t: How to Calculate Heat Load & Recovery Time
s: Heat duty and batch recovery time for solvent recovery, explained with formula and worked example.
x: How to Calculate Heat Load & Recovery Time Chemical Engineering · Process Engineering Once a solvent's boiling point at your working vacuum is known, the next question is a plant one: how much heat does it take to boil it off at a useful rate, and how long will the batch actually take? This is what separates a recovery step that finishes in two hours from one that drags on all shift. The Formula Heat duty (kW) = ṁ × λ Recovery time (hr) = M total / ṁ Where ṁ is the vaporization mass rate (kg/hr), λ is the solvent's latent heat of vaporization (kJ/kg) at the recovery temperature, and M total is the total mass of solvent to be recovered from the batch. Worked Example Recovering 500 kg of a solvent with a latent heat of 360 kJ/kg, using a jacket that can sustainably deliver 40 kW of heating duty to the batch at the vacuum boiling point: ṁ = Duty / λ = 40 / 360 × 3,600 ≈ 400 kg/hr Recove

s: How to Calculate Heat Load & Recovery Time
x: Heat duty (kW) = ṁ × λ Recovery time (hr) = M total / ṁ Where ṁ is the vaporization mass rate (kg/hr), λ is the solvent's latent heat of vaporization (kJ/kg) at the recovery temperature, and M total is the total mass of solvent to be recovered from the batch.

s: How to Calculate Heat Load & Recovery Time
x: Recovering 500 kg of a solvent with a latent heat of 360 kJ/kg, using a jacket that can sustainably deliver 40 kW of heating duty to the batch at the vacuum boiling point: ṁ = Duty / λ = 40 / 360 × 3,600 ≈ 400 kg/hr Recovery time = 500 / 400 ≈ 1.25 hr That's the sustained-boiling estimate. Real recovery time is usually somewhat longer once you account for the initial heat-up to boiling point and the tail end of the batch where the boil-up rate naturally falls off as the last of the solvent is stripped.

s: How to Calculate Heat Load & Recovery Time
x: Available heat duty isn't fixed. It depends on jacket steam pressure (or hot water supply temperature), heat transfer area, and how fouled the jacket surface is. A jacket that delivered 40 kW when clean may only manage 30 kW after a few years of service, stretching recovery time well beyond this calculation.

s: How to Calculate Heat Load & Recovery Time
x: Using latent heat at atmospheric pressure when the batch is actually recovering under vacuum at a lower temperature (latent heat does shift with temperature, though usually modestly); assuming the full nameplate heating duty is available throughout the batch rather than derating for fouling and real steam supply conditions; and not accounting for the slower boil-up rate typical near the end of a batch. t: Mixing Scale-up Rules from Lab to Plant
s: Agitator scale-up rules for a mixing tank from lab to production: constant tip speed, P/V and Reynolds number, with the RPM formula and a worked example.
x: Mixing Scale-up Rules from Lab to Plant Chemical Engineering · Process Engineering Scaling a mixing process from lab to pilot to plant is trickier than it looks because there's no single "correct" way to do it. Constant tip speed, constant power-per-volume (P/V) and constant Reynolds number are different, mutually exclusive scale-up rules. Which one matters depends on your process. Want to run your own numbers? Try the Mixing / Scale-up Calculator . The Core Numbers Re = ρ × N × D² / μ Tip Speed = π × D × N Power = N p × ρ × N³ × D⁵ P/V = Power / Volume Where N is impeller rotational speed (rev/s), D is impeller diameter, ρ and μ are fluid density and viscosity, and N p is the power number (a dimensionless constant depending on impeller type and Reynolds regime). Scale-up Rules at a Glance For geometrically similar vessels (same D/T, same impeller type, same baffling), every common rule

s: Mixing Scale-up Rules from Lab to Plant
x: Re = ρ × N × D² / μ Tip Speed = π × D × N Power = N p × ρ × N³ × D⁵ P/V = Power / Volume Where N is impeller rotational speed (rev/s), D is impeller diameter, ρ and μ are fluid density and viscosity, and N p is the power number (a dimensionless constant depending on impeller type and Reynolds regime).

s: Mixing Scale-up Rules from Lab to Plant
x: For geometrically similar vessels (same D/T, same impeller type, same baffling), every common rule reduces to one formula for the plant agitator speed: N 2 = N 1 × (D 1 / D 2 ) n Scale-up rule n Use it when Constant tip speed 1 Shear matters: crystals, flocs, fragile solids Constant P/V (turbulent) 2/3 Blending, heat transfer, gas–liquid or liquid–liquid dispersion Constant Reynolds number 2 Rarely practical; gives a very low plant RPM

s: Mixing Scale-up Rules from Lab to Plant
x: A lab reactor with a 0.1 m impeller running at 300 rpm (5 rev/s) needs to scale to a plant vessel with a 1.0 m impeller. Scaling on constant tip speed : Tip speed (lab) = π × 0.1 × 5 ≈ 1.57 m/s N (plant) = Tip speed / (π × D) = 1.57 / (π × 1.0) ≈ 0.5 rev/s (30 rpm) Scaling the same jump on constant P/V instead (P/V scales with N³D² in the turbulent regime, so n = 2/3): N (plant) = 300 × (0.1 / 1.0) 2/3 ≈ 300 × 0.215 ≈ 65 rpm And on constant Reynolds number (n = 2): N = 300 × (0.1)² = 3 rpm, which is far too slow to mix a plant vessel. The same lab result gives 3, 30 or 65 rpm depending on the rule, so picking the right one for your chemistry matters more than the arithmetic. At constant P/V the total power also rises with the volume, about 1,000 times here for a tenfold jump in impeller diameter.

s: Mixing Scale-up Rules from Lab to Plant
x: Constant tip speed suits shear-sensitive systems (crystals you don't want to break, some biological materials). Constant P/V suits systems where bulk blend time and heat/mass transfer matter more than shear. Constant Reynolds number is rarely workable at large scale-up ratios since it typically demands an unrealistically low large-vessel RPM.

s: Mixing Scale-up Rules from Lab to Plant
x: Applying one scale-up rule "by default" without checking whether it actually protects the thing that matters for that specific product; comparing power numbers between different impeller types as if they were interchangeable; and forgetting that geometric similarity (same D/T ratio, same baffling) is an assumption behind all of these formulas. If the plant vessel's geometry doesn't match the lab vessel's, none of these scale-up rules apply cleanly.

s: Mixing Scale-up Rules from Lab to Plant
x: What are the main mixing scale-up rules? For geometrically similar vessels, N 2 = N 1 × (D 1 /D 2 ) n , with n = 1 for constant tip speed, n = 2/3 for constant P/V (turbulent) and n = 2 for constant Reynolds number. Which scale-up rule should I use? Constant tip speed when shear damages the product, constant P/V when blending, heat transfer or mass transfer control the result. If you are unsure, calculate both and check what each one does to the property you care about. t: Solvent Recovery Calculation: Boiling Point, Heat Load & Time
s: Find a solvent's boiling point under vacuum with the Antoine equation, then the heat duty and recovery time for a batch. Step-by-step toluene example plus a free calculator.
x: Solvent Recovery Calculation: Boiling Point Under Vacuum, Heat Load and Time Chemical Engineering · Process Engineering Batch solvent recovery under vacuum comes down to one question repeated at every step: at what temperature does this solvent boil at this pressure, and how much heat does it take to get there and keep it boiling? Everything else (condenser sizing, vacuum pump capacity, recovery time) follows from that. Need a number now? The free Solvent Recovery Calculator finds the boiling point under vacuum for thousands of solvents, plus heat load, condenser size and vacuum pump capacity. Boiling Point at Vacuum: the Antoine Equation log₁₀(P) = A − B / (T + C) ⇒ T b = B / (A − log₁₀P) − C Where P is pressure in mmHg, T is temperature in °C, and A, B, C are compound-specific Antoine coefficients fitted from experimental vapor-pressure data. At standard atmospheric pressure (760 mmHg)

t: Boiling Point at Vacuum: the Antoine Equation
s: Solvent Recovery: Boiling Point Under Vacuum
x: log₁₀(P) = A − B / (T + C) ⇒ T b = B / (A − log₁₀P) − C Where P is pressure in mmHg, T is temperature in °C, and A, B, C are compound-specific Antoine coefficients fitted from experimental vapor-pressure data. At standard atmospheric pressure (760 mmHg), this reduces to the solvent's normal boiling point, which is a handy sanity check on any Antoine coefficient set before trusting it at vacuum.

s: Solvent Recovery: Boiling Point Under Vacuum
x: Toluene's Antoine coefficients (in this form) are A = 6.95087, B = 1342.31, C = 219.187. At 100 mmHg vacuum: T b = 1342.31 / (6.95087 − log₁₀100) − 219.187 = 1342.31 / (6.95087 − 2.0) − 219.187 ≈ 271.2 − 219.187 ≈ 52.0°C Compare that to toluene's normal boiling point of 110.6°C at 760 mmHg (the same equation with P = 760). Pulling vacuum drops the boiling point by nearly 60°C. That is the whole reason batch recovery runs under vacuum: it lets you strip solvent at a temperature the batch (and the jacket steam pressure available) can actually sustain.

s: Solvent Recovery: Boiling Point Under Vacuum
x: Once you know the boiling temperature, the heat duty to sustain boiling is governed by the solvent's latent heat of vaporization and the target vapor rate: Duty (kW) = mass vaporization rate (kg/s) × latent heat (kJ/kg). Recovery time then follows from total solvent mass to be recovered divided by that vaporization rate, adjusted for the available heating duty from the jacket or coil.

t: Worked Example: Heat Load and Recovery Time
s: Solvent Recovery: Boiling Point Under Vacuum
x: Continuing with toluene: say 2,000 kg has to be stripped at a steady 500 kg/hr. Toluene's latent heat is about 360 kJ/kg near its normal boiling point (use the value at your actual recovery temperature for design). Vapor rate = 500 / 3,600 ≈ 0.139 kg/s Heat duty = 0.139 × 360 ≈ 50 kW Recovery time = 2,000 / 500 = 4 hours This is the boiling duty alone. Add the sensible heat to bring the batch up to 52°C and an allowance for heat losses. If the jacket can only supply, say, 35 kW, the vapor rate drops in proportion and the recovery takes longer than 4 hours. The condenser has to remove the same ~50 kW, which is the starting point for sizing it.

s: Solvent Recovery: Boiling Point Under Vacuum
x: Antoine coefficients are only valid over the temperature/pressure range they were fitted to. Extrapolating far outside that range (very deep vacuum, or temperatures near a solvent's critical point) can give a boiling point that looks plausible but is wrong. Always check the returned value against a known reference point (like the normal boiling point) before using it to size equipment.

s: Solvent Recovery: Boiling Point Under Vacuum
x: Mixing up mmHg and mbar (a factor of ~1.33 apart) when entering the vacuum level; using latent heat measured at atmospheric pressure without adjusting for the actual recovery temperature; and forgetting that mixed-solvent systems don't follow a single Antoine curve at all. A binary or multi-component mix needs a real VLE calculation, not this single-compound shortcut.

s: Solvent Recovery: Boiling Point Under Vacuum
x: How do you calculate the boiling point of a solvent under vacuum? Rearrange the Antoine equation: T b = B / (A − log₁₀P) − C, with P in mmHg and the A, B, C coefficients for that solvent. For toluene at 100 mmHg this gives about 52°C. How do you calculate heat load for solvent recovery? Heat duty (kW) = vaporisation rate (kg/s) × latent heat (kJ/kg). In the example above, 500 kg/hr of toluene needs roughly 50 kW before sensible heat and losses. Is mmHg the same as mbar? No. 1 mmHg ≈ 1.333 mbar. Check which unit your Antoine coefficients were fitted in before entering the vacuum level. s: Basket centrifuge cake weight and G-force from basket geometry and cake thickness, with formula and worked example.
x: Centrifuge Cake Weight & G-Force Calculation Chemical Engineering · Equipment Two numbers matter most when planning a basket centrifuge batch: how hard the cake is actually being spun (G-force), and how much cake that translates to once the basket is loaded to a given thickness. The Formula G-force = 1.118 × 10 −5 × r × N² Cake weight = Cake volume × bulk density Where r is basket radius (cm) and N is rotational speed (rpm). Cake volume comes from the annular geometry defined by basket radius and cake thickness. In effect it is the basket's cylindrical volume minus the empty core left in the middle. Worked Example A basket with 40 cm radius spinning at 1,200 rpm: G-force = 1.118 × 10 −5 × 40 × 1,200² = 1.118 × 10 −5 × 40 × 1,440,000 ≈ 644 G If that basket carries a 10 cm-thick cake at a bulk density of 1,400 kg/m³, the cake volume comes from the annulus between the full basket radius (40

G-force = 1.118 × 10 −5 × r × N² Cake weight = Cake volume × bulk density Where r is basket radius (cm) and N is rotational speed (rpm). Cake volume comes from the annular geometry defined by basket radius and cake thickness. In effect it is the basket's cylindrical volume minus the empty core left in the middle.

A basket with 40 cm radius spinning at 1,200 rpm: G-force = 1.118 × 10 −5 × 40 × 1,200² = 1.118 × 10 −5 × 40 × 1,440,000 ≈ 644 G If that basket carries a 10 cm-thick cake at a bulk density of 1,400 kg/m³, the cake volume comes from the annulus between the full basket radius (40 cm) and the inner radius left after the cake (40 − 10 = 30 cm) times the basket height. Multiply that volume by the bulk density to get total cake mass for the batch.

Bulk density of a centrifuged cake is not a fixed material property. It depends heavily on particle shape, size distribution, and how well the cake has been de-liquored during the spin. A bulk density measured from a different product, or even a different batch of the same product with different crystal habit, can give a meaningfully wrong cake weight.

Using the full basket radius instead of the cake's actual radial position when computing G-force at the cake surface versus at the basket wall (G-force varies with radius, so the value at the cake's inner surface is lower than at the basket wall); and assuming a bulk density from a handbook table rather than from an actual discharged cake of the real product. t: Pump Power Calculation: Formula, kW from Flow & Head, Examples
s: Pump power calculation step by step: hydraulic power, shaft power and motor kW from flow and head. Two worked examples, the Q×H/367 shortcut and a free pump power calculator.
x: Pump Power Calculation: Formula and Worked Examples Chemical Engineering · Engineering Calculations Sizing a pump motor comes down to three numbers stacked on top of each other: the power the fluid itself needs (hydraulic power), the power the pump has to draw at the shaft to deliver that (shaft power), and the power the motor has to supply to turn that shaft (motor power). Each step loses a bit to inefficiency, which is why a pump moving water at a modest flow and head can still need a noticeably larger motor than the "theoretical" number suggests. Short on time? Use the free Pump Power Calculator . Enter flow, head, density and efficiencies and it returns hydraulic, shaft and motor power. The Formula Hydraulic power (kW) = ρ × g × Q × H / 1,000 Shaft power (kW) = Hydraulic power / η pump Motor power (kW) = Shaft power / η motor Where ρ is fluid density (kg/m³), g is 9.81 m/s², Q is flo

Hydraulic power (kW) = ρ × g × Q × H / 1,000 Shaft power (kW) = Hydraulic power / η pump Motor power (kW) = Shaft power / η motor Where ρ is fluid density (kg/m³), g is 9.81 m/s², Q is flow rate (m³/s), H is total developed head (m), and η pump / η motor are the pump and motor efficiencies as fractions (e.g. 0.65 for 65%).

t: Quick Formula: Pump Power from m³/h
x: On the plant floor, flow is usually read in m³/h, not m³/s. Folding the constants together gives a shortcut that is easy to remember: Hydraulic power (kW) = Q (m³/h) × H (m) × SG / 367 SG is the specific gravity of the liquid (1.0 for water). The 367 comes from 3,600 × 1,000 / (1,000 × 9.81). To get kW in horsepower, divide by 0.7457 (1 hp = 0.7457 kW).

Total head H isn't just the static lift. It's static lift plus friction losses in the piping plus any pressure the destination vessel is already holding, all converted to an equivalent height of fluid. Getting H wrong (usually by forgetting friction losses) is the single most common source of an undersized pump.

Take water (ρ = 1,000 kg/m³) at a flow of 50 m³/hr (0.0139 m³/s) against a total head of 30 m, with a pump efficiency of 65% and motor efficiency of 92%: Hydraulic power = 1,000 × 9.81 × 0.0139 × 30 / 1,000 ≈ 4.09 kW Shaft power = 4.09 / 0.65 ≈ 6.29 kW Motor power = 6.29 / 0.92 ≈ 6.84 kW In practice you'd round up to the next standard motor frame size above 6.84 kW (commonly a 7.5 kW motor) rather than specifying the exact calculated value, to leave margin for wear and off-curve operation. The quick formula gives the same hydraulic power: 50 × 30 × 1.0 / 367 ≈ 4.09 kW.

t: Worked Example 2: Solvent into a Pressurised Vessel
x: Now a case closer to a pharma plant: a solvent with density 870 kg/m³ (SG 0.87) is transferred at 20 m³/hr into a receiver held at 2 bar(g). The static lift is 12 m and the line friction loss is 5 m. Pump efficiency is 60% and motor efficiency 90%. First, convert the receiver pressure to head of this liquid: Pressure head = ΔP / (ρ × g) = 200,000 / (870 × 9.81) ≈ 23.4 m Total head H = 12 + 5 + 23.4 ≈ 40.4 m Then the power: Hydraulic power = 20 × 40.4 × 0.87 / 367 ≈ 1.92 kW Shaft power = 1.92 / 0.60 ≈ 3.20 kW Motor power = 3.20 / 0.90 ≈ 3.55 kW → select a 4 kW motor Notice that the receiver pressure is more than half of the total head here. Leave it out and the motor would be undersized by more than half.

Pump efficiency isn't constant. It peaks at the best-efficiency point (BEP) on the pump curve and drops off the further you run from it. A pump selected purely on this formula using catalog efficiency, but actually operated well off its BEP, will draw more real power than this calculation predicts.

Using static head alone and skipping friction losses; using density from a different fluid than the one actually being pumped; and applying a single "safety factor" on top of an already-conservative efficiency estimate, which can lead to an oversized motor running inefficiently at partial load.

What is the formula for pump power? Hydraulic power (kW) = ρ × g × Q × H / 1,000, with ρ in kg/m³, Q in m³/s and H in m. Divide by pump efficiency for shaft power and by motor efficiency for motor input power. What is the quick formula for pump power in kW from m³/h? Hydraulic power (kW) = Q (m³/h) × H (m) × SG / 367. For 50 m³/h of water at 30 m head this is about 4.1 kW. What is the difference between hydraulic power and shaft power? Hydraulic power is the energy actually given to the fluid. Shaft power (also called brake power) is what the pump draws at its shaft. It is always higher because of losses inside the pump: shaft power = hydraulic power / pump efficiency. How do I convert pressure to head? Head (m) = ΔP (Pa) / (ρ × 9.81). For water, 1 bar is about 10.2 m of head. For a lighter liquid the same pressure is more metres of head, which is why the density matters. Try the Calcula

s: Specific cake resistance and flux from a bench-scale filtration trial, explained with formula and worked example.
x: How to Calculate Filtration Performance Chemical Engineering · Equipment A quick Büchner or Nutsche trial can tell you a lot about how a slurry will filter at production scale, but only if you turn the raw filtrate-volume-vs-time data into two numbers that actually transfer: specific cake resistance and expected flux. The Cake Filtration Equation dV/dt = ΔP × A / [μ × (α × c × V/A + R m )] Where V is filtrate volume, t is time, ΔP is the pressure/vacuum driving force, A is filter area, μ is filtrate viscosity, α is specific cake resistance, c is the mass of dry cake solids per unit volume of filtrate, and R m is the filter medium resistance. In practice, this is rearranged and the trial data (t/V vs V) is plotted to extract α and R m from the slope and intercept. Worked Example A bench trial at 0.5 bar vacuum through a 20 cm² Büchner filter collects 150 mL of filtrate in 90 seconds, with

dV/dt = ΔP × A / [μ × (α × c × V/A + R m )] Where V is filtrate volume, t is time, ΔP is the pressure/vacuum driving force, A is filter area, μ is filtrate viscosity, α is specific cake resistance, c is the mass of dry cake solids per unit volume of filtrate, and R m is the filter medium resistance. In practice, this is rearranged and the trial data (t/V vs V) is plotted to extract α and R m from the slope and intercept.

A bench trial at 0.5 bar vacuum through a 20 cm² Büchner filter collects 150 mL of filtrate in 90 seconds, with a slurry concentration giving c = 40 kg/m³. Plotting t/V against V from several timed readings gives a straight line whose slope yields α and whose intercept yields R m . The regression needs several data points, not just the endpoint, so a single-point trial isn't enough on its own. Once α is known, expected flux at a given ΔP and cake thickness can be estimated directly from the rearranged equation, and specific cake resistance above roughly 10 11 –10 12 m/kg is generally considered slow-filtering, prompting a look at flocculation, filter aid, or a different filter type.

Specific cake resistance for compressible cakes (many organic precipitates and biological solids) isn't constant. It increases with ΔP. A trial run at bench-scale vacuum doesn't automatically predict performance at a much higher production-scale pressure differential; ideally, run the trial at a ΔP close to what production will actually use.

Using only the total volume and total time (a single point) instead of a proper t/V vs V regression across the run; ignoring filter medium resistance when it's actually a significant fraction of total resistance for a thin cake; and assuming bench-scale flux scales linearly to a production filter of different geometry without accounting for the medium and support structure differences. s: Free corrosion coupon calculator: corrosion rate in mils per year (mpy) from coupon weight loss, density, area and exposure time (ASTM G1), with a worked example.
x: Corrosion Coupon Calculator Weight-loss corrosion rate (mils per year, mpy) from coupon exposure data, with an Excellent / Good / Satisfactory / Unsatisfactory rating. Formula Corrosion rate (mpy) = (534 × W) / (D × A × T) Where W is weight loss (mg), D is metal density (g/cm³), A is exposed area (in²), and T is exposure time (hours). This is the standard ASTM G1 weight-loss formula. To report in mm per year: 1 mpy = 0.0254 mm/y. Worked Example A carbon steel coupon (density 7.86 g/cm³) with 2.0 in² exposed area loses 25 mg over 30 days (720 hours): Corrosion rate = (534 × 25) / (7.86 × 2.0 × 720) ≈ 1.18 mpy ≈ 0.030 mm/y Engineering Notes & Assumptions This assumes uniform general corrosion. It won't capture localized attack like pitting or crevice corrosion, which can be far more damaging than the average weight-loss rate suggests. Always inspect the coupon visually for pitting alongsid

This assumes uniform general corrosion. It won't capture localized attack like pitting or crevice corrosion, which can be far more damaging than the average weight-loss rate suggests. Always inspect the coupon visually for pitting alongside the calculated rate.

How is corrosion rate calculated from a coupon? Weigh the cleaned coupon before and after exposure, then use corrosion rate (mpy) = 534 × W / (D × A × T), with W in mg, D in g/cm³, A in in² and T in hours. How do I convert mpy to mm/y? x: Flow patterns Radial impellers throw liquid out to the wall in two loops. Axial impellers pump along the shaft in one loop. Close-clearance agitators move liquid around the vessel near the wall. Baffles In thin liquids, four wall baffles of about one tenth to one twelfth of the tank diameter stop swirl and vortexing. Close-clearance agitators in viscous, laminar batches usually run without baffles. Glass-lined vessels use one or two finger or beavertail baffles. Power Turbulent, baffled: P = Np × ρ × N³ × D⁵. The question is always the same: the cooling fails at the worst possible moment. What happens? Answering it in a structured way gives you the four temperatures of the Stoessel diagram. 1 The reaction runs at the process temperature T p . 2 Cooling fails. Dosing stops (it must be interlocked). The unreacted reagent still in the reactor reacts adiabatically and the temperature climbs to the MTSR . 3 If the MTSR is high enough, a decomposition or secondary reaction starts. How long that takes is the TMR ad at the MTSR. 4 On the way, the batch may reach its boiling point or relief pressure, the MTT , which can act as a barrier (lesson 5).

t: 1 · How much energy? Heat of reaction and ΔT ad
x: Q′ rx = c · (−ΔH r ) / ρ [kJ/kg] (c in mol/m³, ρ in kg/m³) ΔT ad = Q′ rx / c′ p [K] c′ p,mix = Σ m i ·c′ p,i / Σ m i From reaction calorimetry: Q rx = ∫ q rx dt (the area under the heat-flow curve). For a roughly constant heat flow during dosing, Q rx ≈ q rx × t dosing .

t: 2 · Can the plant cool it? Cooling capacity
x: q ex = U · A · (T r − T c ) U is the overall heat-transfer coefficient (typically 100–400 W/m²·K for jacketed vessels with organic batches), A the wetted jacket area (it grows as you dose), T c the coolant temperature. Keep the cooling capacity at least 20 % above the maximum heat release rate. In a semi-batch reaction that keeps pace with the dosing, the heat release rate is roughly the total heat divided by the dosing time. That gives the shortest dosing time the cooling can handle : t dosing,min = Q rx,total / (q ex / 1.2) 🧮 Shortest dosing time for the available cooling From the total reaction heat and the reactor’s cooling capacity. t: 3 · How hot can it get? Accumulation and MTSR
x: In a batch (all reagents charged, then heated) everything is unreacted at the start: X acc = 100 %. In a semi-batch the dosed reagent may react instantly or may pile up. The fraction that has been added but not yet reacted is the accumulation . It is measured in the reaction calorimeter by comparing the heat released with the amount dosed. MTSR = T p + X acc,max · ΔT ad Colder is not automatically safer. Lowering T p slows the reaction, so more reagent accumulates. Many runaways happened in reactions run “cold for safety”, sometimes with a stopped agitator or a forgotten catalyst, where the reagent sat unreacted and then reacted all at once.

t: 4 · How much time is left? TMR ad and TD24
x: For a decomposition with an initial heat release rate q′ 0 (W/kg) at temperature T 0 , the adiabatic time to maximum rate is approximately: TMR ad = c′ p · R · T 0 ² / (q′ 0 · E a ) q′(T) = q′ 0 · exp[ (E a /R)·(1/T 0 − 1/T) ] Zero-order, adiabatic approximation (T in kelvin). TD24 is the temperature at which TMR ad = 24 h: below it, a decomposition develops slowly enough to restore control. As a rough rule the heat release rate doubles every 10 K (van ’t Hoff), so TMR ad roughly halves. 🧮 TMR ad and TD24 from one measurement Enter a heat release rate measured at one temperature (isothermal DSC or ARC) and the activation energy. Cooling-failure scenario: T p → MTSR (accumulated reagent reacts) → decomposition after TMR ad . ΔT ad = Q′ / c′ p ; MTSR = T p + X acc ·ΔT ad . Cooling capacity q ex = UA(T r − T c ), with a ≥ 20 % margin, sets the shortest dosing time. Lower T p can mean more accumulation and a higher MTSR. TD24 (TMR ad = 24 h) is the stability limit to compare the MTSR with.

t: Why a safe lab reaction can be unsafe in the plant
x: A 1 L flask and a 5 m³ reactor run the same chemistry under very different heat-transfer conditions. Volume, and so heat production, grows with the cube of the size; jacket area, and so heat removal, grows only with the square . The area per unit volume falls roughly as 1/D: a 5,000 L reactor has around a tenth of the cooling area per litre of a lab flask. Lab flask (1 L) Plant reactor (5 m³) Area / volume ~50–100 m²/m³ ~2–4 m²/m³ Heat loss when cooling fails High: the flask cools itself in air Almost none: practically adiabatic Mixing time Seconds Tens of seconds to minutes Time to heat / cool Minutes Hours So a reaction that “just got warm” in the lab can run away at scale, and a 10-minute lab addition may need 4 hours in the plant (lesson 4).

t: Things that change reactivity during scale-up
x: Batch vs semi-batch. In an all-in batch there is no control of the rate: all the energy may be released at once. Proving that an addition is dose-controlled (sample just after the end of the addition: little unreacted reagent left) removes most of the risk. Concentration. Reactions in 7–10 volumes of solvent are rarely hazardous; below about 5 volumes, ΔT ad rises and more testing is needed. Large excesses of reagent. Often a sign the chemistry is not understood; the excess may cause side reactions or decompositions and needs a planned quench. Longer times at temperature. Distillations, hold times and filtrations are much longer in the plant. A slow decomposition that was invisible in the lab can matter. Solids and mixing. Poor suspension or a stopped agitator lets a reagent layer accumulate unreacted, then react suddenly when mixing restarts. Materials of construction and contaminants.

t: Changes that need new safety data
x: If the initial assessment was lean, many changes are fine without re-testing. These are not, and should go back to the process safety lab: Anything that increases heat or gas generation, or their rates: new reagents, molar ratios, higher concentration, faster addition, a significantly different reaction or work-up temperature. Changing a dose-controlled step into an all-in process. A change in the composition of a distillation residue . Charging a reactive reagent as a concentrated solution instead of a solid (compatibility: e.g. NBS in NMP or DMF, nitric acid with organic solvents). Management of change (MOC). Every change to chemistry, equipment, procedure or staffing that can affect a hazard must be reviewed before it is made, by people with the right expertise. Flixborough is the textbook case of what happens without it. ✍️ Check yourself: Scaling from a 1 L flask to a 5 m³ reactor,

Heat production scales with volume, cooling with area: plants are nearly adiabatic. Dose-controlled operation, enough dilution and modest excesses reduce scale-up risk. Changes that raise heat or gas generation, all-in charging, new residues or concentrated reagent solutions need new data and MOC.

x: An ARC test of the final reaction mass shows a self-heating rate corresponding to 0.5 W/kg at 150 °C . From a series of isothermal tests, E a = 100 kJ/mol. c′ p = 1.9 kJ/kg·K. The process gives MTSR = 120 °C, and the solvent boils at 140 °C. What is TMR ad at 150 °C? Estimate T D24 and T D8 . What is TMR ad at the MTSR, and the Stoessel class? Show the solution 1. TMR ad = c′ p ·R·T²/(q′·E a ) = 1900 × 8.314 × 423.15² / (0.5 × 100,000) ≈ 56,600 s ≈ 15.7 h . 2. Extrapolating q′ with Arrhenius and solving TMR ad = 24 h and 8 h gives T D24 ≈ 143 °C and T D8 ≈ 161 °C . 3. At 120 °C, TMR ad ≈ 119 h : low probability. Order: MTSR 120 < MTT 140 < T D24 143: 1 Class 1, but with only 3 K between boiling point and T D24 . A development team cannot run every safety test on every step. A high-hazard screen sorts the steps that need a full thermal and process-safety assessment from the ones that need only a basic check. It should happen early, when the route is chosen, because that is when changing the chemistry is still cheap. The checklist below groups the warning signs used by many pharma and fine-chemical companies into four categories. One “high” flag is enough to treat the step as a high-hazard process .

t: How to read the energy numbers
x: Indicator Low Medium High Adiabatic temperature rise ΔT ad < 50 K, no pressure build-up 50–200 K > 200 K Decomposition energy (DSC) < 100 J/g 100–300 J/g 300–500 J/g high; > 500 J/g severe: check explosive properties TMR ad at the worst temperature > 24 h 8–24 h < 8 h The first two measure severity (how bad), the third probability (how likely, how fast). Risk needs both. The Stoessel diagram in lesson 5 puts them together. Don’t forget the “boring” streams. Distillation residues, mother liquors, waste streams and hold tanks are where unstable by-products concentrate. Many incidents happened not in the reaction but while stripping a solvent to dryness. 🧾 Interactive screening checklist Tick everything that applies to your process. Tick everything that applies to your process. Nothing is stored or sent anywhere. Educational screening tool Results are illustrative and depend on the stated assumptions. They are not a substitute for a qualified process-safety assessment, the applicable design code, vendor data, laboratory testing or engineering review. Reactivity Pyrophoric or water-reactive reagents (NaH, LiAlH 4 , n-BuLi, borane complexes, K-tert-butoxide…) ● Molecules with energetic / unstable functional groups (lesson 1), or a positive heat of formation ● Peroxide-forming solvents or reagents, especially if the inhibitor is removed (distillation, base wash) Incompatible materials that may meet (oxidiser + organics, acid + cyanide, water + reactive reagent) High reaction energy: ΔT ad > 200 K (high); 50–200 K counts as medium ● Decomposition can be reached from the MTSR (Stoessel class 3, 4 or 5) ● Fire & explosion

Screen every step early; one high flag means a full assessment. Severity: ΔT ad (50 / 200 K) and decomposition energy (100 / 300 / 500 J/g). Probability: TMR ad (8 / 24 h). Residues, distillations to dryness and all-in heated batches are classic traps.

Class Order What happens after a cooling failure Typical measures 1 T p < MTSR < MTT < T D24 Under the screening assumptions: no boiling and no decomposition expected. The mass would sit at MTSR. Normal process control. Lower thermal-escalation concern (screening result; verify for your process). 2 T p < MTSR < T D24 < MTT Low concern at MTSR, but if the mass is held hot for long it could slowly heat up to the decomposition, and boiling would not stop it. Avoid long hold times at high temperature; alarm on temperature. 3 T p < MTT < MTSR < T D24 The batch boils. Evaporative cooling stops the temperature at MTT, if the condenser / vent can take the vapour at that rate. Check reflux condenser and vapour line capacity; reliable condenser cooling; emergency cooling as an option. 4 T p < MTT < T D24 < MTSR Boiling stops the temperature before T D24 , but only if it works. Four levels: T p , MTSR, MTT, T D24 . Their order gives the class. Class 1–2: lower concern (screening). Class 3–4: the boiling barrier must be reliable and sized. Class 5: redesign or emergency measures. The usual lever is accumulation: feed-controlled dosing, dilution, solvent choice.

The usual flow: DSC screening of all materials and mixtures → if an exotherm is close to process conditions, ARC / TSU for the decomposition → reaction calorimetry for the main reaction → combine the results into the cooling-failure scenario (lesson 4) and the Stoessel class (lesson 5). s: The testing toolkit: DSC, TSU, ARC, RC1
x: Endotherms (down, or up, depending on the plot convention) are melting, evaporation, solvent loss. Look for the arrow marked exo . An exotherm at moderate temperature in a mixture of the reagents is usually the desired reaction . Its area gives Q′ rx . An exotherm at higher temperature is a decomposition. Its area gives Q′ dc and its severity: ΔT ad,dc = Q′ dc / c′ p . A sharp, symmetrical peak after a flat baseline in an isothermal test is the fingerprint of an autocatalytic decomposition. Do not extrapolate it like a normal reaction. Compare thermograms of the right mixtures : final reaction mass, mixture of reagents (worst case of accumulation), and “what if one component is forgotten?” The “100 K rule” is not a safety margin. s: The testing toolkit: DSC, TSU, ARC, RC1
x: DSC screens everything; TSU adds pressure; ARC gives adiabatic kinetics and TMR ad ; reaction calorimetry measures the desired reaction and accumulation. Severity from energy: ΔT ad = Q′ / c′ p . DSC onset temperatures are not safe limits. Use TMR ad / TD24. Watch for autocatalytic signatures and test the mixtures that matter, including mistakes.

t: Static electricity: the usual ignition source
x: Powders become charged whenever they flow, slide, are pneumatically conveyed or poured from a bag. Insulating plastics (liners, FIBCs, funnels) and isolated metal parts store that charge until it discharges as a spark. A typical spark from a person is 10–30 mJ; many fine organic powders and almost all flammable vapours ignite below that. Hybrid mixtures are the trap. Pouring a powder into a reactor that contains flammable solvent vapour creates a hybrid mixture that ignites far more easily than either alone. Charge solids before the solvent, or through an inerted closed system, never by hand into a hot solvent. 🧮 What does this MIE mean for my plant? When a runaway boils the batch, the vapour bubbles swell the liquid and the vent discharges a foaming two-phase mixture , not clean vapour. Two-phase flow carries far less energy per unit area, so a vent sized with the vapour formula can be several times too small . Runaway relief is sized with the DIERS methods (e.g. Leung’s method) from adiabatic test data: the self-heating rate (dT/dt) at the set pressure, and whether the system is “tempered” (vapour), “gassy” or hybrid. That is specialist work, done from ARC / VSP2-type data. T2 Laboratories (2007): the reactor’s rupture disc was far too small for a runaway. The reactor burst and the explosion killed four people. See the case study . ✍️ Check yourself: Why is a vent sized with the vapour formula often too small for a runaway reaction? Level swell turns the discharge into a two-phase flow. Two-phase venting needs much larger areas. Us

Start from the scenario: blocked outlet, fire, utility failure, thermal expansion, runaway, gas evolution. Vapour: A ∝ W·√(TZ/M)/(C·K d ·P 1 ). Fire: Q = 43,200 or 70,900·F·A w 0.82 W. Liquid: A ∝ Q·√(G/ΔP). Runaway relief is two-phase: use DIERS methods and adiabatic test data. Never the vapour formula alone. Discharge to a safe place: catch tank, scrubber, flare.

x: Process Safety · Lesson 9 of 9 · 12 min read Toxic and flammable releases Source terms, dispersion, AEGL and LFL zones, pool fires, and emergency response. Educational overview. The principles here are general and simplified, and the figures and rules of thumb are typical values, not limits for your plant. Decisions need process-specific data, the applicable codes and standards, and a qualified assessment. From leak to consequence Consequence analysis follows the material: source term (how much escapes, how fast) → pool and evaporation (for liquids) → dispersion in the wind → effect on people (toxic dose, flash fire, heat radiation, overpressure). Liquid through a hole: Q = C d · A · √(2·ρ·ΔP) (C d ≈ 0.61) ΔP = pad / pump pressure + ρ·g·h (liquid head) Gases and liquefied gases (Cl₂, NH₃) escape much faster and partly flash; a 6 mm hole in a chlorine tonner can empty it in well under an

Consequence analysis follows the material: source term (how much escapes, how fast) → pool and evaporation (for liquids) → dispersion in the wind → effect on people (toxic dose, flash fire, heat radiation, overpressure). Liquid through a hole: Q = C d · A · √(2·ρ·ΔP) (C d ≈ 0.61) ΔP = pad / pump pressure + ρ·g·h (liquid head) Gases and liquefied gases (Cl₂, NH₃) escape much faster and partly flash; a 6 mm hole in a chlorine tonner can empty it in well under an hour.

Level Meaning (60-minute exposure) AEGL-1 Notable discomfort, irritation; reversible AEGL-2 Irreversible or serious long-lasting effects, or impaired ability to escape AEGL-3 Life-threatening effects or death Example 60-min values: chlorine 0.5 / 2 / 20 ppm; ammonia 30 / 160 / 1,100 ppm. Chlorine’s are tiny, which is why a small chlorine leak needs a far larger emergency zone than a large solvent leak.

LFL / UFL : a vapour–air mixture burns only between the lower and upper flammable limits (methanol 6–36 %, toluene 1.1–7.1 %). Zones are usually drawn to ½ LFL to allow for pockets of richer mixture. Flash fire : a cloud ignites and burns back to the source. Deadly inside the cloud, little effect outside. Vapour cloud explosion : the same cloud in a congested area (pipe racks, buildings) can accelerate into a damaging blast (Flixborough, Buncefield). Pool fire : harm is by heat radiation: 37.5 kW/m² damages equipment and is fatal; 12.5 kW/m² ignites wood and is lethal within minutes; 4 kW/m² causes pain within about 20 s.

The same leak is far more dangerous on a calm, clear night (Pasquill stability class F, low wind) than on a windy afternoon (class D): the cloud stays concentrated and travels further. Dense gases (chlorine) hug the ground and flow into drains and basements.

Detect fast: gas detectors, CCTV, manual call points, siren. Evacuate crosswind, then upwind , to the assembly point the control room names for the current wind. Head count at the assembly point. Isolate from a safe place: remote shut-off valves, king valves, emergency kits (e.g. chlorine kit B). Water curtains knock down soluble clouds (NH 3 , HCl, Cl 2 ); foam blankets cut evaporation from solvent pools. Never spray water onto a leaking chlorine container: it forms acid and enlarges the hole. See all of this in 3D: open the virtual plant tour , choose What-If Leak , pick a scenario and press Play the emergency response . ✍️ Check yourself: A chlorine leak and a methanol leak give the same concentration (in ppm) 200 m downwind. Which is more dangerous to people there? Chlorine AEGL-3 (60 min) is 20 ppm; methanol AEGL-3 is 7,200 ppm. The same concentration means very different harm. ✍️ C

Source term → pool / evaporation → dispersion → effect. AEGL-1/2/3 for toxic effects; LFL / ½ LFL for flammable clouds; 37.5 / 12.5 / 4 kW/m² for fires. Stable night-time weather gives the largest zones; dense gases hug the ground. Respond: detect, alarm, evacuate crosswind → upwind, isolate remotely, knock down.

t: Process safety is not personal safety
x: Personal (occupational) safety is about slips, falls, cuts and PPE: frequent, usually small events that affect one person. Process safety is about keeping hazardous materials and energy inside the equipment: rare events, but when they happen they can kill many people at once, destroy a plant and reach the neighbourhood. A plant can have an excellent lost-time injury record and still be one valve away from disaster. That was true at Bhopal, Flixborough and Buncefield. In pharma and fine-chemical plants the largest source of energy is usually not a pressurised gas or a flammable inventory. It is the chemistry itself : an exothermic reaction, or a molecule that can decompose.

t: The runaway problem in one picture
x: An exothermic reaction stays under control only while heat is removed as fast as it is produced. Heat production rises exponentially with temperature (Arrhenius), while heat removal through the jacket rises only linearly (UA × ΔT). Above a certain temperature, production wins: the batch heats itself, which speeds the reaction, which heats it faster. That positive feedback is a thermal runaway . If the batch reaches a temperature where a decomposition starts, the energy and gas released can be many times larger than the main reaction. Heat production: q rx = k 0 ·e −Ea/RT · V · c · (−ΔH r ) (exponential in T) Heat removal: q ex = U · A · (T − T c ) (linear in T)

t: Terms you will meet in every lesson
x: Term Meaning Exothermic reaction Releases heat: the reaction enthalpy ΔH r is negative. Adiabatic No heat exchange with the surroundings. A large, well-insulated reactor with failed cooling is close to adiabatic, so it is the worst case. Adiabatic temperature rise, ΔT ad How much the temperature would rise if all the remaining reaction heat stayed in the mass: ΔT ad = Q′ / c′ p . Activation energy, E a Sets how strongly the rate rises with temperature. A higher E a means a steeper rise once things get hot. Runaway A thermally unstable system in which temperature and rate keep accelerating, possibly to an explosion. Induction time / TMR ad The time, under adiabatic conditions, from a given temperature until the reaction or decomposition reaches its maximum rate. It is the time you have to act. Autocatalytic reaction A reaction sped up by its own products or intermediates. It can sit quiet

Some groups of atoms store a lot of energy or release gas when they break down. If one of them is in a starting material, intermediate, product or residue, treat the process as potentially hazardous until thermal testing says otherwise. Family Examples of energetic groups Nitrogen-rich Azides (–N 3 ), diazo and diazonium compounds, azo (–N=N–), triazenes, tetrazoles and triazoles, hydrazines, N-halo compounds Oxygen-rich Peroxides and hydroperoxides (–O–O–), peracids, ozonides, epoxides (strained ring) Nitrogen + oxygen Nitro (–NO 2 ), nitrate esters (–ONO 2 ), nitrites, nitroso, N-oxides, oximes, hydroxylamine and its salts Halogen + oxygen Chlorates, perchlorates, hypochlorites, perchloryl compounds Unsaturated carbon Acetylenes and metal acetylides, allenes, conjugated dienes (polymerisation) Metal compounds Organometallics and metal hydrides (pyrophoric), heavy-metal salts of energet

Process safety is about keeping energy and hazardous material inside the equipment. It is measured differently from personal safety. Runaway = exponential heat production beating linear heat removal. ΔT ad , E a and TMR ad describe how big, how steep and how fast a runaway is. Energetic functional groups (azides, nitro, peroxides, diazo, N–O, acetylenes…) mean: test before you scale up.

s: Flixborough, 1974: the temporary bypass: process safety case study
x: The plant oxidised cyclohexane in a train of six reactors at about 155 °C and 8.8 bar. In March 1974 a crack was found in reactor 5, so it was removed and a 20-inch bypass pipe was installed between reactors 4 and 6 to keep production going. Because the reactor nozzles were at different heights, the bypass had a “dog-leg” shape and was supported on scaffolding, with bellows at each end. No design calculation was made, no drawing beyond a chalk sketch on the workshop floor, no pressure test of the assembly, and the bellows manufacturer’s guidance was not followed. On 1 June the bypass failed. About 30–40 tonnes of hot cyclohexane flashed into a vapour cloud, which ignited and exploded.

s: Flixborough, 1974: the temporary bypass: process safety case study
x: Mar 1974 Crack found in reactor 5. Decision to bypass it and restart quickly. Days later Bypass designed and built by site staff; no qualified mechanical engineer in post. Apr–May Plant runs with the bypass. 1 Jun, 16:53 Bypass ruptures during a pressure rise. Vapour cloud forms and explodes within about a minute. The control room is destroyed.

s: Flixborough, 1974: the temporary bypass: process safety case study
x: No management of change : a major modification treated as a quick repair; no hazard review. No engineering design : forces on the dog-leg and bellows not calculated; no reference to the design code; no pressure test. Missing expertise : the works engineer post was vacant and nobody with the right competence was involved. Production pressure : restarting fast took priority over understanding the original crack. Large inventory under pressure and an occupied control room close to the plant. s: T2 Laboratories, 2007: a runaway nobody expected: process safety case study
x: T2 made methylcyclopentadienyl manganese tricarbonyl (MCMT) in a 2,450-gallon batch reactor. The first step, metalation with sodium in diglyme, is exothermic, and above about 390 °F (199 °C) an undesired, much more energetic reaction starts. The company relied on cooling water in the jacket to control the temperature, with no backup. On the 175th batch, the cooling failed, probably because of a blockage in the water supply or a valve failure. The temperature rose into the range of the side reaction. The 4-inch rupture disc opened but was far too small for a runaway. About ten minutes after the operator reported a cooling problem, the reactor burst. Debris was thrown up to a mile and buildings were damaged within a quarter mile.

s: T2 Laboratories, 2007: a runaway nobody expected: process safety case study
x: Hazard not recognised : the owners were chemists and chemical engineers, but did not recognise the runaway potential of the side reaction, nor that scale-up removed the safety margin seen in small batches. Single safeguard : the whole protection was the cooling water. No redundant cooling, no automatic shutdown, no quench. Relief not sized for the runaway : the rupture disc was sized for normal operation, not two-phase runaway relief. No reactive-hazard testing or formal hazard analysis of the process. x: Process Safety · Case study Bhopal, 1984: methyl isocyanate release Water entered a storage tank of methyl isocyanate (MIC). x: The plant made the pesticide carbaryl using MIC, a volatile, highly toxic and water-reactive intermediate stored in large underground tanks. Late on 2 December 1984, water got into tank E610. MIC reacts exothermically with water; the temperature and pressure rose, the relief valve lifted, and MIC vapour poured out of the vent stack for about two hours. The way the water got in has been disputed (a pipe-washing operation without a blind, or deliberate introduction), but the scale of the disaster came from what failed to stop it.

By morning The cloud has covered large parts of the city; thousands are dead or dying.

s: Buncefield, 2005: filling blind: process safety case study
x: Both layers of overfill protection failed : a gauge known to stick, and an independent switch left inoperative after testing. No alarm on “no level change while filling” , and limited control of incoming flow by the site. Containment failed : bund walls and joints leaked and fire-water and fuel escaped, polluting groundwater. Unexpected severity : a vapour cloud in a moderately congested area exploded far more strongly than models of the time predicted. Lessons for your plant Overfill protection must be truly independent, tested properly, and returned to service after testing (functional safety, SIL). Treat repeated instrument faults as warnings, not nuisances. Design secondary and tertiary containment (bunds, drainage) to hold fuel and fire-water. Do not assume a vapour cloud will only flash: congestion can make it explode. Learn more on PharmaChemE Lesson 9 · Toxic and flammable releas

Distillation separates the components of a liquid mixture by differences in volatility (boiling point). The mixture is heated so the more volatile component vaporizes preferentially, and that vapor is then condensed back to a liquid richer in that component. It's one of the most common separation and purification techniques in chemical and pharmaceutical processing, used both to purify a product and to recover or remove solvents.

t: What is evaporation, and how is it different from distillation?
x: Evaporation removes a volatile solvent from a solution by vaporizing it, leaving behind a more concentrated solution or, if carried far enough, a solid residue. Unlike distillation, evaporation isn't mainly about collecting the vapor as a purified product; the vapor is often just discarded or recovered as a byproduct. Distillation uses that vapor deliberately to separate two or more components.

Filtration separates solid particles from a liquid (or gas) by passing the mixture through a porous medium that retains the solids while letting the liquid pass through. In chemical and pharmaceutical processing it's the standard way to isolate a crystallized or precipitated solid product from its mother liquor.

t: What is drying, in a process engineering sense?
x: Drying removes residual liquid (usually solvent or water) from a wet solid, typically by applying heat, reducing pressure, or both, until the material reaches an acceptable residual moisture or solvent specification. It's usually the final step before a solid product is packaged, and it needs to balance thorough solvent removal against avoiding thermal degradation of the product.

t: What is absorption, and how is it different from adsorption?
x: Absorption is when a gas (or sometimes a liquid) is taken up into the bulk volume of a liquid or solid, becoming dissolved or incorporated throughout, like carbon dioxide absorbing into water. Adsorption is when a substance sticks to the surface of a solid (or sometimes liquid) without going into the bulk, like activated carbon adsorbing color bodies from a solution. The difference matters because it changes what controls the rate and capacity: bulk solubility for absorption, surface area for adsorption.

t: What is centrifugation used for in process engineering?
x: Centrifugation uses rapid rotation to generate centrifugal force that separates components of different density. It's commonly used to separate solids from a liquid (as an alternative or complement to filtration) or to split two immiscible liquid phases faster than gravity settling alone would. In pharmaceutical and fine chemical manufacturing, centrifuges are often used to isolate crystallized solids from their mother liquor.

x: Size reduction mechanically breaks larger solid particles into smaller ones, using equipment ranging from simple mechanical mills to jet mills that use high-velocity gas to shatter particles through collisions. In pharmaceutical processing, controlling final particle size is often important for how a drug substance dissolves, flows, and is handled during formulation.

t: What is agitation/mixing, and why does it matter?
x: Agitation is the mechanical action of stirring a liquid or slurry, typically with a rotating impeller, to blend materials, suspend solids, disperse gases or a second liquid phase, or improve heat transfer. Many reactions and physical processes (like crystallization or extraction) depend on bringing materials into close contact at the rate the process needs. Poor mixing can become the rate-limiting step even when the underlying chemistry is fast.

t: What is heat exchange, and what's a heat exchanger?
x: Heat exchange is the transfer of thermal energy from a hotter fluid to a cooler one without the two fluids mixing, typically across a solid wall (like a metal tube or plate). A heat exchanger is the equipment that does this, from a simple jacketed vessel to dedicated shell-and-tube or plate heat exchangers. Heating, cooling, condensing and evaporating all over a chemical plant depend on it.

t: What is scrubbing, in the context of chemical plant operations?
x: Scrubbing removes unwanted gases, vapors, or particulates from a gas stream by contacting it with a liquid (or sometimes a solid) that absorbs or reacts with the contaminant, commonly used to treat vent gases before they're released to the atmosphere or to recover a valuable solvent vapor. A scrubber is the equipment that provides this gas-liquid contact, often using packing or trays to maximize contact area.

Decantation separates two immiscible liquids, or a liquid from settled solids, simply by carefully pouring or draining off the upper layer once the mixture has been allowed to settle and separate by gravity. It's one of the simplest separation techniques, often used as a quick first step before a more thorough separation like filtration or centrifugation.

t: What's the difference between a batch process and a continuous process?
x: A batch process takes a fixed quantity of material through a complete sequence of steps before the next batch starts. It's common in pharmaceutical and fine chemical manufacturing, where flexibility, smaller volumes and traceability of each batch matter. A continuous process runs material through the system steadily without starting and stopping, which is typically more efficient at very large scale and consistent product volumes, but less flexible for making different products or smaller quantities.

t: What is a theoretical plate (or theoretical stage) in distillation?
x: A theoretical plate is one full equilibrium contact between vapor and liquid: the ideal case where the vapor and liquid leaving that stage are in perfect equilibrium with each other. Real distillation columns are rated by how many theoretical plates' worth of separation they achieve. It's the standard way to compare and design separation equipment, even though no real tray reaches perfect equilibrium.

Residence time is how long material actually spends inside a piece of equipment or a process step. For a continuous process it's typically the vessel volume divided by the volumetric flow rate; for a batch process it's simply the duration of that step. Many processes (reactions, drying, heat transfer) need a minimum residence time to reach completion, and too little residence time is a common cause of incomplete processing.

t: What's the difference between yield, conversion, and selectivity?
x: Conversion is the fraction of starting material that has reacted at all; selectivity is the fraction of that converted material that went to the desired product rather than side products; and yield is the overall fraction of theoretical product actually obtained, which combines both conversion and selectivity (yield equals conversion times selectivity, roughly speaking). A reaction can have high conversion but poor yield if selectivity to the desired product is low.

t: What is viscosity, in practical terms?
x: Viscosity is a fluid's resistance to flow. A high-viscosity fluid (like honey) flows sluggishly and resists being pumped or stirred, while a low-viscosity fluid (like water) flows easily. It directly affects pump selection, mixing, heat transfer rates and filtration behavior, which is why it's one of the first physical properties checked when handling an unfamiliar material.

t: What is vapor pressure, and why does it matter for process engineering?
x: Vapor pressure is the pressure exerted by a substance's vapor when it's in equilibrium with its liquid at a given temperature, and it increases with temperature. A substance boils when its vapor pressure equals the surrounding pressure. Vapor pressure sets a solvent's volatility, flammability risk and evaporation rate, and how distillation or vacuum operations will behave for that material.

t: What is boiling point, and how does pressure affect it?
x: Boiling point is the temperature at which a liquid's vapor pressure equals the surrounding (ambient or system) pressure, causing it to vaporize throughout the bulk liquid rather than just at the surface. Reducing the surrounding pressure (as in vacuum distillation) lowers the boiling point, which is exactly why vacuum is used to distill heat-sensitive materials at a lower, safer temperature.

A slurry is solid particles suspended in a liquid, thick but still able to flow, with a significant proportion of undissolved solids. Slurries are common in crystallization (crystals suspended in mother liquor) and when solid raw materials are charged as a pumpable mix rather than a dry powder. Pumps, valves and agitators need to be suited to slurry service, since standard liquid-handling equipment can struggle with abrasive or settling solids.

t: What's the difference between a suspension and an emulsion?
x: A suspension is solid particles dispersed in a liquid (like a slurry), while an emulsion is one liquid dispersed as tiny droplets within another liquid it doesn't naturally mix with (like oil droplets dispersed in water). Both are inherently unstable over time and will eventually separate unless stabilized, which is why suspensions and emulsions often need continued agitation or a stabilizing agent to remain uniform.

t: What's the difference between an exothermic and an endothermic reaction?
x: An exothermic reaction releases heat as it proceeds (the products have lower energy than the reactants), while an endothermic reaction absorbs heat from its surroundings to proceed (the products have higher energy than the reactants). This difference is central to process safety. An exothermic reaction can self-accelerate and potentially run away if the heat it generates isn't removed fast enough, which is why reaction calorimetry is done before scaling up a new exothermic process.

t: What does validation mean in a pharmaceutical manufacturing context?
x: Validation is documented evidence that a process, piece of equipment, or analytical method consistently does what it's intended to do, produced by executing predefined tests or trial runs against predetermined acceptance criteria. It's a core regulatory requirement in pharmaceutical manufacturing. A process isn't considered proven because it worked once; it has to be shown to work reliably and reproducibly under real operating conditions.

t: What's the difference between a raw material, an intermediate, and an API?
x: A raw material is a starting substance brought into the process from outside (a reagent, solvent, or starting chemical); an intermediate is a substance produced partway through a multi-step synthesis that isn't the final desired product but is used to make it; and the API (Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient) is the final biologically active substance that goes into a drug product. A single synthesis might pass through several intermediates before reaching the API.

t: What is a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP)?
x: An SOP is a documented, step-by-step set of instructions for carrying out a specific task or process the same way every time, covering everything from equipment setup to the exact sequence of actions and the acceptance criteria for each step. SOPs are central to GMP manufacturing because consistency and reproducibility depend on everyone following the same validated procedure, not on individual judgment each time.

t: What does 'unit operation scale-up' actually mean, in plain terms?
x: Scale-up means taking a process that's been developed and proven at small (lab or pilot) scale and getting the same result at a much larger, commercially useful scale. That's harder than it sounds, because many physical effects (mixing time, heat transfer rate, addition time) don't change in proportion to size. Good scale-up work identifies which of these effects actually control the process outcome, then designs the larger equipment and procedure to preserve those conditions.

t: Why does a reaction that works perfectly in the lab behave differently at pilot scale?
x: Scale-up changes physical parameters that don't scale linearly with volume: mixing time typically increases, heat transfer surface area per unit volume decreases, and addition/charging times get longer relative to the reaction rate. A reaction that's mixing-limited or heat-transfer-limited at large scale can behave completely differently even though the chemistry itself hasn't changed. Always ask what's actually controlling your reaction rate at lab scale before assuming it will scale directly.

t: What are the most important factors to check before scaling up a reaction?
x: Focus on heat transfer capability (can the plant reactor add/remove heat as fast as the reaction needs?), mixing time versus reaction rate, addition/charge time relative to reaction kinetics, and whether the reaction is adiabatic-safe if cooling is lost. Reaction calorimetry data (heat of reaction, adiabatic temperature rise) is usually the single most valuable piece of information before committing a new reaction to a larger vessel.

t: Why does mixing take longer at larger scale even with a similarly powerful agitator?
x: Mixing time generally scales unfavorably with vessel size for a fixed impeller tip speed or fixed power per unit volume. Larger vessels have proportionally longer blend times because the ratio of impeller-swept volume to total volume shrinks. This is one of the most common reasons a reaction that seemed instantaneous on the bench becomes addition-rate or mixing limited in the plant.

t: Why is reaction calorimetry important before running a new process?
x: Calorimetry measures the heat of reaction and the rate at which heat is generated, which tells you whether your reactor's cooling capacity can keep up with the reaction, and what the adiabatic temperature rise would be if cooling were lost. Without this data you don't actually know whether a runaway is possible, so it's the single most important safety screening step before scaling up an exothermic reaction. This explains why calorimetry matters in general. The specific safety screening tests required for a given reaction should be determined by a qualified process safety specialist based on the actual chemistry involved.

t: What should a batch record capture?
x: A batch record should capture every material charged (with lot numbers and quantities), every process step performed with actual times and observed conditions (temperature, pressure, pH, etc.), in-process sample results, deviations from the procedure, and who performed and verified each step. It needs to be complete enough that someone could reconstruct exactly what happened without being present.

t: What's the purpose of a process flow diagram in pilot plant work?
x: A process flow diagram shows the sequence of unit operations, the equipment involved, and the major streams (raw materials, intermediates, waste) flowing between them. It's the reference document operators and engineers use to understand how the whole process fits together, and it's usually the starting point for a Haz-Op.

t: What are common mistakes to avoid when developing a process meant to be scaled up?
x: Common ones: relying on very fast additions or instantaneous mixing that won't be achievable at scale, using lab techniques that don't translate (like swirling a flask by hand), not characterizing the heat of reaction, assuming filtration or drying rates from a Buchner funnel will hold at plant scale, and not building in enough margin for longer hold times and addition times.

t: Why do batches typically take longer at pilot or plant scale than at the bench?
x: Charging, heating, cooling, and phase separations all take proportionally longer as equipment gets larger, because heat transfer area and addition rates don't scale at the same rate as volume. A charge that takes seconds from a pipette can take an hour from a plant-scale addition vessel, and a reaction that seemed to run to completion instantly on the bench may take hours to reach the same conversion once mixing and heat transfer become rate-limiting.

t: What does GMP mean for pilot plant operations?
x: Good Manufacturing Practice means documented, reproducible procedures, calibrated and qualified equipment, traceability of materials and actions (who did what, when), and a quality system that reviews deviations. Even in early-stage pilot work, building GMP-friendly habits (good batch records, equipment logs, clear procedures) makes the eventual transfer to full GMP manufacturing much smoother.

t: Why does my reaction seem to be mixing-limited at larger scale?
x: If a reaction's rate depends on how quickly two phases or reagents are brought into contact, blend time becomes the limiting factor once the mixing rate falls below the intrinsic reaction rate. Signs of this include yield or selectivity dropping as scale increases even though temperature and stoichiometry are unchanged. The fix is usually to slow the addition rate, improve impeller design, or add the reagent closer to the impeller discharge.

t: What causes poor reaction control (temperature excursions) during scale-up?
x: Usually a mismatch between the rate of heat generation (which can scale faster than expected if addition is fast) and the rate of heat removal (which is often limited by jacket area per unit volume, which shrinks as the vessel gets bigger). Slowing the addition rate, using a controlled semi-batch addition, or pre-cooling reagents are the standard fixes.

t: How do I know if a process sample is representative of the whole batch?
x: Sample from a well-mixed zone, ideally while the agitator is running, and avoid sampling right after a charge before it's had time to distribute. For heterogeneous or viscous systems, take samples from more than one location or depth and compare. If results vary noticeably between samples, that's a sign the batch isn't fully mixed yet.

t: What makes an extraction efficient or inefficient?
x: Extraction efficiency depends on the partition coefficient of the solute between the two phases, the volume ratio of the phases, and the number of extraction stages. A single extraction with a favorable partition coefficient can still leave significant product behind. Several smaller extractions are almost always more efficient than one large one for the same total solvent volume.

t: Why does batch distillation performance change when I scale it up?
x: Larger stills often have proportionally less surface area for heat input relative to the batch volume, meaning distillation takes longer. Column efficiency (theoretical plates) can also differ if the plant column's packing or trays aren't equivalent to whatever was used at bench scale, changing the separation you actually achieve for the same reflux ratio.

t: What causes poor crystal quality: too many fines or hard agglomerates?
x: Fines are usually caused by excessive supersaturation (cooling or antisolvent addition too fast, or too much local supersaturation at the addition point), which favors nucleation over growth. Agglomerates often come from poor mixing that lets locally over-concentrated zones stick particles together, or from seeding technique issues. Slower, better-controlled addition rates and adequate seeding usually improve both problems.

t: What's the difference between cake filtration and depth filtration, and when do I use each?
x: Cake filtration collects a visible layer of solids on a filter medium and is used when you want to recover a solid product (like isolating a crystallized API). Depth filtration passes liquid through a thick porous medium to capture fine particulates for clarification, typically used for polishing a solution rather than recovering solids. Choosing the wrong one either clogs quickly (using depth media for heavy solids loading) or fails to clarify properly (using cake filtration for trace particulates).

t: Why does drying take so much longer at production scale than in a lab oven?
x: Larger cake beds have longer diffusion paths for moisture or solvent to escape, and heat transfer to the center of a large cake or through a jacketed dryer wall is slower per unit mass than in a thin lab tray. Poor airflow or vacuum distribution across a larger surface area makes it worse. Bed depth and agitation (if using an agitated dryer) are usually the first things to check when drying is slower than expected. These are the usual suspects, but drying behavior is often product-specific, so verify with actual scale-down or pilot trials before settling on a cause.

t: What's the right way to clean a reactor between batches of different products?
x: Use a validated cleaning procedure suited to the residue's solubility (solvent rinse, caustic wash, or dedicated cleaning agent), verify cleanliness with a rinse sample or swab test where cross-contamination matters, and pay special attention to dead legs, gaskets, and agitator shafts where residue can hide. For potent or highly reactive residues you need documented cleaning validation, not just a visual check.

t: What causes a rotary (gear or lobe) pump to stop delivering flow?
x: Common causes include excessive clearance from wear letting liquid slip back internally, a relief valve stuck open or set too low, entrained air or vapor in the pumped fluid, or the fluid viscosity being outside the pump's design range. Rotary pumps depend on close internal clearances, so wear is a very common root cause of gradually declining output.

t: What's the difference between a diaphragm pump and a peristaltic pump, and when should I use each?
x: A diaphragm pump uses a flexing membrane and check valves to move fluid and can handle higher pressures and a wide range of chemical compatibility depending on diaphragm material; a peristaltic pump squeezes fluid through flexible tubing with rollers, keeping the fluid completely isolated from any pump internals, which is ideal for sterile, shear-sensitive, or highly corrosive fluids at lower pressures and flow rates. Choose peristaltic when you need to avoid any fluid contact with pump internals, and diaphragm when you need higher pressure or flow capability.

t: Why won't my diaphragm pump prime?
x: Common causes are a worn or torn diaphragm, a stuck or fouled check/ball valve, air trapped on the suction side that the pump can't purge, or a suction lift beyond the pump's dry-priming capability. Diaphragm pumps rely on their check valves sealing properly to build suction, and a valve held open by debris is one of the most common culprits.

t: What causes excessive pressure drop in a transfer line?
x: Undersized pipe diameter for the flow rate, too many fittings and elbows (each adds equivalent length), a partially closed or fouled valve, or a highly viscous fluid all increase pressure drop. Pressure drop increases roughly with the square of velocity, so a line sized even slightly too small can cause a disproportionate increase in required pump head.

t: How do I select the right gasket material for a flange?
x: Match the gasket material's chemical compatibility to the process fluid first (this rules out most options quickly), then confirm it can handle the operating temperature and pressure, and consider whether the flange faces are smooth or serrated, which affects which gasket types will seal properly. When in doubt, check a material compatibility chart for the specific chemical against the elastomer or fluoropolymer first, instead of just picking a common general-purpose gasket. This is only a general starting point. Always verify against the gasket manufacturer's chemical compatibility data at your actual operating temperature and concentration before final selection.

t: How do I pick the right size O-ring to fix a leaking seal?
x: Measure the groove's inner diameter and cross-section width (or measure the failed O-ring itself if it hasn't distorted too much) and match against a standard O-ring size chart (AS568 dash sizes are the common reference). Always confirm the elastomer is chemically compatible with the process fluid, not just that the dimensions match. A correctly sized but incompatible O-ring will still fail.

t: How do I estimate how much liquid a storage tank or drum actually holds?
x: For a vertical cylindrical vessel, volume is simply cross-sectional area times liquid height, but always subtract for any dished or sloped bottom, and never plan to fill to 100% of nominal capacity. Leave enough freeboard for thermal expansion and to prevent overflow during filling. For common container sizes, standard drum and tank capacity references (by diameter and standard sizes) are a faster check than calculating from scratch.

t: Why does my reactor take longer to heat up or cool down as batch size increases?
x: Heat transfer area (jacket surface) scales with the square of a vessel's linear dimension, while volume scales with the cube. So larger vessels have proportionally less jacket area per unit volume, which directly increases heating and cooling times. This is one of the most predictable and unavoidable effects of scale-up, and it's why plant-scale temperature ramps are almost always slower than lab-scale ones.

t: How do I estimate the heat transfer coefficient of a jacketed reactor?
x: The overall coefficient combines the inside film coefficient (driven by agitation and fluid properties), the wall and jacket-side resistances, and any fouling. In practice, it's most reliable to determine it experimentally by measuring the actual heating or cooling rate of a known mass and comparing to the temperature driving force, rather than relying solely on theoretical correlations, since fouling and real agitation conditions vary significantly from vessel to vessel.

t: What is LMTD and why does it matter for heat exchanger sizing?
x: Log mean temperature difference is the properly-averaged temperature driving force between two fluids exchanging heat when that difference changes along the length of the exchanger (as it does in any real heat exchanger). Using a simple arithmetic average instead of LMTD will give an inaccurate (usually optimistic) estimate of the required heat transfer area, especially when the temperature difference varies a lot between the inlet and outlet ends.

t: Why won't my temperature control unit (TCU) reach its setpoint?
x: Check first whether the heat transfer fluid flow rate through the jacket is adequate (a partially closed valve or air-locked line will starve heat transfer), whether the TCU's own heating or cooling capacity is actually sufficient for the vessel size and duty, and whether the fluid has degraded or lost its heat transfer properties over time. An undersized TCU relative to the vessel's heat duty is a very common root cause, especially after moving a process to a larger reactor.

t: How do I choose the right heat transfer fluid for my application?
x: Match the fluid's useful temperature range to your process's full operating range (including any planned excursions), check viscosity at the coldest temperature you'll see (high viscosity kills circulation and heat transfer), and consider flammability and toxicity if a leak into the process is a credible scenario. Glycols are common for moderate temperature ranges; specialized synthetic heat transfer fluids or silicone oils are used for wider or more extreme ranges.

t: What's the difference between using a glycol solution and using a brine for cooling?
x: Glycol/water mixtures are generally less corrosive and easier to handle but have a practical low-temperature limit around -30 to -40°C depending on concentration; brines (like calcium chloride solutions) can reach lower temperatures but are more corrosive to many common materials. Choose based on the coldest temperature you actually need and the material compatibility of your cooling loop.

t: Why does my process chiller lose cooling capacity in hot weather?
x: Chillers reject heat to ambient air or cooling water, and their capacity drops as the temperature difference between the condenser and ambient shrinks. A chiller rated for a cold winter day can lose a significant fraction of its rated capacity on a hot summer day. Always check a chiller's capacity curve at the worst-case (highest) ambient or cooling water temperature you expect, not just the nominal rating.

t: How does cooling water inlet temperature affect condenser performance?
x: Higher cooling water inlet temperature reduces the temperature driving force across the condenser and directly cuts its heat rejection capacity. This can show up as poor vacuum distillation performance or incomplete condensation on hot summer days even when nothing else in the system has changed. If condenser performance is seasonal, cooling water temperature is usually the first thing to check.
