x: Continuous and Flow Chemistry Scale-up · Continuous Processing · October 2026 Instead of filling a 6,000 L reactor and waiting, a flow reactor pumps reagents through a tube a few millimetres wide, and product comes out continuously at the other end. It sounds like a lab curiosity, but flow chemistry is now used at production scale for reactions that are too fast, too hot or too hazardous to run safely in batch. This article explains how it works and where it fits. In this article The idea: time becomes distance Basics Why flow can do things batch cannot Basics Sizing a simple flow reactor Working level What flow does badly Working level Scaling up and running a flow process Going deeper Questions people ask The idea: time becomes distance Basics In a batch reactor, the reaction proceeds in time: so many hours at temperature. In a flow reactor, it proceeds along the tube: each bit of flui

t: The idea: time becomes distance Basics
x: In a batch reactor, the reaction proceeds in time: so many hours at temperature. In a flow reactor, it proceeds along the tube: each bit of fluid enters, reacts as it travels, and leaves after the residence time: Residence time τ = reactor volume V / volumetric flow Q A 6 mm tube 40 m long holds about 1.1 L. At 100 mL/min, the residence time is about 11 minutes. Run it continuously and it processes 144 L a day, from a reactor you can carry. Try it: change the tube diameter, length and flow and see the residence time, throughput and heat transfer area per volume compared with batch reactors.

t: Why flow can do things batch cannot Basics
x: Heat transfer: area per volume is 4/d for a tube. A 6 mm tube has about 670 m²/m³; a 6 kL batch reactor has about 2. Strongly exothermic reactions that would need hours of slow dosing in batch can run in seconds to minutes. Small inventory: only a litre or so is reacting at any moment. If something goes wrong, the energy available is tiny compared with a full batch. Hazardous intermediates (diazonium salts, azides, organolithiums) can be made and used immediately without accumulating. Precise residence time: stopping a reaction at exactly the right point helps with consecutive side reactions. See reactor selection . Extreme conditions: temper

t: Sizing a simple flow reactor Working level
x: Find the residence time needed from batch kinetics or small flow trials at the chosen temperature. Choose the throughput: product per day = flow × concentration × molar mass × time. At 100 mL/min, 0.5 mol/L and a molar mass of 250 g/mol, that is about 18 kg per day. Reactor volume = flow × residence time. Check mixing at the inlet: fast reactions need a good mixer (T-piece, static mixer or micromixer), because laminar flow in small tubes mixes slowly by itself. Check pressure drop through the tube and mixers, and that the pumps can deliver steady, pulse-free flow.

t: What flow does badly Working level
x: Solids: precipitates and slurries block narrow channels. This is the most common reason flow projects fail. Keep everything in solution, or use reactors designed for slurries (CSTR cascades, oscillatory baffled reactors). Slow reactions: a 10-hour reaction needs a very long tube or very low flow. Batch is usually simpler. Many steps with different conditions can be linked, but every step adds pumps, mixers and control, and the slowest step sets the pace. Start-up and shut-down produce off-specification material, which must be planned for.

t: Scaling up and running a flow process Going deeper
x: Flow processes scale by running longer, by using a larger reactor of the same design (keeping heat transfer and mixing similar), or by numbering up : several identical reactors in parallel. Each keeps the same conditions that worked in development, which avoids many of the scale-up surprises of batch. See lab to plant scale-up . Continuous processes also need continuous quality control. Process analytical technology (inline IR, UV or Raman) watches the product stream in real time, and a diverter valve sends out-of-specification material to waste or recycling. In GMP manufacture, the batch is defined by time or quantity, with traceability of a

Choosing flow for a reaction that forms solids. Ignoring mixing at the inlet of a fast reaction. Pulsing pumps that make residence time uneven. No plan for start-up and shut-down material. Converting a whole process when one hazardous step would do.

x: Cooling Tower Calculations Explained Utilities · Cooling Water · Updated October 2026 The cooling tower decides the condenser water temperature for every chiller, solvent condenser and reactor jacket in the plant, and it is usually the biggest single user of fresh water on site. Four numbers describe it: range, approach, evaporation and cycles of concentration. Here is how to calculate each one and what it tells you. In this article How a cooling tower cools water Basics Range, approach and effectiveness Basics Heat load Working level Water balance Working level A water-saving case: raising the cycles Working level Why the approach matters to the whole plant Going deeper Monthly checks Going deeper Questions people ask Short on time? The Cooling Tower calculators work out all of these from your readings. How a cooling tower cools water Basics Hot water is spread over the fill so that a l

t: How a cooling tower cools water Basics
x: Hot water is spread over the fill so that a large surface of water meets moving air. About 1 % of the water evaporates for every 6–7 °C of cooling, and the latent heat it takes cools the rest. Because the cooling comes from evaporation, the limit is the air's wet bulb temperature, not its dry bulb. On a humid monsoon day with a 29 °C wet bulb, no tower can deliver 28 °C water. Hot water falls over the fill while the fan draws air through it. A small part of the water evaporates into the air, and that evaporation is what cools the rest.

Range = hot water in - cold water out Approach = cold water out - wet bulb Effectiveness = Range / (Range + Approach) = Range / (hot water in - wet bulb) The range is fixed by the plant: heat load divided by water flow. The approach is what the tower controls. A tower designed for 4 °C approach that now gives 7 °C at the same wet bulb has a problem: scaled or broken fill, blocked distribution nozzles, a fan with the wrong blade angle or a slipping belt, or air short-circuiting from the outlet back to the inlet.

Heat rejected (kW) = flow (m³/h) × 1,000 / 3,600 × 4.186 × Range In TR: kW / 3.517 In kcal/h: kW × 860 For 500 m³/h cooled from 37 to 32 °C: 500 × 1,000 / 3,600 × 4.186 × 5 ≈ 2,907 kW, about 827 TR. A cooling tower serving a chiller rejects the chiller's cooling load plus its compressor power, about 1.2–1.25 times the chiller TR. For a VAM it is about 1.8 times, because it also rejects the steam's heat.

Evaporation E (m³/h) = 0.00085 × 1.8 × circulation (m³/h) × Range (°C) Drift D = drift % × circulation Cycles of concentration COC = conductivity (or chloride) of circulating water / that of make-up Blowdown B = E / (COC - 1) - D Make-up M = E + B + D = E × COC / (COC - 1) The evaporation formula is a field approximation: about 0.15 % of the flow per degree of range. It assumes all the heat leaves as latent heat; in dry weather a little leaves as sensible heat and actual evaporation is slightly lower. Worked example 500 m³/h, range 5 °C, COC 4, drift 0.02 % E = 0.00085 × 1.8 × 500 × 5 ≈ 3.8 m³/h D = 0.0002 × 500 = 0.1 m³/h B = 3.8 / 3 - 0.1 ≈

t: A water-saving case: raising the cycles Working level
x: A 1,000 m³/h tower with a 6 °C range evaporates about 9.2 m³/h. At 3 cycles the make-up is 9.2 × 3/2 ≈ 13.8 m³/h. At 5 cycles it is 9.2 × 5/4 ≈ 11.5 m³/h: about 55 m³ a day less make-up, and about 55 m³ a day less blowdown going to the ETP. Above about 6 cycles the saving per extra cycle gets small, while the scaling and corrosion risk keeps rising. What limits the cycles is the make-up water: hardness and alkalinity (calcium carbonate scale), silica, chloride (corrosion of stainless and carbon steel) and the treatment programme. Ask your water treatment supplier for the maximum safe cycles for your make-up analysis, and control the blowdown

t: Why the approach matters to the whole plant Going deeper
x: Every degree the cooling water runs warmer costs energy and capacity elsewhere. An electric chiller uses roughly 2–3 % more power for each 1 °C rise in condenser water temperature. Solvent condensers lose capacity, vacuum systems lose vacuum, and batch cooling times stretch. A 2 °C approach improvement on the tower is often worth more in the chiller house than in the cooling tower itself.

Log hot water, cold water and wet bulb every shift; trend the approach against the wet bulb. Measure the circulating flow at least once a year (ultrasonic meter) to confirm the heat load. Inspect the hot water basin and nozzles, the fill, the drift eliminators and the fan blade angle. Compare make-up meter readings with the calculated make-up; a big gap means leaks or uncontrolled overflow. Check the conductivity controller and the blowdown valve actually work. Run fans on cold-water temperature, with VFDs where possible, so they slow down in winter.

s: Crystallisation scale-up: solubility and supersaturation, metastable zone width, seeding, cooling profiles, oiling out and what changes at plant scale.
x: Crystallisation Scale-up Scale-up · Solids · October 2026 In API manufacturing, crystallisation is where the product gets its purity, its form and its particle size. It is also the step that most often behaves differently in the plant: the lab gave nice prisms that filtered in minutes, and the plant gives a paste that blocks the centrifuge. The cause is nearly always supersaturation: how much of it was created, how fast, and where in the vessel. This article explains crystallisation from that one idea. In this article Solubility and supersaturation Basics Nucleation vs growth Basics The metastable zone Working level Seeding and cooling profiles Working level Antisolvent and reactive crystallisation Working level What changes at plant scale Going deeper Oiling out, polymorphs and other surprises Going deeper Questions people ask Solubility and supersaturation Basics Every compound has a s

Every compound has a solubility in a solvent: the most that can stay dissolved at a given temperature. For most organic compounds it rises with temperature. Dissolve the product hot, cool it, and the solution ends up holding more than it can at the lower temperature. That excess is supersaturation , and it is the driving force for crystallisation: Supersaturation ΔC = C - C*(T) or as a ratio S = C / C*(T) C: concentration in solution; C*: solubility at the current temperature. We create supersaturation by cooling, by evaporating solvent, by adding an antisolvent in which the product is poorly soluble, or by a reaction that forms the less solu

Supersaturation can be used up in two ways: Nucleation: new crystals form from nothing. It needs high supersaturation and happens suddenly, in a burst, producing a large number of tiny crystals. Growth: dissolved molecules attach to crystals that already exist. It works at low supersaturation and makes existing crystals bigger. A good crystallisation is mostly growth: few crystals, growing large and evenly. A bad one is mostly nucleation: a shower of fines that are hard to filter and wash, hold more mother liquor (and its impurities) and dry slowly. Controlling crystallisation means keeping supersaturation in the range where growth wins.

A clear solution can be cooled some way below its saturation temperature without crystallising. The region between the solubility curve and the point where it finally nucleates on its own is the metastable zone . Its width (MSZW) is typically a few degrees to about 20 °C of undercooling. It is not a fixed property: faster cooling, weaker agitation and higher purity all make it wider. Inside the zone, crystals that are already present grow, but new ones form only slowly. Cross the upper limit and the solution nucleates suddenly, usually at a temperature that varies from batch to batch. Try it: a solution saturated at 70 °C is cooled to 10 °C.

t: Seeding and cooling profiles Working level
x: Seeding takes nucleation out of the hands of chance. You add crystals of the right form at a chosen point inside the metastable zone, so growth starts on them at low supersaturation. Good practice: Seed about a quarter to a third of the way into the metastable zone: past saturation so the seed doesn't dissolve, but far from the limit. Use 0.5–2 % by weight of seed, milled or sieved to a known size, and of the correct polymorph. Add it as a slurry in the same solvent, not as a dry powder that floats on the surface. Hold for 30–60 minutes after seeding before cooling further, so the seed surface “heals” and starts to grow. Then cool. At the sta

t: Antisolvent and reactive crystallisation Working level
x: With an antisolvent (water into a methanol solution, heptane into ethyl acetate), supersaturation is created where the antisolvent meets the solution: at the feed point. Local supersaturation there can be far higher than the average in the vessel. The same applies to reactive crystallisation, such as adding acid to form a salt. So: Add slowly, especially at first; seed after the first portion. Feed into a well-mixed zone near the impeller, not onto the surface or down the wall. Consider reverse addition (solution into antisolvent) only if the lab has shown it gives the right form.

t: What changes at plant scale Going deeper
x: Cooling is slower and less even. The plant can't cool as fast as the lab, which is often good for crystal size, but the jacket wall is much colder than the bulk. Supersaturation near the wall causes encrustation and fines. Limit the jacket-to-batch temperature difference (often 10–15 °C) during crystallisation. Mixing is slower. Antisolvent and reagent feed points matter much more. See the mixing scale-up article . Agitator tip speed is higher. At the same power per volume, the plant impeller tip moves faster and can break needle-like crystals, creating fines. Check the crystal habit under the microscope. Time is longer. Holds at the end of c

t: Oiling out, polymorphs and other surprises Going deeper
x: Oiling out (liquid-liquid phase separation) happens when the product separates as an oil instead of crystals, usually because supersaturation is too high or the temperature is above the product's melting point in that solvent mixture. The oil later solidifies into a lump that traps impurities. Seed above the oiling-out temperature, and add antisolvent more slowly. Polymorphs are different crystal forms of the same molecule, with different solubility, stability and bioavailability. The form that crystallises can depend on solvent, temperature, supersaturation and seed. Always seed with the right form, confirm the form by XRD on plant batches,

Cooling at a fixed rate with no seed and accepting whatever nucleates. Adding dry seed powder onto the surface. Cooling fast right after seeding. Pouring antisolvent onto the surface or down the wall. Scaling up without checking the plant's jacket temperature difference and agitator tip speed.

s: Distillation basics: VLE, relative volatility, theoretical stages, McCabe-Thiele, minimum reflux and Fenske, tray efficiency and batch distillation.
x: Distillation Basics Process Design · Separation · October 2026 Distillation is the workhorse of every chemical plant: solvent recovery, purification, removing water before a reaction. Most engineers can run a still, but fewer can say why one separation needs five trays and another needs fifty, or why turning up the reflux sometimes fixes the purity and sometimes doesn't. This article builds the picture from one idea: vapour is richer in the more volatile component than the liquid it boils from. In this article The one idea behind distillation Basics Relative volatility: how easy is the separation? Basics What a theoretical stage is Basics McCabe-Thiele: counting the stages Working level Choosing the reflux ratio Working level From theoretical stages to a real column Working level Batch distillation in pharma plants Going deeper Questions people ask The one idea behind distillation Basics

t: The one idea behind distillation Basics
x: Boil a mixture of methanol and water and the first vapour that comes off is richer in methanol than the liquid was, because methanol has the higher vapour pressure. Condense that vapour, boil it again, and it gets richer still. A distillation column simply does this boiling and condensing many times over, in one piece of equipment. Vapour rises, liquid falls, and on each tray or each bit of packing they meet, swap some molecules, and part again. That is all. Everything else in distillation design is about how many of those contacts you need and how much liquid you must send back down the column to make them work.

t: Relative volatility: how easy is the separation? Basics
x: Relative volatility, α, measures how strongly the light component prefers the vapour compared with the heavy one: α = (yA/xA) / (yB/xB) ≈ P^satA / P^satB (for ideal mixtures) x is the mole fraction in the liquid, y in the vapour. The equilibrium curve is y = αx / (1 + (α - 1)x). Some feel for the numbers: α above 3: easy. A few stages do the job. Acetone from water is in this range at low acetone concentrations. α around 1.5 to 2.5: normal. Ten to thirty stages. α below 1.2: hard. Many stages and high reflux; ask whether another method would be cheaper. α = 1: an azeotrope. Ordinary distillation cannot pass it, whatever the column. Ethanol an

t: What a theoretical stage is Basics
x: A theoretical stage (or ideal stage) is a contact where vapour and liquid mix long enough to reach equilibrium and then separate cleanly. Real trays don't quite get there, so a real column needs more trays than theoretical stages. But theoretical stages are the right way to think first, because they depend only on the chemistry and the reflux, not on the hardware. The reboiler counts as one theoretical stage. A partial condenser also counts as one; a total condenser does not.

t: McCabe-Thiele: counting the stages Working level
x: The McCabe-Thiele diagram is the classic way to see a binary separation. It has three lines: the equilibrium curve : what composition of vapour sits above each liquid; the operating lines : a mass balance that links the liquid leaving one stage with the vapour coming up from the one below. Above the feed (rectifying section) the slope is R/(R + 1), where R is the reflux ratio; below the feed (stripping section) it is steeper; the 45° diagonal, where x = y. Starting at the top product composition, step horizontally to the equilibrium curve (one stage of equilibrium), then vertically to the operating line (mass balance to the next stage down),

t: Choosing the reflux ratio Working level
x: Two limits frame every design: Nmin = ln[ (xD/(1 - xD)) × ((1 - xB)/xB) ] / ln α (Fenske, at total reflux) Rmin: the reflux at which the operating line touches the equilibrium curve (a pinch) For our example: Nmin = ln(19 × 19) / ln 2.5 ≈ 6.4 stages, and Rmin ≈ 1.1. At total reflux you need the fewest stages but produce nothing; at minimum reflux you need infinite stages. Between them is a trade-off: Every unit of reflux has to be boiled in the reboiler and condensed again. Reboiler duty ≈ (R + 1) × D × latent heat, so steam and cooling water costs rise in step with R + 1. Fewer stages means a shorter, cheaper column. The economic optimum is

t: From theoretical stages to a real column Working level
x: Trays: real trays = theoretical stages ÷ overall efficiency. Typical efficiencies are 0.5 to 0.8 for solvent systems, lower for viscous liquids. Tray spacing is usually 450–600 mm. Packing: packed height = theoretical stages × HETP. Structured packing gives HETP of roughly 0.3–0.5 m; random packing (rings) 0.4–0.8 m. Packing has a low pressure drop, so it is the usual choice for vacuum distillation and for the small columns on top of batch stills. Diameter is set by the vapour load: too small and the column floods; too large and liquid doesn't distribute evenly on packing or trays weep at low load. Design around 70–80 % of flooding. Add a mar

t: Batch distillation in pharma plants Going deeper
x: Most solvent distillation in API and intermediate plants is batch: a reactor acts as the reboiler, with a short packed column, a condenser, a reflux divider and receivers. The pot composition keeps changing, so the top composition falls during the run unless the reflux ratio is raised. Operators usually run it in cuts: total reflux to establish the column; a low-boiler fore-cut, collected separately; the main solvent cut at a moderate reflux ratio, raising it as the top temperature starts to climb; an intermediate cut (slop) to be recycled into the next batch; the residue left in the pot. Watch the top temperature, not just the time. For a so

Designing from a single relative volatility for a mixture with water. Expecting distillation to break an azeotrope. Turning up reflux on a column that is already flooding. Ignoring liquid distribution in packed columns. Running batch cuts by the clock instead of the top temperature.

s: Drying of wet cakes: drying curves, why plant drying is slower than lab, dryer types (VTD, ANFD, RCVD, FBD), residual solvent and endpoints.
x: Drying and Dryer Scale-up Scale-up · Solids · October 2026 Drying looks like the simplest step in the process: put the wet cake in, heat it, wait. Yet it is often the bottleneck of the whole plant, and where batches fail on LOD, residual solvent or degradation. The reason is that drying happens in two very different stages, and the second one, which barely shows in the lab, can take most of the time in the plant. This article explains drying from the basics and what to expect when you scale it up. In this article What happens when a cake dries Basics The drying curve Basics Why the plant is so much slower Working level Choosing a dryer Working level Temperature, form and residual solvent Working level Knowing when it's dry Going deeper Questions people ask What happens when a cake dries Basics A wet cake from a centrifuge or filter holds solvent in two places: free solvent in the spaces

t: What happens when a cake dries Basics
x: A wet cake from a centrifuge or filter holds solvent in two places: free solvent in the spaces between particles and on their surfaces, and bound solvent inside pores, in crystal defects or held as a solvate. Free solvent evaporates easily once heat reaches it. Bound solvent first has to travel out of the particle, which is slow and doesn't speed up much however hot the jacket is. To evaporate solvent you need heat (its latent heat) and a way to carry the vapour away (vacuum or a gas stream). Vacuum lowers the boiling point, so the solvent evaporates at a temperature the product can tolerate.

Plot LOD (loss on drying) against time and you see two periods: Constant-rate period: particle surfaces are wet, and solvent evaporates as fast as heat arrives. The product sits near the solvent's boiling point at the dryer pressure, well below the jacket temperature. LOD falls in a straight line. Falling-rate period: below the critical moisture content , the surfaces dry out. Now the rate is set by how fast solvent moves out from inside the particles. The rate falls, LOD approaches its final value slowly, and the product temperature rises toward the jacket temperature. The falling-rate period is the trap. It has little solvent left to remove

t: Why the plant is so much slower Working level
x: In a contact dryer (a vacuum tray dryer, filter-dryer or conical dryer), heat comes through the heated wall or plates. The drying rate per kilogram of cake depends on how much heated area each kilogram has, and that falls as the bed gets deeper: Drying rate per kg ∝ U × A × (Tjacket - Tproduct) / mcake ∝ ΔT / bed depth A lab tray of 2 cm cake dried at 60 °C reaches 0.5 % LOD in about 1.4 hours. The same cake in a filter-dryer with a 30 cm bed has 15 times less area per kilogram and takes about 22 hours, 14 of them in the falling-rate period. Raising the jacket to 80 °C, if the product allows, brings it to about 14 hours. Reducing the bed dept

Dryer Good for Watch out for Vacuum tray dryer (VTD) Small batches, sticky or heat-sensitive products, many products Manual loading and unloading, operator exposure, slow Agitated nutsche filter-dryer (ANFD) Filtration, washing and drying in one closed vessel; potent and toxic products Deep beds, slow falling-rate period, agitator causing agglomerates or attrition Rotary cone vacuum dryer (RCVD) Free-flowing powders, gentle tumbling, good mixing Lumps and balling with sticky cakes Fluid bed dryer (FBD) Fast drying of granular, free-flowing solids with hot gas Dust explosion risk with solvents and fines; needs inert gas for flammable solvents

t: Temperature, form and residual solvent Working level
x: Product temperature limit: below the temperature where it melts, sinters, degrades or changes form. During the constant-rate period the product stays cool even with a hot jacket, but in the falling-rate period it heats up toward the jacket temperature. Many plants run a hot jacket first and lower it later. Solvates and hydrates: some products hold solvent or water in the crystal. Drying too hard can remove it and change the form; drying too gently can leave too much. The form must be checked by XRD at the end of drying. Residual solvent limits: ICH Q3C sets limits for solvents in drug substances. For example, toluene is limited to 890 ppm and

t: Knowing when it's dry Going deeper
x: The definitive answer is a sample tested for LOD or residual solvent. But samples take time, so watch the online signs too: Product temperature rising toward the jacket temperature: the constant-rate period is over. Dryer pressure falling toward the pump's no-load vacuum: little vapour is being produced. Condensate collection in the receiver slowing to a stop. Sample at the point the trend says it should be dry, not on a fixed clock. If the falling-rate period is the bottleneck, look at reducing particle porosity in crystallisation, at better deliquoring, or at a short slurry wash with a lower-boiling solvent to displace a high-boiling one be

Estimating plant drying time from a lab oven tray. Running the jacket at full temperature into the falling-rate period without checking product temperature limits. Passing LOD but never testing residual solvent. Drying a 30 % LOD cake when better deliquoring could bring it to 20 %. Fluid-bed drying flammable solvent-wet product with air.

s: Dust explosions explained: the pentagon, Kst and Pmax, MIE, hybrid mixtures with solvent, secondary explosions and controls: inerting, venting, suppression.
x: Dust Explosions Process Safety · Fire and Explosion · October 2026 Most people in a solvent plant respect solvent vapour, but treat powder as harmless: it is just the product, sitting in a bag. Yet many organic powders, APIs, intermediates, sugar and starch among them, explode as violently as a gas when they are dispersed as a cloud. This article explains when and why a dust explodes, how to read the test data, and the controls that actually protect a plant. In this article How a powder can explode Basics The explosion pentagon Basics Reading the test data: Kst, Pmax, MIE Working level Hybrid mixtures: powder plus solvent Working level Prevention and protection Working level Secondary explosions and Imperial Sugar Going deeper Questions people ask How a powder can explode Basics A lump of sugar burns slowly. Grind it to a fine powder and blow it into the air, and every particle is surrou

t: How a powder can explode Basics
x: A lump of sugar burns slowly. Grind it to a fine powder and blow it into the air, and every particle is surrounded by oxygen with a huge surface area to react. A flame can then pass from particle to particle fast enough to build pressure inside equipment or a building: a dust explosion. Roughly, any solid that can burn can explode as a dust if it is fine enough, typically below about 500 µm, and especially below 100 µm. That includes most organic chemicals, APIs, excipients, food powders, plastics and metal powders such as aluminium. Inert inorganic salts don't.

A fire needs the three sides of the fire triangle: fuel, oxygen and ignition. A dust explosion needs two more: the dust must be dispersed as a cloud, and the cloud must be confined so pressure can build. Take away any one of the five and there is no explosion. Try it: tap a side of the pentagon to remove it, and see how plants remove each one in practice. Dispersion is what makes dust different from a vapour. A layer of powder on a floor is not an explosion hazard by itself; the same powder blown into the air is. That's why the places to worry about are where powder is airborne: inside mills, sieves, blenders, fluid bed dryers, cyclones, bag

t: Reading the test data: Kst, Pmax, MIE Working level
x: A powder's explosion behaviour is measured in standard tests. The main numbers: Property What it means Typical range KSt (bar·m/s) How violent the explosion is: maximum rate of pressure rise, normalised to volume St 1: up to 200; St 2: 200–300; St 3: above 300 Pmax (bar g) Highest pressure in a closed vessel Usually 7–10 bar g MIE (mJ) Smallest spark that ignites the dust cloud From below 3 mJ (very sensitive) to above 1,000 mJ MIT (°C) Minimum ignition temperature of a cloud and of a 5 mm layer Cloud often 400–600 °C; layers much lower LOC (% O2) Oxygen below which the dust cannot explode Often 9–14 % with nitrogen MEC (g/m³) Minimum explosi

t: Hybrid mixtures: powder plus solvent Working level
x: Pharma and fine chemical plants have a special problem: powders that are wet with solvent, or charged into vessels containing solvent vapour. A dust cloud mixed with flammable vapour is a hybrid mixture . Even solvent vapour well below its LFL makes the dust far easier to ignite, often reducing the MIE to that of the solvent, and makes the explosion more violent. Practical rules: Charging powder into a reactor containing solvent: treat it as a solvent vapour hazard first, and inert the vessel. See inerting and LOC . Drying solvent-wet product in a fluid bed: use nitrogen in a closed loop, not air, unless testing shows the hybrid mixture can't

Prevention stops an explosion starting: Avoid clouds and layers: closed transfer systems, dust extraction at charging points, and housekeeping with industrial vacuum cleaners rated for combustible dust, never compressed air or brooms. Control ignition sources: earthing and bonding, Type C or D FIBCs, magnets and metal detectors ahead of mills, temperature limits for equipment surfaces, and hazardous area zoning (Zone 20, 21, 22 for dust) with suitably rated electrical equipment. Inert equipment where clouds are unavoidable and the dust is sensitive: mills, blenders, dryers. Protection limits the damage when one does start: Explosion venting:

t: Secondary explosions and Imperial Sugar Going deeper
x: A primary explosion inside equipment is often fairly small. But its pressure wave shakes loose dust settled on beams, ducts, cable trays and floors, raising a large cloud through the building, and the flame from the primary ignites it. This secondary explosion causes most of the deaths and damage in major dust incidents. On 7 February 2008, at the Imperial Sugar refinery in Port Wentworth, Georgia, a primary explosion in a steel belt conveyor under the sugar silos set off secondary explosions that spread through the packing buildings. Fourteen workers died and dozens were injured. The US Chemical Safety Board found heavy accumulations of suga

Assuming a powder is safe because it is “just the product”. No dust explosion test data for products that are milled, sieved or fluid-bed dried. Cleaning with compressed air, which creates the cloud. Ignoring hybrid mixtures when charging powders into solvent. Explosion vents that discharge into a work area or are blocked.

x: Equipment Qualification: URS, DQ, IQ, OQ and PQ Plant Engineering · GMP · October 2026 A new reactor arrives at the site, and before it makes a single batch of drug substance, it has to be qualified: a documented trail showing it was specified properly, built and installed as designed, works as intended and performs consistently with the real process. To engineers new to pharma it can look like paperwork for its own sake. Done well, it is simply good engineering written down. This article explains each stage and what it is really checking. s: Equipment Qualification: URS, DQ, IQ, OQ and PQ
x: GMP rules (EU GMP Annex 15, WHO and Schedule M in India, US FDA expectations) require that equipment used to make medicines is shown to be fit for its intended use, with documented evidence. The aim is simple: if a batch fails, you should be able to rule out the equipment, because you know it was built right, installed right and works right. Qualification is that evidence. Qualification applies to equipment and utilities (reactors, dryers, purified water, HVAC, compressed air and nitrogen that contact product). Validation is the related term for processes, cleaning and computer systems. Qualified equipment is a precondition for process valida

s: Equipment Qualification: URS, DQ, IQ, OQ and PQ
x: The stages are usually drawn as a V. Down the left side you specify what you want and design it; at the bottom it is built; up the right side you test it, and each test stage checks the specification opposite it. Try it: tap each stage of the V to see what it covers. The dashed lines show which specification each test verifies.

t: URS and DQ: getting the specification right Working level
s: Equipment Qualification: URS, DQ, IQ, OQ and PQ
x: The user requirement specification (URS) is the most important document in the chain, and the one most often rushed. Write it in the user's terms, with numbers that can be tested: working volume and minimum stir volume, temperature and pressure range, materials of construction for every wetted part, surface finish, cleanability (drainability, spray ball coverage), instruments and their accuracy, interlocks, data integrity needs for any control system, and safety requirements such as ATEX zone and relief. Design qualification (DQ) is the documented review that the supplier's design (drawings, datasheets, P&IDs, functional specification) meets

s: Equipment Qualification: URS, DQ, IQ, OQ and PQ
x: The factory acceptance test (FAT) is done at the supplier's works before dispatch: dimensions, materials certificates, welding records, pressure test, surface finish, agitator run, control sequences. Faults found here are cheap to fix. The site acceptance test (SAT) repeats the key checks after installation. Well-documented FAT and SAT results can be referenced in IQ and OQ instead of repeating every test.

t: IQ, OQ and PQ Working level
s: Equipment Qualification: URS, DQ, IQ, OQ and PQ
x: Installation qualification (IQ): the equipment is installed as designed. Check model and serial numbers, materials certificates, P&ID walk-down, utilities connected correctly, instruments calibrated and tagged, drawings as-built, manuals, spare parts lists and SOPs received. Operational qualification (OQ): every function works across its operating range. Agitator speed range, heating and cooling rates, temperature control and uniformity, vacuum and pressure hold tests, alarms and interlocks proven by simulating the trip condition, sequence and recipe functions, and data recording and audit trail for computerised systems. Performance qualifica

s: Equipment Qualification: URS, DQ, IQ, OQ and PQ
x: Modern guidance (Annex 15, ICH Q9, ASTM E2500) expects the depth of qualification to follow risk: test thoroughly what affects product quality and patient safety, and rely on good engineering practice and supplier documentation for the rest. A jacket's cooling rate matters for a crystallisation step; the colour of the motor does not. Qualified status has to be maintained. Periodic review (often yearly) checks that the equipment is still in a qualified state: calibrations current, changes controlled, deviations and breakdowns reviewed. Any change goes through change control, and the impact assessment decides what must be requalified. A like-fo

s: Effluent treatment basics: COD, BOD, TDS, stream segregation, stripping, MEE and ATFD, biological and tertiary treatment, ZLD and discharge limits.
x: Effluent Treatment Basics Plant Engineering · Environment · October 2026 Pharmaceutical effluent is difficult: high COD, high salt, residual solvents and compounds that bacteria don’t like to eat. Treating it all together usually fails. Treating it well starts long before the ETP, with knowing which stream is which. This article explains the key parameters, the treatment steps, and why segregation is the most important design decision. In this article The numbers that describe effluent Basics Segregation: the first decision Basics High-COD and high-TDS streams Working level Biological treatment Working level Tertiary treatment and ZLD Going deeper Questions people ask The numbers that describe effluent Basics COD (chemical oxygen demand): the oxygen needed to oxidise everything organic chemically, in mg/L. The overall organic load. BOD (biochemical oxygen demand, usually 3 days at 27 °C

t: The numbers that describe effluent Basics
x: COD (chemical oxygen demand): the oxygen needed to oxidise everything organic chemically, in mg/L. The overall organic load. BOD (biochemical oxygen demand, usually 3 days at 27 °C in India): the oxygen bacteria use to eat the organics. The biodegradable part. BOD/COD ratio: above about 0.4, the effluent is reasonably biodegradable; below about 0.2, biology alone won't do much. TDS (total dissolved solids): salts from neutralisations and work-ups. High TDS, above roughly 1–2 %, inhibits normal biological treatment. pH, TSS, oil and grease, ammoniacal nitrogen and specific toxic compounds. Typical general discharge standards for inland surface

A small volume of mother liquor or aqueous layer can carry most of a site's COD and salt. Mixing it with large volumes of washings dilutes the concentration, but not the load, and turns it into a big stream that is hard to treat. Separate streams at the source: High-COD / high-TDS: aqueous layers, mother liquors, scrubber blowdowns. Send to stripping and evaporation. Low-COD / low-TDS: equipment washings, utility blowdowns, floor washings. Send to biological treatment. Collect high-strength streams in separate, labelled tanks with an analysis for each batch. The material balance of each process tells you in advance what each stream carries.

t: High-COD and high-TDS streams Working level
x: Solvent stripping: a steam stripper removes volatile solvents, recovering them and cutting COD. A few percent of methanol in an aqueous stream can be a large share of its COD. Neutralisation and pre-treatment: pH adjustment, removal of oil and suspended solids. Multiple effect evaporator (MEE): evaporates the water using steam several times over; a four-effect MEE typically evaporates around 3–3.5 kg of water per kg of steam. The condensate goes to biological treatment or reuse. Agitated thin film dryer (ATFD): dries the MEE concentrate to a solid salt, which goes to a hazardous waste facility.

Low-strength streams and MEE condensate go through a conventional sequence: equalisation (to even out swings in flow and composition), neutralisation, primary clarification, aeration (activated sludge or MBBR) and secondary clarification. Bacteria need steady conditions: sudden slugs of solvent, high salt or toxic compounds kill the biomass, and recovery takes weeks. Equalisation and stream control protect them. Try it: change the inlet COD and biodegradability (BOD/COD) and see whether the treated effluent meets a 250 mg/L COD limit. A rough model, but it shows why low-BOD/COD streams need segregation.

t: Tertiary treatment and ZLD Going deeper
x: After biology, tertiary steps polish the water: pressure sand filters, activated carbon, sometimes ozonation, and ultrafiltration plus reverse osmosis for reuse. In a zero liquid discharge scheme, RO permeate is reused as cooling tower or boiler feed make-up, and the RO reject goes back to the MEE, so no liquid leaves the site. ETP operating cost is dominated by steam for the MEE and ATFD, power for aeration, chemicals and hazardous solid disposal. The cheapest reduction is at source: recover solvents better, reduce salt by choosing reagents and work-ups carefully, and keep high-strength streams small. On the plant Track COD load (kg/day), no

Mixing high-strength mother liquors with large washing streams. Sending high-TDS effluent straight to biological treatment. Ignoring solvent content as a source of COD. Shock loading the aeration tank. Watching concentration instead of load.
