s: Falling film evaporator basics: film formation, distributor, minimum wetting rate, heat transfer and area, multiple effects, MVR and common problems.
x: Falling Film Evaporator: How It Works and How It Is Sized Process Design · Evaporation · October 2026 A falling film evaporator looks like a shell-and-tube exchanger standing on end, and that is nearly what it is. Liquid runs down the inside of the tubes as a thin film while steam condenses outside, and the vapour separates at the bottom. Because each drop spends only seconds in the heated tube, it is a favourite for heat-sensitive liquids and for effluent concentration in MEE plants. Its weak point is the film itself: if it breaks, the tube runs dry and fouls. This article explains how it works and how to keep the film whole. In this article How it works Basics Why choose a falling film Basics The distributor and the wetting rate Working level Sizing the heat transfer Working level Multiple effects and MVR Going deeper Common problems Going deeper Questions people ask How it works Basic

s: Falling Film Evaporator: How It Works and How It Is Sized
x: Feed enters the top head, above the tube sheet, and a distributor spreads it evenly over every tube. It runs down the inside wall as a thin film, typically a millimetre or less, heated by steam condensing on the shell side. The liquid boils at the film surface; vapour flows down the tube centre with the liquid, and both leave the bottom into a separator, where the vapour goes to a condenser or the next effect and the concentrate is pumped out, partly recirculated to the top if needed.

t: Why choose a falling film Basics
s: Falling Film Evaporator: How It Works and How It Is Sized
x: Short residence time , seconds per pass, so heat-sensitive products degrade less. Small temperature difference works well, because there is no hydrostatic head raising the boiling point at the bottom of the tube (unlike a rising film or natural circulation evaporator). That suits multiple effects and vapour recompression. High heat transfer coefficients for clean, low-viscosity liquids. It is a poor choice for liquids that crystallise or foul heavily in the tube, or are very viscous; forced circulation evaporators and agitated thin film dryers handle those. See the ATFD article .

t: The distributor and the wetting rate Working level
s: Falling Film Evaporator: How It Works and How It Is Sized
x: Everything depends on every tube getting enough liquid, all the way down. The measure is the wetting rate Γ: liquid flow per metre of tube perimeter. Γ = m / (N × π × d) m liquid flow (kg/s), N number of tubes, d tube inside diameter (m). Evaporation reduces Γ down the tube, so the bottom is the critical point. Below a minimum wetting rate the film breaks into rivulets, leaving dry patches that overheat and foul. The minimum depends on the liquid, surface and heat flux; designers often work with figures in the region of a few tenths of a kg/m·s for water-like liquids and check with the supplier. The figure uses 0.25 kg/m·s as an illustration.

t: Sizing the heat transfer Working level
s: Falling Film Evaporator: How It Works and How It Is Sized
x: Q = mevap × λ + mfeed × cp × (Tboil - Tfeed) A = Q / (U × ΔT) ΔT is the steam saturation temperature minus the boiling temperature of the liquid at the evaporator pressure, adjusted for boiling point elevation of concentrated solutions. Overall U for clean aqueous duty is often 1,500–3,000 W/m²K, falling with viscosity and fouling. Preheat the feed to its boiling point before it enters the tubes; otherwise the top of the tubes acts as a heater, not an evaporator. See heat exchanger design basics .

t: Multiple effects and MVR Going deeper
s: Falling Film Evaporator: How It Works and How It Is Sized
x: In a multiple effect evaporator (MEE) the vapour from one effect heats the next, which runs at a lower pressure and temperature. A four-effect plant evaporates roughly 3 to 3.5 kg of water per kg of steam. In mechanical vapour recompression (MVR) , a compressor or fan raises the vapour pressure slightly so it can heat the same evaporator, using electricity instead of steam. Falling film designs suit both because they work with small temperature differences. In pharma effluent plants, an FFE often forms the first effects of the MEE, followed by forced circulation effects as the liquid concentrates and an ATFD to dry it. See ETP basics .

s: Falling Film Evaporator: How It Works and How It Is Sized
x: Falling capacity : scaling in the tubes (check the ΔT needed for the same evaporation) or non-condensables blanketing the shell side (vent it). Dry tubes and fouling at the bottom : wetting rate too low; add recirculation. Carry-over of droplets into the condensate: separator overloaded, demister damaged or foaming. Uneven tube performance : distributor out of level or partly blocked.

s: Falling Film Evaporator: How It Works and How It Is Sized
x: Feeding below the boiling point so the top of the tubes only heats. No recirculation when most of the feed is evaporated. Distributor not levelled or inspected. Using an FFE for crystallising or very viscous liquids. Ignoring boiling point elevation of concentrated solutions.

s: Fault tree analysis for process plants: top and basic events, AND and OR gates, top event frequency, minimal cut sets and links to HAZOP and LOPA.
x: Fault Tree Analysis (FTA) Process Safety · Risk Assessment · October 2026 A HAZOP finds that a runaway is possible. LOPA estimates how likely it is with simple multiplication. But when the protection is a complicated system, two pumps, redundant trips, shared power supplies, you need a way to see exactly which combinations of failures lead to the accident. That is fault tree analysis: working backwards from the accident to every route that gets there. In this article The idea: start from the accident Basics AND and OR gates Basics Calculating the top event Working level Minimal cut sets Working level Common cause failures and where FTA fits Going deeper Questions people ask The idea: start from the accident Basics A fault tree starts with one undesired top event , such as “runaway reaction with reactor damage”, and asks: what must happen for this to occur? Each answer is broken down agai

t: The idea: start from the accident Basics
x: A fault tree starts with one undesired top event , such as “runaway reaction with reactor damage”, and asks: what must happen for this to occur? Each answer is broken down again, until you reach basic events whose failure rates you can estimate: a pump fails, a valve sticks open, an operator makes an error, a trip fails on demand. The result is a tree that shows, on one page, every route to the accident.

OR gate : the event above happens if any one of the events below happens. Too much reagent is dosed if the pump speed is wrong, or the control valve fails open, or the operator doses the wrong quantity. AND gate : the event above happens only if all the events below happen together. Damage occurs only if excess dosing happens and both protections fail. OR: P = 1 - (1 - P1)(1 - P2)… ≈ P1 + P2 + … (for small P) AND: P = P1 × P2 × … OR gates add up; AND gates multiply down. That is why protection works: putting independent protections under an AND gate makes the top event much rarer. Try it: change the frequency or probability of each basic even

t: Calculating the top event Working level
x: In the example, the three causes of excess dosing (0.05, 0.1 and 0.1 per year) combine through the OR gate to about 0.23 per year. The high-temperature trip fails on 1 demand in 100, and the relief is undersized for this case with a probability of 0.1, so both protections fail together with a probability of 0.001 per demand. The top event frequency is 0.23 × 0.001 ≈ 2.3 × 10^-4 per year. Halving the operator error rate barely changes this; improving the trip to SIL 2 (0.001) cuts it tenfold. Mixing units is the common trap: initiating causes are frequencies (per year), while protections are probabilities of failure on demand (no units). Only

A cut set is a combination of basic events that together cause the top event. A minimal cut set is one where removing any event stops it being a cut set. In the example the minimal cut sets are {A, D, E}, {B, D, E} and {C, D, E}. Two things to look for: Single-event cut sets : one failure alone causes the accident. These need attention first. Events that appear in every cut set , like D and E here: improving them reduces every route at once.

t: Common cause failures and where FTA fits Going deeper
x: The AND gate only multiplies if the events are independent. Two trips on the same instrument air supply, two pumps fed from one electrical panel, or two sensors calibrated with the same faulty reference can fail together. These common cause failures often dominate the real risk and must be added as their own basic events. See LOPA and SIL on independence. FTA sits alongside other methods: HAZOP finds the scenarios, LOPA screens them with quick arithmetic, and FTA is used where the protection logic is complex, for SIL verification of redundant systems, or for investigating an incident to see which combinations of failures occurred. See HAZOP m

Putting two frequencies under an AND gate. Assuming protections are independent when they share a utility or a sensor. Using precise-looking numbers without stating where they came from. Improving events on OR branches when the AND gate matters more. Drawing a tree so detailed that nobody reviews it.

s: kLa and gas-liquid mass transfer: Henry's law, when a hydrogenation is mass-transfer limited, why plant kLa is lower, and how pressure and agitation help.
x: Gas-Liquid Reactions and kLa Scale-up · Reaction Engineering · October 2026 A hydrogenation that finishes in an hour in the lab autoclave takes six hours in the plant, and the impurity profile changes too. The catalyst is the same, the temperature and pressure are the same. What changed is how fast hydrogen gets from the gas into the liquid. This article explains gas-liquid mass transfer and the one number, kLa, that describes it. In this article The path of a hydrogen molecule Basics kLa and the transfer rate Basics Which step limits the rate? Working level Why plant kLa is lower Working level Improving mass transfer Going deeper Questions people ask The path of a hydrogen molecule Basics For hydrogen to react, it has to travel: from the gas bubble across a thin liquid film into the bulk liquid, then through the liquid to a catalyst particle, into its pores and onto the metal surface. E

t: The path of a hydrogen molecule Basics
x: For hydrogen to react, it has to travel: from the gas bubble across a thin liquid film into the bulk liquid, then through the liquid to a catalyst particle, into its pores and onto the metal surface. Each step has a resistance. The slowest one sets the overall rate. In most hydrogenations with an active catalyst, the slow step is the first: gas into liquid.

t: kLa and the transfer rate Basics
x: Rate of transfer = kLa × (C* - C) kLa: volumetric mass transfer coefficient (1/s), the product of the liquid-film coefficient kL and the bubble surface area per volume a. C*: gas solubility at the interface; C: dissolved concentration in the bulk. C* follows Henry's law: proportional to the gas partial pressure. Hydrogen is poorly soluble; in methanol roughly 0.004 mol/L per bar. At 5 bar, C* ≈ 0.02 mol/L. With kLa = 0.1 s^-1, the maximum transfer rate (when C is near zero) is 0.1 × 0.02 × 3,600 ≈ 7 mol/L per hour.

t: Which step limits the rate? Working level
x: Compare the maximum transfer rate with the rate the catalyst could achieve if hydrogen were plentiful (the kinetic rate): Mass-transfer limited: the catalyst could go faster, but hydrogen can't arrive fast enough. Dissolved hydrogen is near zero. The rate rises with pressure and agitation, but not with more catalyst. Kinetically limited: hydrogen is plentiful; the catalyst is the bottleneck. The rate rises with catalyst loading and temperature, but not with agitation. Try it: change the pressure, kLa and catalyst-limited rate. See which one limits, and how long it takes to take up 3 mol/L of hydrogen (a nitro reduction at 1 mol/L). A simple l

t: Why plant kLa is lower Working level
x: Typical values: lab autoclaves with gas-inducing stirrers reach 0.1–1 s^-1; plant hydrogenators often 0.02–0.2 s^-1. The reasons: Plant agitators run at lower power per volume than small lab stirrers. Gas enters from the headspace by surface entrainment, which becomes much less effective in tall vessels. Gas-inducing impellers lose efficiency with depth. So a reaction that was kinetically limited in the lab can become mass-transfer limited in the plant, with a longer cycle time and a different impurity profile. With the default values in the figure, lowering kLa from 0.1 to 0.03 s^-1 stretches the reaction from about 40 minutes to over an hou

Raise the pressure within the vessel rating: C* rises in proportion. Improve gas dispersion: gas-inducing hollow-shaft impellers, a sparger below a Rushton-type turbine, or an external loop reactor with an ejector. Increase agitator power where the motor and seal allow. Use the right fill level: too full and the surface entrainment drops; too empty and the impeller is uncovered. Mass transfer also gives a safety handle: in a mass-transfer limited hydrogenation, cutting the hydrogen supply or stopping the agitator stops the reaction and its heat quickly. But it works in reverse too: restarting a stopped agitator with hydrogen pressure on can r

Adding more catalyst to a mass-transfer limited reaction. Assuming lab reaction times will hold in the plant. Ignoring hydrogen starvation as a source of impurities. Restarting the agitator under hydrogen pressure without thought. Overfilling a hydrogenator with a gas-inducing impeller.

s: Glass-lined reactor care: thermal shock and temperature limits, chemical attack by alkali and HF, electrostatic damage, spark testing and repairs.
x: Glass-Lined Reactor Care Plant Engineering · Equipment Care · October 2026 A glass-lined reactor costs a lot, takes months to replace, and can be ruined in seconds by a dropped spanner or a blast of steam into a cold jacket. Yet it will last decades if a handful of rules are followed. This article explains how the lining works, what damages it, and how to inspect and repair it. In this article How a glass lining works Basics Thermal shock Basics Mechanical and chemical damage Working level Electrostatic damage Working level Inspection and repair Going deeper Questions people ask How a glass lining works Basics A glass-lined reactor is a carbon steel vessel with a layer of special glass, typically about 1–2 mm thick, fused onto the inside at high temperature. The glass is applied so that it is held in compression by the steel as they cool; glass is very strong in compression and weak in t

t: How a glass lining works Basics
x: A glass-lined reactor is a carbon steel vessel with a layer of special glass, typically about 1–2 mm thick, fused onto the inside at high temperature. The glass is applied so that it is held in compression by the steel as they cool; glass is very strong in compression and weak in tension. Anything that puts the glass in tension, such as a sudden temperature change, an impact or flexing of the steel, can crack or chip it. Once the glass is breached, the process liquid reaches the steel and corrodes it quickly.

Glass and steel expand at different rates. A sudden temperature difference between the glass surface and the steel behind it creates stress in the glass. Manufacturers publish charts of the allowable temperature difference, which depend on the vessel temperature and on whether you are heating or cooling. Typical dangerous situations: Charging cold liquid into a hot empty vessel, or hot liquid into a cold one. Switching the jacket from steam straight to brine, or brine to steam. Spraying cold wash water onto a hot wall. Ramp the jacket temperature in steps, clamp the jacket set point within the allowed difference in the DCS, and drain the jack

t: Mechanical and chemical damage Working level
x: Impact: dropped tools, sample thieves, scrapers, solids charged from height. Use protective covers on the manhole and non-metallic tools. Agitator problems: a bent shaft or worn bearing lets the impeller strike the wall or baffle. Check runout after maintenance. External damage: welding on the outside of the jacket or nozzles destroys the glass behind it. Never weld on a glass-lined vessel. Chemicals: glass resists almost all acids, but is attacked by hydrofluoric acid and fluorides, hot concentrated phosphoric acid, and alkali, increasingly so with temperature and pH. Prolonged boiling water also slowly attacks glass.

Glass is an insulator. When non-conductive liquids such as toluene or heptane are stirred, filtered or sprayed into a glass-lined vessel, charge can build up on the glass surface until it discharges through the lining to the steel, leaving a pinhole. It is also an ignition risk. Remedies include conductive glass, earthed tantalum or PTFE-coated probes in contact with the liquid, slower filling through dip pipes, and adding conductive solvents where the process allows. See static electricity .

Visual inspection at every opportunity: chips, dull or rough patches (chemical attack), rust stains (breach). Spark (holiday) testing: a high-voltage brush passed over the glass shows sparks where there is a pinhole or crack to the steel. Use the voltage recommended by the manufacturer for the glass thickness. Thickness measurement of the glass with a magnetic gauge shows gradual chemical wear. Repairs: small defects are sealed with tantalum plugs and screws or tantalum patches, with PTFE gaskets; larger areas with repair cements or sleeves. Repairs are compatible with fewer chemicals than the original glass, so note them in the vessel histor

Steam straight into the jacket of a cold vessel, or brine into a hot one. Metal tools and sample thieves inside the vessel. Hot caustic cleaning. Welding on the jacket or nozzles. Ignoring static with non-conductive solvents.

s: Safe handling of NaH, LiAlH4, thionyl chloride, azides and other hazardous reagents, and how to design a quench with controlled heat and gas release.
x: Hazardous Reagents and Quench Design Process Safety · Hazardous Operations · October 2026 A small group of reagents causes a large share of the incidents in API plants. They are not exotic: sodium hydride, lithium aluminium hydride, thionyl chloride, sodium azide. What they share is that their hazard is greatest at the end of the reaction, when the excess has to be destroyed. This article covers the main ones and the principles of a safe quench. In this article Why the quench is the dangerous step Basics The usual suspects Basics Designing a safe quench Working level Gas evolution and venting Working level Before scale-up Going deeper Questions people ask Why the quench is the dangerous step Basics During the reaction, the reagent is consumed under conditions somebody designed carefully. The quench is different: it destroys whatever is left, often an uncertain amount, with water or an al

t: Why the quench is the dangerous step Basics
x: During the reaction, the reagent is consumed under conditions somebody designed carefully. The quench is different: it destroys whatever is left, often an uncertain amount, with water or an alcohol, releasing heat and gas. It is often written in the batch record as a single line (“quench with water”) and done near the end of a long shift. Many incidents follow that pattern.

Reagent Main hazards Key precautions Sodium hydride (usually 60 % in mineral oil) Hydrogen with water, alcohols and acids; known thermal runaways in DMF, DMSO and DMAc Avoid NaH with DMF/DMSO at elevated temperature unless tested; quench slowly with IPA before water; inerted vessel and safe H2 vent Lithium aluminium hydride Violent reaction with water, hydrogen; ether solvents Controlled quench (for example the Fieser method: water, 15 % NaOH, water in a 1:1:3 ratio by weight of LAH); keep cold; vent H2 Thionyl chloride Releases SO2 and HCl; violent with water Distil off the excess before quench; route vents to a caustic scrubber sized for th

t: Designing a safe quench Working level
x: Know how much is left. Use the stoichiometry and an in-process check, not “excess”. The amount of reagent left decides the heat and gas. Control by addition rate. The quench should be dose-controlled: heat and gas come out as you add, and stop when you stop. That needs the quench reagent to react quickly at the quench temperature. Too cold and it accumulates, then reacts all at once. Choose the direction. Adding quench to the reaction (normal quench) or the reaction to the quench (reverse quench) gives very different local concentrations. Reverse quench into a large volume of cold quench solution often gives better control of heat and gas. Us

t: Gas evolution and venting Working level
x: Every mole of NaH gives a mole of hydrogen. Six kilograms of NaH (250 mol) releases about 5.6 Nm³ of hydrogen. Over 2 hours that averages 2.8 Nm³/h, but the peak rate is often higher. The vent line, flame arrester and scrubber must handle the peak without pressurising the vessel, and the headspace must stay inerted so the hydrogen has no oxygen to burn with inside the vessel. Try it: change the amount of excess NaH and the addition time. The curve shows the average hydrogen rate; compare it with what the vent can take. The same logic applies to CO2 from bicarbonate quenches (foaming), SO2 and HCl from thionyl chloride, and nitrogen from azide

Run the quench in the reaction calorimeter at the plant addition rate, measuring heat and gas. See how to read RC1 data . DSC the reaction mixture before quench, especially reagent/solvent combinations with known incidents. Calculate peak gas rate and check the vent and scrubber capacity. See scrubber design . Write the quench into the batch record as a controlled step with rate, temperature limits and stop conditions, not a single line. On the plant If a quench “isn't doing anything”, stop adding. A quench that seems not to react is the most dangerous kind: the reagent is accumulating, and when it starts, it will all go at once.

Quenching an unknown excess. Quenching too cold, so the quench reagent accumulates. Adding the quench faster because nothing seems to happen. Vent lines sized for normal breathing, not for quench gas. Using DMF or DMSO with NaH at elevated temperature without testing.

s: A practical HAZOP guide: nodes and design intent, guidewords, causes, consequences and safeguards, risk ranking, batch HAZOP and closing actions.
x: HAZOP Made Practical Process Safety · Hazard Studies · October 2026 Most engineers first meet a HAZOP as a long meeting with a projector, a stack of P&IDs and a spreadsheet that grows by a hundred rows a day. Done well, it is the single best way to find out how a design can go wrong before it does. Done badly, it is a box-ticking exercise that misses the one scenario that matters. This article explains how a HAZOP works, step by step, and what separates a useful one from a ritual. In this article The idea behind a HAZOP Basics The method: node, intent, guideword, deviation Basics Filling one row properly Working level Ranking risk and deciding actions Working level HAZOP for batch processes Going deeper What makes a HAZOP good Going deeper Questions people ask The idea behind a HAZOP Basics A process design describes how the plant is supposed to behave. Accidents happen when it behaves d

t: The idea behind a HAZOP Basics
x: A process design describes how the plant is supposed to behave. Accidents happen when it behaves differently: too much flow, no cooling, the wrong material, a step done out of order. A HAZOP (hazard and operability study) is a disciplined way of imagining those departures from design, one at a time, with a team that between them knows the chemistry, the equipment and how the plant is really operated. The method was developed at ICI in the 1960s and is now described in IEC 61882. Its strength is that it doesn't rely on anyone's memory of past incidents: it forces the team to consider deviations systematically, including ones nobody has seen ye

t: The method: node, intent, guideword, deviation Basics
x: Pick a node. A section of the P&ID with one clear purpose: the reagent dosing line and reactor, the condenser and receiver, the transfer to the centrifuge. State the design intent. What the node is meant to do, with numbers: “Dose 800 kg of reagent into R-101 over 4 hours at 60 °C, with the agitator running and the jacket on cooling water.” Combine a guideword with a parameter to get a deviation. Guidewords: No, More, Less, As well as, Part of, Reverse, Other than . Parameters: flow, temperature, pressure, level, composition, agitation, time. For each meaningful deviation, ask: What could cause it? What would happen? What protects us now? Is

t: Filling one row properly Working level
x: Take More flow of reagent during dosing. A weak row reads: “Cause: pump problem. Consequence: high temperature. Safeguard: operator.” It is useless, because nobody can act on it. A good row is specific enough that someone who wasn't in the room understands it: Causes: dosing pump speed set too high after maintenance; control valve FCV fails open; operator increases rate to finish before shift change. Consequence (without safeguards): reagent accumulates faster than it reacts; heat release exceeds jacket cooling; batch temperature rises; if cooling then fails, the MTSR exceeds the solvent boiling point and the reactor pressurises. Existing saf

t: Ranking risk and deciding actions Working level
x: Most companies rank each scenario on a risk matrix: severity of the consequence (from minor injury to multiple fatalities or a major release) against likelihood (from “has happened on this site” to “not expected in the plant's life”). The ranking decides whether the existing safeguards are enough or an action is needed. For high-severity scenarios, a matrix alone is too coarse. Layer of Protection Analysis (LOPA) is the usual next step: it counts the independent protection layers, gives each a credit (typically a tenfold risk reduction for a good alarm with operator response or a basic trip), and checks whether the total meets the company's t

t: HAZOP for batch processes Going deeper
x: A continuous plant runs in one steady state, so nodes based on equipment work well. A batch plant runs through a sequence of steps, and the same reactor is a charging vessel, a reactor, a distillation pot and a crystalliser on the same day. For batch processes, it works better to take the batch record steps as nodes and add timing guidewords: Early / Late: sampling done before the reaction is complete; quench added late. Before / After: solvent charged before the vessel is inerted; heating started before the agitator. Longer / Shorter: hold time extended over a weekend; dosing completed in half the time. Other than: wrong drum, wrong reactor,

t: What makes a HAZOP good Going deeper
x: Up-to-date P&IDs. A HAZOP on drawings that don't match the plant reviews a plant that doesn't exist. Walk the line first. The right people. An independent facilitator, a good scribe, the process engineer, and an operator or supervisor who knows how things are really done at 3 a.m. Process safety data in hand. Reaction heat, MTSR, TD24, gas evolution, flash points, toxicity. Without them, the team guesses at consequences. Short sessions. Four to five hours a day. After that, quality drops sharply and rows become copy-paste. Actions closed, not just raised. Track them with owners and dates, and review the closure. An open HAZOP action is a know

Writing consequences with the safeguards working, so every scenario looks minor. Counting the alarm and the trip on the same sensor as two layers. Skipping “obvious” deviations because the team is experienced. No reaction hazard data, so runaway scenarios are judged by feel. Actions that say “be careful”.

s: Heat exchanger sizing basics: heat duty, LMTD, counter vs co-current flow, overall U, typical U values, fouling, the F factor and a worked example.
x: Heat Exchanger Design Basics Process Design · Heat Transfer · October 2026 Every heat exchanger, from a reactor jacket to a shell-and-tube condenser, is sized with one short equation: Q = U × A × ΔT. The skill is in the three pieces: how much heat you must move, what temperature difference you really have, and how well heat crosses the wall once the exchanger has been in service a year. This article walks through each one and finishes with a full sizing example. In this article Step 1: the heat duty Basics Step 2: the temperature difference (LMTD) Basics Counter-current vs co-current Working level Step 3: the U value Working level Fouling: designing for the dirty exchanger Working level A full worked example Working level F factor, pinch and choosing the type Going deeper Questions people ask Step 1: the heat duty Basics The duty is the heat that must move from the hot stream to the cold

The duty is the heat that must move from the hot stream to the cold stream per second. With no phase change: Q = m × cp × (Tin - Tout) Q in kW when m is in kg/s and cp in kJ/kg·K. With condensation or boiling, add m × latent heat. The duty must balance: what the hot side loses, the cold side gains (minus a few percent lost to the surroundings). Use this to find the flow you need on the other side. If 4,000 kg/h of a solvent stream with cp 2.0 cools from 120 to 60 °C, the duty is (4,000/3,600) × 2.0 × 60 ≈ 133 kW. Cooling water warming from 30 to 40 °C then needs 133 / (4.18 × 10) ≈ 3.2 kg/s, about 11.5 m³/h.

The temperature difference between the two streams is not constant: it is large at one end of the exchanger and smaller at the other. The right average is not the simple arithmetic mean but the log mean : LMTD = (ΔT1 - ΔT2) / ln(ΔT1 / ΔT2) ΔT1 and ΔT2 are the hot-minus-cold temperature differences at the two ends. The log mean is always smaller than the arithmetic mean, and the difference grows as the two end differences move apart. When one end difference gets very small, the LMTD falls sharply and the area shoots up: that is the “temperature pinch” designers watch for.

In counter-current flow the streams enter at opposite ends; in co-current (parallel) flow they enter at the same end. For our example, hot 120 → 60 °C and cold 30 → 40 °C: Counter-current: ΔT1 = 120 - 40 = 80, ΔT2 = 60 - 30 = 30. LMTD = 50 / ln(2.67) ≈ 51.0 °C . Co-current: ΔT1 = 120 - 30 = 90, ΔT2 = 60 - 40 = 20. LMTD = 70 / ln(4.5) ≈ 46.5 °C . Counter-current needs about 9 % less area here. The bigger advantage is that it allows the cold outlet to get hotter than the hot outlet (a “temperature cross”), which co-current can never do. Co-current is still used where you want to limit the wall temperature for a heat-sensitive product, because t

t: Step 3: the U value Working level
x: U, the overall heat transfer coefficient (W/m²·K), is how easily heat crosses from one fluid to the other. It combines the film on the hot side, the wall, the film on the cold side and any fouling, all as resistances in series: 1/U = 1/hhot + twall/kwall + 1/hcold + Rf The worst resistance dominates. A gas or a viscous liquid on one side caps U, whatever you do on the other side. Typical overall values for preliminary sizing: Service Typical U (W/m²·K) Water to water, shell-and-tube 800 – 1,500 Organic solvent to cooling water 300 – 600 Condensing steam to water 1,500 – 4,000 Condensing solvent vapour to cooling water 500 – 1,000 Gas to water

t: Fouling: designing for the dirty exchanger Working level
x: A clean exchanger only stays clean for a few weeks. Scale from cooling water, polymer or tar from process streams and corrosion products all add resistance. Designers allow for this with a fouling factor: 1/Udirty = 1/Uclean + Rf With Uclean = 500 W/m²·K and Rf = 0.0005 m²K/W: 1/U = 0.002 + 0.0005 = 0.0025, so Udirty = 400. The exchanger needs 25 % more area. Typical Rf values: treated cooling tower water 0.0002–0.0004, river or untreated water 0.0005–0.001, clean organic solvents 0.0002, heavy or polymerising streams 0.0005 and up. Be careful not to stack margins: a generous fouling factor, plus a 20 % area margin, plus a conservative U, can

t: A full worked example Working level
x: Cool 4,000 kg/h of process stream (cp 2.0 kJ/kg·K) from 120 to 60 °C with cooling water from 30 to 40 °C, in a shell-and-tube exchanger E-101. Duty: Q = 1.111 × 2.0 × 60 = 133 kW. Cooling water: 133 / (4.18 × 10) = 3.2 kg/s, about 11.5 m³/h. LMTD, counter-current: 51.0 °C. U: organic to water, clean 500, with Rf 0.0005 gives 400 W/m²·K. Area: A = Q / (U × LMTD) = 133,000 / (400 × 51.0) ≈ 6.5 m² . Co-current would need 133,000 / (400 × 46.5) ≈ 7.2 m². Specify the exchanger at 6.5 m² plus a modest margin (10–15 %), and check the tube-side velocity: cooling water below about 1 m/s fouls fast.

t: F factor, pinch and choosing the type Going deeper
x: The F correction factor. Real shell-and-tube exchangers with more than one tube pass are neither pure counter-current nor co-current. The LMTD is multiplied by a correction factor F (from charts or equations, based on the four temperatures): Q = U × A × F × LMTD. If F falls below about 0.8, the design is inefficient and sensitive; use more shells in series or a true counter-current design. Approach temperature. The smallest temperature difference anywhere in the exchanger. Below about 5–10 °C for liquids, area grows very fast for little extra heat recovered. That is why a cooling water exchanger rarely cools a process stream below about 38–40

Using the arithmetic mean temperature difference instead of the LMTD. Forgetting the latent heat when a solvent vapour condenses. Stacking fouling factor, area margin and conservative U on top of each other. Ignoring non-condensables in vacuum condensers. Taking U from a table for a viscous or gas service where it can be ten times lower.

s: How to read a P&ID: equipment tags, line numbers, valve and line symbols, ISA 5.1 instrument letters, control loops and interlocks. Interactive explorer.
x: How to Read a P&ID Plant Engineering · Drawings · October 2026 The first time someone hands you a P&ID, it looks like a circuit diagram that fell into a bowl of alphabet soup. A week later you can't imagine working without it. The P&ID is the one drawing that shows how the plant is really put together: every line, valve, instrument and interlock. This article teaches you to read one, using a simple reactor example with generic tags. In this article What a P&ID is (and is not) Basics Equipment and their tags Basics Lines and line numbers Basics Valves and fittings Working level Instrument bubbles and ISA letters Working level Control loops and interlocks Going deeper How to trace a line on site Going deeper Questions people ask What a P&ID is (and is not) Basics A PFD (process flow diagram) tells the story of the process: main equipment, main streams, temperatures, pressures and flows fro

t: What a P&ID is (and is not) Basics
x: A PFD (process flow diagram) tells the story of the process: main equipment, main streams, temperatures, pressures and flows from the heat and material balance. It fits a whole plant on a few sheets. A P&ID (piping and instrumentation diagram) tells you how to build and run it: every pipe with its size and class, every valve, every instrument and what it is connected to, every vent, drain, sample point, utility connection, interlock and relief device. It is drawn schematically, not to scale: a pump drawn next to a reactor might be 30 metres away on site. For where things physically are, you need the layout and isometric drawings. The P&ID is

Each piece of equipment gets a tag: a letter code for its type and a number, often starting with the area or block. Codes differ between companies, but a common pattern is: Code Equipment Example R Reactor R-101 V / T Vessel / storage tank V-102, T-103 E Heat exchanger, condenser E-101 P Pump P-101A/B (A and B: duty and standby) C / K Centrifuge / compressor C-101 F / D Filter / dryer F-101, D-101 The legend sheet, usually the first sheet in the set, defines the codes and symbols for that project. Read it before anything else.

A thick solid line is a main process line; a thinner solid line is a secondary or utility line. Instrument signals are drawn differently: dashed lines for electrical signals, lines with short cross-hatches for pneumatic (air) signals, and a line of small circles or a dash-dot pattern for software or data links. Arrows show the direction of flow, and an off-page connector (an arrow-shaped box) shows where the line continues on another sheet. Every pipe has a line number. A typical format: 50 – PS – 101 – A1 50: nominal size in mm (or 2″). PS: service code, here process solvent. 101: sequence number. A1: piping class, which fixes material, pres

Most valve symbols start from two triangles touching at their tips (a “bow-tie”), which is a gate valve. Variations on it: Globe valve: bow-tie with a solid dot in the middle. Used for throttling. Ball valve: bow-tie with a circle in the middle. Quick on/off. Butterfly valve: a line with a short bar across it, or a bow-tie with a vertical line. Check (non-return) valve: a bow-tie with one triangle filled, or an arrow with a bar, pointing in the allowed flow direction. Control valve: a bow-tie with an actuator drawn on top: a dome for a diaphragm actuator. Labels FC (fail closed) or FO (fail open) tell you what it does when air or power fails.

t: Instrument bubbles and ISA letters Working level
x: Instruments are drawn as circles (bubbles). The line through the middle tells you where the instrument is seen: No line: mounted in the field, locally. Solid line: in the main control room panel. Dashed line: behind the panel or in a local panel. A circle inside a square: a function in the DCS or PLC, shown on the operator screen. Inside the bubble are letters and a loop number, following ISA-5.1. The first letter is what is measured; the following letters are what the instrument does. First letter (measured) Following letters (function) F flow, L level, P pressure, T temperature I indicate, R record, C control A analysis (O2, pH), S speed, W

t: Control loops and interlocks Going deeper
x: All instruments with the same number form one loop. Follow it: TE-101 senses the batch temperature, TT-101 sends it to the DCS, TIC-101 compares it with the set point, and TV-101 on the jacket cooling water opens or closes. Once you see a loop as sensor, controller and final element, every loop on the drawing reads the same way. Safety functions are drawn separately. An interlock or trip often appears as a diamond or a hexagon with a number (I-101) and a note, or as a separate safety instrumented function with its own sensor, such as TSHH-105 tripping the dosing valve XV-105. Check two things: Independence. Does the trip have its own sensor,

t: How to trace a line on site Going deeper
x: Start from a piece of equipment you can find on site, such as the reactor nozzle. Follow the line on the P&ID valve by valve, writing down the line number and each valve. On site, follow the same line. Every valve, instrument, reducer and branch should match the drawing, in the same order. Mark differences in red on a copy: a valve that doesn't exist, a bypass nobody drew, a temporary hose that became permanent. Send the marked-up copy for as-built correction through change control. On the plant New engineers learn a plant fastest by tracing lines with an experienced operator. It is also the cheapest HAZOP preparation there is: most surprises

Reading the P&ID as a layout and expecting things to be where they are drawn. Ignoring the piping class at the end of the line number. Missing the FC/FO label on a control valve. Treating a control alarm and a trip on the same sensor as two protections. Trusting a drawing that hasn't been walked since commissioning.

x: How to Read DSC, ARC, RC1 and TSU Data Process Safety · Thermal Hazards · October 2026 A thermal safety report lands on your desk: a DSC trace, an ARC plot on a log scale, an RC1 curve and a TSU pressure chart. Each says something different about the same chemistry, and each can mislead you if read carelessly. This article explains, from the basics, what each instrument does, how to read its key features, and which questions each one can and cannot answer. First, the desired reaction : how much heat does it release

s: How to Read DSC, ARC, RC1 and TSU Data
x: Two questions decide whether a process is thermally safe. First, the desired reaction : how much heat does it release, how fast, and how much could still be released if cooling failed? Second, the undesired reaction : at what temperature does the mixture start to decompose, how much energy and gas does that release, and how quickly does it run away? No single instrument answers both well, so we use a set: Test Sample What it measures Main question it answers DSC 2–10 mg, sealed crucible Heat flow while heating at a fixed rate Is there an exotherm, where, and how big? TSU A few grams, closed cell Temperature and pressure while heating Does dec

s: How to Read DSC, ARC, RC1 and TSU Data
x: Differential scanning calorimetry heats a few milligrams of sample and an empty reference side by side at a steady rate, typically 2–10 °C/min, and records the extra heat the sample absorbs or gives out. It is fast, cheap and needs very little material, so it is the first test for every intermediate, reaction mixture, distillation residue and isolated solid. Use a sealed high-pressure crucible (gold-plated steel is common) for anything containing solvent. In an open pan, the solvent evaporates with a large endotherm that can hide a decomposition exotherm completely.

t: Reading a DSC trace Working level
s: How to Read DSC, ARC, RC1 and TSU Data
x: Try it: pick an instrument and tap the numbered points on its curve. The curves are illustrative, not from a real compound. On a DSC trace (check the axis label: most safety labs plot exo up ), read four things: Endotherms (downward peaks): melting, boiling, desolvation. Not hazards themselves, but a melt just before a decomposition often means the decomposition is fast. Onset : where the exotherm leaves the baseline. It depends on heating rate and sensitivity. A DSC at 5 °C/min detects onset much later than the temperature at which a large, insulated plant batch would start to self-heat. It is a marker, never a safe operating limit. Energy :

t: TSU: screening for gas Working level
s: How to Read DSC, ARC, RC1 and TSU Data
x: A thermal screening unit (TSU) heats a few grams of sample in a closed metal cell, usually at a slow ramp (often around 1–2 °C/min), recording both temperature and pressure. It fills the gap between DSC and ARC. The pressure trace is the valuable part: Below the onset, pressure rises gently and reversibly with the solvent's vapour pressure. At the exotherm, temperature and pressure jump together. The rates dT/dt and dP/dt show how violent it is. After cooling back to room temperature, any pressure left is non-condensable gas . Gas generation often decides relief sizing and can be more dangerous than the heat itself.

t: RC1: the reaction as it runs Working level
s: How to Read DSC, ARC, RC1 and TSU Data
x: A reaction calorimeter such as the RC1 is a small jacketed reactor that runs the real process (same charges, temperatures and dosing) and measures the heat flow from the difference between reactor and jacket temperatures: q = UA × (Tr - Tj). A calibration heater of known power, fired before and after the reaction, gives UA. From one run you get: Reaction heat ΔHr in kJ/mol, from integrating the heat flow, and the adiabatic temperature rise. Heat release rate : the plateau during dosing tells you the cooling the plant must provide per kg. Thermal conversion and accumulation : heat still coming out after dosing stops is unreacted material. That

t: ARC: the runaway in slow motion Going deeper
s: How to Read DSC, ARC, RC1 and TSU Data
x: An accelerating rate calorimeter puts a few grams in a strong spherical bomb inside a heated chamber and runs heat-wait-search : heat by about 5 °C, wait for temperatures to settle, then search for self-heating above a threshold of about 0.02 °C/min. Once found, the heaters track the sample so it heats itself as if insulated. The result is the runaway in slow motion, plotted as self-heat rate (log scale) against temperature, plus pressure. Phi factor : the bomb absorbs part of the heat, so the sample looks milder than it would in a plant reactor. φ = 1 + (m·cp)bomb / (m·cp)sample, often 1.5–3 in an ARC and close to 1 for a plant vessel. Resul

s: How to Read DSC, ARC, RC1 and TSU Data
x: DSC every material and mixture, including residues and mother liquors that will be stored or distilled. If DSC shows a significant exotherm within reach of process conditions, run TSU or ARC for gas and kinetics. For every exothermic step, run RC1 under the planned dosing to get heat, accumulation and MTSR. Combine MTSR, MTT and TD24 into the criticality class, and size relief for the worst credible case. On the plant Ask for the raw curves, not only the summary table. A table that says “onset 228 °C, 650 J/g” hides whether the exotherm was sharp, whether a melt came first, and whether the sample was in a sealed crucible. Five minutes with th

x: Treating the DSC onset as a safe temperature. Testing solvent-containing samples in open DSC pans. Using ARC results without the phi-factor correction. Ignoring gas generation because the heat looked small. Testing only the pure product, not the reaction mixture, residues and mother liquors.

s: Safe hydrogenation: the N2-H2-N2 purge sequence, pyrophoric Pd/C and Raney nickel catalysts, charging and filtering, heat release and leak detection.
x: Hydrogenation Safety Process Safety · Hazardous Operations · October 2026 Hydrogenation is one of the most useful reactions in API manufacturing and one of the most unforgiving. It combines a gas that ignites from almost any spark with catalysts that can catch fire on their own in air, usually in a flammable solvent, under pressure. Most hydrogenation fires happen not during the reaction but before and after it: at charging, purging and filtration. This article explains why, and the procedures that prevent them. In this article Why hydrogen is different Basics The purge sequence Basics Pyrophoric catalysts Working level Charging and filtering catalyst safely Working level Heat, pressure and leaks Going deeper Questions people ask Why hydrogen is different Basics Very wide flammable range: about 4 to 75 % in air, compared with roughly 1 to 7 % for toluene. Tiny ignition energy: about 0.02

Very wide flammable range: about 4 to 75 % in air, compared with roughly 1 to 7 % for toluene. Tiny ignition energy: about 0.02 mJ, around ten times less than most solvent vapours. A static spark you would never feel is enough. Low LOC: about 5 % oxygen with nitrogen, lower than most solvents, so inerting must be tighter. Leaks easily: the smallest molecule, so it escapes through joints that hold other gases. It is lighter than air and collects under roofs. Nearly invisible flame in daylight.

The rule is simple: hydrogen and air must never meet in the vessel . Every hydrogenation follows the same pattern: Charge the vessel and inert it: pressure-purge with nitrogen, typically three cycles, until oxygen is below about 1 %. Pressure-purge with hydrogen to displace the nitrogen. React under hydrogen pressure. Vent the hydrogen to a safe location and purge with nitrogen until hydrogen is below a safe level (often under 1 %). Only then open the vessel or transfer the slurry for filtration. Try it: run the correct sequence, then skip the first nitrogen purge. The headspace passes through the flammable range as hydrogen enters air. Each

Palladium, platinum and nickel catalysts are pyrophoric: dry, and especially when they have absorbed hydrogen, they can heat up and ignite on contact with air. Add a flammable solvent and you have the fuel, the ignition source and the oxygen together. Pd/C and Pt/C are supplied about 50 % water-wet to reduce this risk. Keep them wet. Raney nickel is stored under water and is strongly pyrophoric when dry. Spent catalyst is more dangerous than fresh: it carries absorbed hydrogen and organic residue.

t: Charging and filtering catalyst safely Working level
x: Charge wet catalyst into an inerted vessel, ideally as a slurry in water or the reaction solvent through a closed charging system. Never sprinkle dry catalyst into a solvent in air. Filter under nitrogen in a closed filter: candle, sparkler or enclosed Nutsche. Open-top filtration of a catalyst slurry is a classic fire scenario. Never let the catalyst cake suck dry while air can reach it. Wash with solvent and then water, and keep the cake covered. Store spent catalyst under water in closed, labelled containers, and send it for recovery promptly. Earth the filter and the receiving vessel: catalyst slurry in a low-conductivity solvent charges

t: Heat, pressure and leaks Going deeper
x: Many hydrogenations are strongly exothermic; nitro reductions release over 500 kJ per mol of nitro group. Because the reaction usually can't go faster than hydrogen dissolves, the hydrogen feed rate and agitation control the heat release. That is useful, but it means an agitator restart after a stop, or a sudden pressure increase, can release accumulated heat quickly. See gas-liquid mass transfer . Pressure relief sized for the worst case, including runaway of the substrate if it is thermally unstable. Leak test the system with nitrogen at operating pressure before every campaign. Hydrogen detectors at high points, with ventilation and alarms

Introducing hydrogen into a vessel that was never purged with nitrogen. Letting the catalyst cake dry on the filter. Opening the reactor before purging out the hydrogen. Leak testing only once, at commissioning. Venting hydrogen inside a building or under a canopy.

s: Nitrogen inerting basics: the flammability diagram, LOC and safe oxygen targets, pressure, vacuum and sweep purging, blanketing and O2 measurement.
x: Inerting and Limiting Oxygen Concentration Process Safety · Fire and Explosion · October 2026 “The reactor is under nitrogen.” Everyone in a solvent plant has said it, and it is one of the most reassuring and least checked sentences in process safety. Inerting is powerful: take enough oxygen away and solvent vapour simply cannot burn, whatever sparks fly. But it only works if the oxygen really is low, and the only way to know is to understand the numbers and measure them. This article explains both. In this article Why removing oxygen works Basics The flammability diagram Basics How low is low enough? Working level Getting there: three ways to purge Working level Staying there: blanketing and leaks Working level Measuring oxygen, and the hazard to people Going deeper Questions people ask Why removing oxygen works Basics A fire needs fuel, oxygen and an ignition source. In a solvent plant

A fire needs fuel, oxygen and an ignition source. In a solvent plant, fuel is always present and ignition sources are hard to eliminate completely: static, hot surfaces, sparks from metal, a pyrophoric catalyst. Oxygen is the one side of the triangle we can control reliably, by replacing air with nitrogen. You don't need to remove all the oxygen. Below a certain level, the flame can't sustain itself because there isn't enough oxygen to release heat faster than the surrounding gas absorbs it. That level is the limiting oxygen concentration (LOC) .

Picture a chart with solvent vapour along the bottom and oxygen up the side. Mixtures of solvent with plain air lie on a line that starts at 21 % oxygen and falls slightly as vapour displaces air. Along that line, the mixture burns only between the lower flammable limit (LFL) and the upper flammable limit (UFL) : around 1–7 % for toluene, 6–36 % for methanol. Add nitrogen and you move downward. The flammable range narrows as oxygen falls, until the LFL and UFL boundaries meet at a nose. The oxygen level at that nose is the LOC. Below it, no solvent concentration can burn. Try it: the shaded region is flammable for a typical solvent. Move the

t: How low is low enough? Working level
x: Operating right at the LOC leaves no room for error: a small leak, a slow analyser or a gust of air through a manhole would put you into the flammable region. NFPA 69 sets the margin: With continuous O2 monitoring: operate at least 2 percentage points below LOC Without continuous monitoring: no more than 60 % of LOC For LOC = 10 %: 8 % with an analyser and interlock, 6 % without. Many plants simply use 5 % as a standard target for all solvent work. That is easier to remember and gives margin for hydrogen-free systems, but check it against the LOC if hydrogen or another low-LOC gas can be present.

t: Getting there: three ways to purge Working level
x: Pressure purging Pressurise the vessel with nitrogen, let it mix, vent back to atmosphere, repeat. Each cycle reduces the oxygen by the ratio of the absolute pressures: O2 after n cycles = O2 initial × (Plow / Phigh)^n Purging to 2 barg (3.01 bar abs) and venting to 1.01 bar abs multiplies the oxygen by 0.34 each cycle: 21 → 7.1 → 2.4 %. Two cycles reach a 5 % target. Check the vessel's rating first: a glass-lined reactor or a vessel with a sight glass may not take 2 barg. Try it: change the nitrogen pressure and run the purge. Higher pressure means fewer cycles, but more nitrogen per cycle. Vacuum purging Pull a vacuum, break it with nitroge

t: Staying there: blanketing and leaks Working level
x: Purging gets the oxygen down; blanketing keeps it down. A small nitrogen pressure (typically 20–100 mbarg) held by a regulator stops air coming in as the vessel breathes. Every time something happens, ask whether oxygen came in: Opening a manhole to charge solids lets air in. Keep a nitrogen flow at the manhole while it is open, or use a closed charging system, and re-purge before heating. Cooling a vessel under a fixed amount of gas pulls a vacuum, which pulls air through any leak. Keep the blanket supply open while cooling. Drawing liquid out lowers the pressure the same way. Vacuum distillation pulls in air through every leaking gland and

t: Measuring oxygen, and the hazard to people Going deeper
x: Without a measurement, “inerted” is a hope. Options range from a portable analyser used to check after each purge, to a fixed analyser on the vent line, interlocked to stop heating or charging if oxygen rises. Calibrate it regularly, check that the sample point represents the vessel (not just the nitrogen inlet), and remember that solvent vapour in the sample can affect some sensors. The same nitrogen that protects the vessel kills people. Air with less than about 18 % oxygen impairs judgement, and a few breaths of near-pure nitrogen cause collapse without warning, because the body senses carbon dioxide, not low oxygen. Treat an inerted vesse

Assuming the vessel is inert because nitrogen was connected, without measuring. Forgetting to re-purge after opening a manhole for charging. Breaking vacuum with air after distillation. Assuming a mixture above the UFL is safe. Treating nitrogen as harmless around people.

s: How plant instruments measure pressure, temperature, level and flow: RTDs, thermocouples, DP, radar, magnetic, Coriolis and vortex meters, calibration.
x: Process Instrumentation Basics Plant Engineering · Instrumentation · October 2026 Every decision on a plant starts with a number from an instrument. When that number is wrong, everything built on it is wrong too: the batch goes off temperature, the tank overflows, the yield seems to fall. Instrument engineers don’t need to be the only ones who understand how these readings are made. This article covers the four main measurements, how each instrument works, and where each one fools people. In this article Pressure Basics Temperature Basics Level Working level Flow Working level Accuracy, turndown and calibration Going deeper Questions people ask Pressure Basics Know which pressure you are reading. Gauge pressure (barg) is relative to the atmosphere; absolute pressure (bar abs, mbar abs) is relative to vacuum. For vacuum work always use absolute transmitters: a gauge reading of -0.95 bar m

Know which pressure you are reading. Gauge pressure (barg) is relative to the atmosphere; absolute pressure (bar abs, mbar abs) is relative to vacuum. For vacuum work always use absolute transmitters: a gauge reading of -0.95 bar means a different absolute pressure on different days and at different altitudes. Bourdon gauges for local reading; transmitters (strain gauge or capacitance sensors) send 4–20 mA signals to the DCS. Diaphragm seals protect the sensor from corrosive, crystallising or viscous fluids. The fill fluid adds temperature error and slows the response. A pressure gauge on the suction of every important pump is worth its cost

RTD (Pt100): platinum resistance; accurate and stable, the usual choice up to about 400 °C. Thermocouple: two dissimilar metals produce a voltage; robust, wide range, less accurate. Type K is common for high temperatures. Thermowell: protects the sensor but adds delay. A heavy thermowell in a slow-moving liquid can lag the real temperature by minutes, which matters a great deal in an exothermic reaction. In glass-lined reactors the temperature probe is usually inside a baffle. If the baffle isn't covered by liquid at low volume, it reads vapour temperature, not batch temperature.

Differential pressure: level = ΔP / (ρ g). Accurate only if the density is right; a change from water to toluene (1,000 to 867 kg/m³) shifts the reading by 15 %. Radar (non-contact) and guided-wave radar: unaffected by density; foam, vapour and agitators can confuse non-contact radar. Load cells: weigh the whole vessel; excellent for batch charging and mass balances, but piping stresses, nitrogen pressure and agitator vibration affect them. Sight glass and level gauges: local check; keep them clean and protected. Level switches for high-high trips should be independent of the level transmitter used for control.

Meter How it works Good for Limitations Orifice plate (DP) Flow ∝ √ΔP across a restriction Clean liquids, gases, steam; cheap Narrow turndown (about 3–4:1); permanent pressure loss Magnetic Voltage induced in a conductive liquid moving through a magnetic field Water, aqueous solutions, slurries Does not work with solvents and other non-conductive liquids Coriolis Mass flow from the twisting of vibrating tubes Mass flow and density of any liquid; batch dosing Cost; pressure drop in small sizes Vortex Frequency of vortices shed from a bluff body Steam, gases, clean liquids Needs a minimum velocity Rotameter Float rises in a tapered tube Local i

t: Accuracy, turndown and calibration Going deeper
x: Read the accuracy statement carefully. “±0.1 % of span” means the same absolute error at every reading, so the relative error grows at low readings. “±0.2 % of reading” stays proportional. For an orifice meter at 10 % flow, the DP is only 1 % of span, and a ±0.1 % of span transmitter gives about ±5 % error in flow. Turndown is the ratio of maximum to minimum flow the meter can measure accurately. Size meters for the normal flow, not the design maximum times a safety factor, or the plant will spend its life at the bottom of the range. Calibration checks the instrument against a reference; a loop check confirms that the value in the DCS matches

Magnetic flowmeters on solvent lines. DP level transmitters left calibrated for the wrong density. Gauge-pressure transmitters for vacuum control. Orifice meters sized for the maximum and run at 10 % flow. Control and trip sharing one level transmitter.

s: Reactor jackets, limpet (half-pipe) coils, dimple jackets and internal coils: jacket velocity, film coefficients, overall U and multi-fluid service.
x: Reactor Jackets and Limpet Coils Process Design · Heat Transfer · October 2026 Heat-up and cool-down times on a plant reactor are often blamed on the vessel size or the glass lining. Sometimes the real culprit is the jacket: cooling water creeping through a wide annulus at a few centimetres per second. This article explains the main jacket types, why velocity on the jacket side matters, and when it stops mattering. In this article Jacket types Basics Why jacket-side velocity matters Basics Film coefficients and overall U Working level Steam, water, brine and thermic fluid Working level Multi-fluid jackets and practical problems Going deeper Questions people ask Jacket types Basics Conventional jacket: an outer shell around the vessel, with a gap of typically 50–100 mm. Simple and cheap, good for steam. For liquids, the flow area is huge and the velocity very low unless agitation nozzles

Conventional jacket: an outer shell around the vessel, with a gap of typically 50–100 mm. Simple and cheap, good for steam. For liquids, the flow area is huge and the velocity very low unless agitation nozzles or a spiral baffle are fitted. Half-pipe or limpet coil: a pipe cut in half lengthwise and welded in a spiral around the vessel. Small flow area, so high velocity and good heat transfer with liquids. Strong, so it suits high-pressure utilities and thin vessel walls. Dimple jacket: a thin sheet with pressed dimples welded to the vessel. Light and cheap, used for moderate pressures. Internal coils: extra area inside the vessel, at the cos

Take a 3 m³ vessel, 1.6 m in diameter. A 50 mm conventional jacket has a flow area of about 0.27 m². Twenty m³/h of cooling water flows through it at about 0.02 m/s: barely moving. The jacket-side film coefficient is then only a few hundred W/m²K, set mostly by natural convection. The same 20 m³/h through an 80 NB half-pipe coil (flow area about 0.0024 m²) runs at over 2 m/s, and the film coefficient rises to around 7,500 W/m²K. Agitation nozzles in a conventional jacket, which inject water tangentially to create swirl, give something in between. Try it: change the cooling water flow and compare the overall U for three jacket designs on the s

t: Film coefficients and overall U Working level
x: 1/U = 1/hprocess + twall/kwall + Rfouling + 1/hjacket The overall coefficient is limited by the worst resistance. With a slow conventional jacket, the jacket side dominates and U is about 220 W/m²K. With agitation nozzles, U roughly doubles. With a half-pipe coil, the jacket side almost disappears from the sum, and U is limited by the process side and the wall: about 550 W/m²K in this example. Going faster on the jacket side beyond this gains little. For glass-lined vessels, the glass layer (about 1–2 mm, with thermal conductivity around 1 W/m·K) adds a resistance of the same order as the process film, so U is usually 200–400 W/m²K whatever t

t: Steam, water, brine and thermic fluid Working level
x: Steam: condensing film coefficients are very high, so a conventional jacket is fine. Inlet at the top, condensate out at the bottom through a steam trap. Air and non-condensables must be vented or they blanket the surface. Cooling water and chilled water: velocity matters, as above. Inlet at the bottom so the jacket stays full and air is pushed out at the top. Brine and glycol: more viscous at low temperature, so film coefficients are lower; velocity matters even more. Thermic fluid (hot oil): for temperatures above about 180 °C without high-pressure steam. Lower film coefficients than steam; usually in half-pipe coils.

t: Multi-fluid jackets and practical problems Going deeper
x: Most multi-purpose reactors switch the same jacket between steam, water and brine. That is convenient but causes trouble if not done carefully: Drain and blow out the previous fluid before switching. Water left in a jacket that receives brine dilutes the brine and can freeze; steam into a jacket full of brine causes water hammer. Thermal shock: switching from steam to cold brine on a glass-lined vessel can crack the glass. Respect the manufacturer's temperature-difference limits. See glass-lined reactor care . Fouling: cooling tower water scales jackets over the years. A periodic acid clean of the jacket, done under a permit, can restore a su

Expecting good cooling from water in a conventional jacket with no nozzles. Feeding cooling water from the top and trapping air. Switching utilities without draining the previous fluid. Blaming the glass for slow cooling without checking the jacket side. Never cleaning scaled jackets.

t: Lab to Plant Scale-up: What Changes
s: Why reactions behave differently at plant scale: area to volume, heat-up, mixing, dosing and solids, with a practical tech transfer checklist.
x: Lab to Plant Scale-up: What Changes Scale-up · Technology Transfer · October 2026 The chemist hands over a procedure that works perfectly in a 1-litre flask. The first plant batch takes three times longer, gives a sticky solid that won't filter and misses the impurity limit. Nobody did anything wrong. The chemistry is the same, but almost everything around it has changed. This article explains what changes with scale, why, and how to check it before the first plant batch instead of after. What does

t: The chemistry stays, the physics changes Basics
s: Lab to Plant Scale-up: What Changes
x: Reaction kinetics, equilibrium and solubility don't depend on the size of the vessel. What does depend on size is everything that moves heat and material around: how fast you can heat or cool, how quickly a drop of reagent mixes in, how long a transfer takes, how deep the filter cake is. In the lab these are so fast that they disappear. In the plant they can become slower than the chemistry, and then they control the result. So the question for every step is: in the lab, which was faster, the chemistry or the physics? And will that still be true in the plant?

s: Lab to Plant Scale-up: What Changes
x: Make a vessel twice as wide (keeping the same shape) and its volume grows eight times, but its wall area only four times. Volume grows with the cube of size, area with the square. So the cooling area per litre falls as the vessel gets bigger: Area per volume ∝ V^-1/3 From 1 L to 6,000 L: 6,000^1/3 ≈ 18, so about 18 times less jacket area per litre. That has three consequences. Heating and cooling take roughly 18 times longer for the same temperature difference (and plant jackets often have a lower U than a thin glass flask in a bath, so it can be worse). An exotherm that a flask absorbed easily may exceed the plant's cooling. And a quench or

s: Lab to Plant Scale-up: What Changes
x: A magnetic stirrer in a flask blends in a few seconds. A plant reactor at a typical power input takes tens of seconds to a few minutes; at the same power per volume, blend time grows roughly with V^2/9, about 7 times from 1 L to 6,000 L, and much more if the agitator is less powerful per litre than the lab. This matters when: a fast reaction competes with a side reaction , and local excess reagent near the feed point favours the impurity. Feed below the surface near the impeller, not onto the surface; two liquid phases need to stay dispersed for the reaction to proceed; solids need to stay suspended , especially dense catalysts or heavy cryst

t: Solids: crystallisation, filtration and drying Working level
s: Lab to Plant Scale-up: What Changes
x: Solids cause more scale-up failures than reactions do. Slower cooling in the plant changes the supersaturation profile, so crystals nucleate differently: often finer, sometimes a different polymorph. Fines filter slowly; filtration time grows with the square of the cake depth, and a plant centrifuge or filter-dryer cake is far deeper than a Buchner funnel's. Wash efficiency falls in deep cakes, and drying a deep bed takes much longer than a thin layer in a lab oven. Run the lab crystallisation at the plant's real cooling rate and agitation, and measure filtration resistance (see the filtration article ). Seed at a defined temperature to contr

s: Lab to Plant Scale-up: What Changes
x: Everything takes longer in the plant: charging 200 kg of solid by hand, transferring 4,000 L through a 50 mm line, sampling and waiting for the lab, heating, cooling. A reaction mixture that sat for 20 minutes in the lab may sit for 8 hours in the plant, sometimes overnight. If the product, an intermediate or a reagent degrades in that time, the impurity profile changes. Ask the chemists for hold-time studies : keep each key mixture at its process temperature for several times the expected plant duration and measure what happens. It is cheap in the lab and saves batches. On the plant The best technology transfer meetings I've seen include an

s: Lab to Plant Scale-up: What Changes
x: Safety Reaction calorimetry for every exothermic step: heat, accumulation, MTSR, gas evolution. DSC/ARC on reaction mixtures, isolated intermediates and residues. Criticality class for each step, and the relief scenario it implies. Flash points, static risk, inerting needs and dust explosion data for powders. Equipment fit Minimum stir volume and maximum working volume of each vessel at every step, including after distillation. Jacket service (steam, hot water, brine) and the temperatures it can reach. Materials of construction: glass-lined, SS316, Hastelloy; gaskets and seals compatible with every chemical and solvent. Filter or centrifuge a

s: Lab to Plant Scale-up: What Changes
x: Copying lab addition times into the plant batch record. Assuming the lab crystallisation will filter the same at plant scale. No hold-time data, so a weekend stop becomes a failed batch. Checking that the batch fits the reactor at the start, but not after a distillation or a dilution. Reaction safety data done after the first plant batch instead of before.

s: Line sizing basics: recommended velocities, Reynolds number, friction factor, the Darcy equation, fittings and static-safe velocities for solvents.
x: Line Sizing and Pressure Drop Process Design · Fluid Flow · October 2026 Choosing a pipe size looks like a small decision, but it fixes the pump head, the energy bill, whether the pump cavitates, whether a solvent line charges up with static, and whether the line erodes or blocks. Most of it comes down to one number, velocity, and one equation for friction. This article goes through both, with the rules of thumb engineers actually use.
