Typical design velocities for liquids: Service Ty

v = Q / A = 4Q / (π D²) v in m/s, Q in m³/s, D the pipe's inside diameter in m (not the nominal size). Typical design velocities for liquids: Service Typical velocity Why Pump suction 0.6–1.5 m/s Low friction keeps NPSH available high Pump discharge 1.5–3 m/s Balance of pipe cost and pumping energy Gravity drain 0.3–1 m/s Little head available; avoid running full of vapour Cooling water headers 1.5–2.5 m/s High enough to limit fouling Low-conductivity solvent into a tank ≤ 1 m/s until the inlet is submerged Static charge generation For 20 m³/h of water: 40 NB gives 4.2 m/s (too fast), 50 NB 2.6 m/s (good for a discharge), 80 NB 1.2 m/s (good

t: Reynolds number: laminar or turbulent Basics
x: Re = ρ v D / μ Below about 2,300 the flow is laminar: smooth layers, friction proportional to velocity. Above about 4,000 it is turbulent: eddies, friction roughly proportional to velocity squared. Water at 2.6 m/s in a 50 NB line has Re ≈ 135,000, well into turbulence. A 100 cP oil at the same velocity has Re ≈ 1,200, which is laminar, and behaves very differently.

t: Friction loss: the Darcy equation Working level
x: ΔP = f × (L / D) × ρ v² / 2 f is the Darcy friction factor: 64/Re for laminar flow; for turbulent flow from the Moody chart or the Colebrook or Swamee-Jain equations, depending on Re and the pipe roughness (about 0.045 mm for commercial steel). For 20 m³/h of water in 50 NB steel, f ≈ 0.02 and the loss is about 1.3 bar per 100 m. In 80 NB it falls to about 0.18 bar per 100 m. That is the trade-off: friction falls steeply with diameter (roughly as D^-5 at constant flow), while pipe cost rises with diameter. Velocities of 1.5–3 m/s for pumped liquids sit near the economic optimum for typical plant lengths.

t: Fittings, valves and equivalent length Working level
x: Elbows, tees, valves, strainers and entrances add loss. Two ways to include it: K values: ΔP = K × ρ v²/2 for each fitting. Typical K: standard 90° elbow 0.3–0.75, open gate valve 0.15, open globe valve 6–10, swing check 2, tank entrance 0.5, exit 1. Equivalent length: each fitting adds the friction of a straight length, for example about 30 pipe diameters for an elbow. In compact plant piping, fittings often account for more loss than the straight pipe. A Y-strainer that is half blocked can account for more than everything else together; that's why strainers get differential pressure gauges.

t: Special cases: solvents, slurries, viscous liquids, gases Going deeper
x: Solvents and static: keep low-conductivity solvents at 1 m/s or less into tanks until the fill pipe is submerged, and at most about 7 m/s anywhere. See static electricity . Slurries: keep velocity above the settling velocity of the solids, often 1.5–2.5 m/s, and avoid dead legs and low points where solids collect. Viscous liquids: flow is often laminar and loss rises with viscosity; heat tracing or a larger line can save a lot of pump power. Use a positive displacement pump. Gases and vapours: much higher velocities (10–30 m/s for process gas, lower for vacuum lines where every millibar matters). Vacuum lines from a condenser to the pump shou

Using the nominal size instead of the inside diameter. Sizing pump suction lines like discharge lines. Ignoring fittings and strainers in compact piping. Filling solvent tanks at high velocity through a top nozzle. Forgetting that viscous liquids may be laminar.

s: LOPA basics: scenarios, initiating event frequencies, independent protection layers, tolerable risk targets, and what SIL 1 and SIL 2 really mean.
x: LOPA and SIL Basics Process Safety · Risk Assessment · October 2026 A HAZOP finds a scenario: cooling water fails during dosing and the reactor could run away. Everyone agrees it is serious. But is the alarm enough? Do we need a trip? How reliable must it be? LOPA, layer of protection analysis, answers those questions with simple arithmetic instead of opinion. This article shows how it works and what a SIL rating actually means. In this article The idea: layers like slices of cheese Basics What counts as a protection layer Basics The LOPA arithmetic Working level Closing the gap: SIF and SIL Working level Keeping the SIL real Going deeper Questions people ask The idea: layers like slices of cheese Basics No single safeguard is perfect. The alarm might be ignored, the trip valve might stick, the rupture disc might be the wrong size. A plant is safe when there are enough independent layers

t: The idea: layers like slices of cheese Basics
x: No single safeguard is perfect. The alarm might be ignored, the trip valve might stick, the rupture disc might be the wrong size. A plant is safe when there are enough independent layers that the chance of all of them failing together is very small. Picture slices of Swiss cheese: an accident happens only when the holes line up. LOPA puts numbers on this. Start with how often the cause happens, multiply by the chance each layer fails when needed, and compare the result with what the company accepts as tolerable.

t: What counts as a protection layer Basics
x: Only independent protection layers (IPLs) get credit. A safeguard is an IPL only if it is: Independent of the initiating event and of the other layers. A high-temperature alarm on the same sensor as the control loop that failed is not independent. Effective : able to stop the scenario on its own, in time, if it works. An operator needs a clear alarm and enough time, often at least 10 minutes, to act. Auditable : tested and maintained, with records. Typical credits, as probability of failure on demand (PFD): Layer Typical PFD Risk reduction Alarm with operator response (enough time, clear procedure) 0.1 10× Basic process control system functio

Frequency of outcome = initiating event frequency × PFD1 × PFD2 × … × conditional modifiers Conditional modifiers include the probability that someone is present (occupancy) or that a release ignites. Use them with care and only where justified. Take the scenario: cooling water fails during exothermic dosing (0.1 per year, a typical value for a utility failure), leading to a runaway that could rupture the reactor and kill an operator. The company's tolerable frequency for a single fatality is 10^-5 per year. High-temperature alarm, operator stops dosing: × 0.1 Area manned half the time: × 0.5 Result: 0.1 × 0.1 × 0.5 = 5 × 10^-3 per year, 500

t: Closing the gap: SIF and SIL Working level
x: When the existing layers don't reach the target, the usual answer is a safety instrumented function (SIF) : its own sensor, logic solver and final element, separate from the control system. Its safety integrity level (SIL) is set by the risk reduction still needed: Gap up to 10×: no SIF needed if another IPL can do it; otherwise SIL 1 is ample. Gap of 10–100×: SIL 1. Gap of 100–1,000×: SIL 2. Gap above 1,000×: SIL 3 is possible but rare and expensive in chemical plants; usually it is better to change the process (smaller batch, slower dosing, a different solvent). SIL is a property of the whole function, not of a transmitter. A SIL 2 sensor c

t: Keeping the SIL real Going deeper
x: Proof testing at the interval the calculation assumed, testing the whole loop from sensor to valve, with results recorded. Bypass management : a bypassed SIF provides no protection. Bypasses need permits, compensating measures and a time limit. Demand tracking : if the SIF trips more often than the LOPA assumed, the initiating frequency was wrong and the analysis must be redone. Management of change for set points, logic and hardware. See management of change . On the plant The most useful LOPA output is often not the SIL number but the list of layers you were already relying on. Each one becomes a safety-critical element with an owner and a

Giving credit to two layers that share a sensor or valve. Counting procedures and training as protection layers. Using a fire-sized relief valve as a layer for a runaway. Specifying a SIL and never proof testing the loop. Stacking optimistic conditional modifiers to make the numbers work.

s: Management of change in process plants: what counts as a change, temporary and organisational changes, MOC steps to PSSR, and Flixborough lessons.
x: Management of Change (MOC) Process Safety · Safety Management · October 2026 A plant that is safe on the day it is commissioned does not stay safe by itself. Every week someone swaps a valve, changes a set point, tries a new supplier or adds a hose “for now”. Each change on its own looks harmless. Management of change is the habit of stopping for a moment before each one and asking: what else does this affect? This article explains what counts as a change, how a good MOC works, and why it fails. In this article Why changes cause accidents Basics What counts as a change Basics The MOC steps Working level What a good review asks Working level Temporary, emergency and organisational changes Going deeper Flixborough: a temporary pipe Going deeper Questions people ask Why changes cause accidents Basics When a plant is designed, engineers think through how each part interacts with the others:

When a plant is designed, engineers think through how each part interacts with the others: the relief valve is sized for the nitrogen regulator, the pump for the line, the trip for the reaction. Those links are rarely written on the equipment. When one part is changed without looking at the links, the plant quietly loses protection it used to have, and nobody notices until the day it is needed. Investigations of major accidents keep finding the same thing: a change made with good intentions, by competent people, without anyone asking what else it affected.

t: What counts as a change Basics
x: Anything that alters the plant, the process or the way it is run, compared with what was reviewed and approved. That includes: Equipment and piping: new or modified equipment, a different material, a bigger pump, removed or added valves. Process conditions: temperatures, pressures, dosing times, batch sizes, beyond the approved range. Chemistry and materials: new solvents, reagents, suppliers or grades; a new product in an existing reactor. Controls and safeguards: set points, alarm limits, interlock logic, bypasses, relief devices. Procedures: changed sequences, skipped steps, new cleaning methods. Organisation: fewer operators per shift, a

Request: describe the change, why it is needed and what it replaces. Attach marked-up drawings. Classify: is it in kind? Minor or major? Permanent or temporary? The class decides how deep the review goes. Hazard review: a checklist for small changes, a what-if or HAZOP for larger ones, and reaction safety data for chemistry changes. Approve: by people with the authority and the knowledge, from production, engineering and safety, and quality where product is affected. Implement: build or change it as approved, not as convenient on the day. Pre-startup safety review (PSSR): walk it down before use. Built as approved? Drawings, SOPs and batch re

t: What a good review asks Working level
x: Does it change the relief scenarios or the relief load? (A bigger nitrogen regulator, a higher steam pressure.) See relief valve sizing . Does it change the reaction hazard : heat, gas, accumulation, MTSR? Does it remove or weaken a safeguard , even temporarily? Does it bring a new ignition source , flammable atmosphere or static risk? Are the materials compatible: pressure rating, temperature, corrosion, gaskets? Who needs to know? Procedures, drawings and training to update. On the plant The best MOC systems are quick for small changes and thorough for big ones. If filling in the form for a gasket takes a week, people stop filling it in, an

t: Temporary, emergency and organisational changes Going deeper
x: Temporary changes need the same hazard review as permanent ones, plus an expiry date and a named person responsible for removing them. Temporary hoses, bypasses and jumpers have a way of becoming permanent. Emergency changes , made at night to keep a batch safe, can be approved by a shift manager under a short procedure, but must go through the full review within a defined time, typically a day or two. Organisational changes are the most often missed: cutting a shift crew, outsourcing maintenance, or losing the one engineer who understood an old process. Ask the same question: which safeguards depended on these people or this knowledge?

t: Flixborough: a temporary pipe Going deeper
x: On 1 June 1974, at the Nypro plant in Flixborough, England, a cracked cyclohexane reactor was removed from a train of six. To keep production going, the engineers bridged the gap with a 20-inch temporary pipe with bellows at each end, supported on scaffolding. No design calculation was done for the bellows or the pipe under pressure, and no qualified engineer reviewed it. Two months later the bypass failed, releasing tonnes of cyclohexane, and the vapour cloud exploded. Twenty-eight people died and the site was destroyed. The investigation's lesson shaped modern MOC: a modification must be designed and reviewed to the same standard as the ori

Calling a different specification “like for like”. Temporary changes with no end date. Changing set points and alarm limits without MOC. MOC closed before drawings and SOPs are updated. Never applying MOC to staffing or organisational changes.

t: Material and Energy Balance for Batch Plants
s: Material and energy balances for batch plants: boundaries, batch mass balance and closure, solvent component balances and a distillation energy balance.
x: Material and Energy Balance for Batch Plants Plant Engineering · Fundamentals · October 2026 Every chemical engineer learns material balances in the first year, then meets a real plant where the numbers never add up. 3,800 kg go into the reactor and only 3,670 kg come out the other end, and nobody can say where the rest went. Those missing kilograms are money, solvent emissions and sometimes a safety problem. This article shows how to do a balance that is useful on a real batch plant, and how to find what is missing. In this article The idea: what goes in comes out Basics Draw the boundary first Basics A batch mass balance Working level Component balances: following the solvent Working level The energy balance of a distillation Working level Finding the missing kilograms Going deeper Questions people ask The idea: what goes in comes out Basics Mass is conserved. For any part of a plant o

t: The idea: what goes in comes out Basics
s: Material and Energy Balance for Batch Plants
x: Mass is conserved. For any part of a plant over any period: In - Out + Generated - Consumed = Accumulated For total mass, nothing is generated or consumed by a chemical reaction, so for a complete batch (empty to empty) the balance is simply In = Out . For a single chemical, reactions do create and destroy it, so its balance needs the generation and consumption terms from the stoichiometry. Energy follows the same rule: heat in from steam, plus heat released by reaction, equals heat out to cooling water and surroundings, plus the change in the batch's own heat content.

s: Material and Energy Balance for Batch Plants
x: Most balance arguments are really arguments about the boundary. Before writing any numbers, draw a box on the process flow diagram and decide: What is inside: one reactor, a whole stage, or the whole plant? Over what period: one batch, a campaign, a month? Monthly balances smooth out batch-to-batch hold-up. Every stream crossing the line: raw materials, solvents, washes, nitrogen, water, steam condensate, vents, samples, effluent, product, residues. The streams people forget are almost always the small ones crossing the boundary sideways: the line wash, the sample, the vent to the scrubber, the water used to rinse the filter.

t: A batch mass balance Working level
s: Material and Energy Balance for Batch Plants
x: Take a reaction stage. Into the reactor go 500 kg of starting material, 300 kg of reagent, 400 kg of caustic lye, 2,000 kg of toluene and 600 kg of water: 3,800 kg in total. Out come 520 kg of dry product, 1,850 kg of recovered toluene, 1,160 kg of aqueous layer to the ETP and 140 kg of distillation residue: 3,670 kg. Closure = total out / total in × 100 = 3,670 / 3,800 = 96.6 % 130 kg unaccounted per batch. A batch balance closing within about 97–103 % is good, given weighing and level-gauge accuracy. Below that, something is being missed or lost. Try it: change how much toluene is recovered and how much dry product is made. Watch the unacco

t: Component balances: following the solvent Working level
s: Material and Energy Balance for Batch Plants
x: A total balance can close even when individual components don't, because errors cancel. To reduce consumption you need a balance on each important component, and toluene is the obvious one here: In: 2,000 kg charged (fresh plus recovered). Out: 1,850 kg recovered, plus toluene dissolved in the aqueous layer (toluene's solubility in water is about 0.05 %, so under 1 kg), plus toluene in the wet cake before drying, plus toluene in the residue, plus vapour lost through vents and vacuum. Analyse each stream: GC on the aqueous layer and residue, LOD and GC on the wet cake, and a vent estimate from the condenser outlet temperature (see the vacuum s

t: The energy balance of a distillation Working level
s: Material and Energy Balance for Batch Plants
x: Energy balances answer questions like “how much steam does this distillation need?” and “is the condenser big enough?”. Heat needed = mbatch × cp × (Tboil - Tstart) + mdistilled × λsolvent Steam = heat needed / λsteam × (1 + losses) Distilling 1,850 kg of toluene (λ ≈ 360 kJ/kg at atmospheric pressure) takes 1,850 × 360 ≈ 666 MJ of latent heat. With steam at about 3.5 barg (λ ≈ 2,130 kJ/kg) that is 313 kg of steam, plus roughly 10–15 % for losses and heating the vessel: about 360 kg. Add the sensible heat to bring the batch up to boiling if it starts cold. The condenser has to remove the same 666 MJ. With cooling water warming by 8 °C: 666,00

t: Finding the missing kilograms Going deeper
s: Material and Energy Balance for Batch Plants
x: Check the measurements. Load cells drift; level gauges on agitated, foaming or jacketed vessels are often several percent out; drum weights are sometimes assumed rather than weighed. Calibrate before chasing losses. Check hold-up. A batch balance is only exact from empty to empty. Material left in the reactor, filter, lines and dryer from one batch shows up in the next. Use campaign balances to average it out. List the unrecorded streams. Line washes, filter washes, samples, spillage, nitrogen sweeping vapour to the vent. Look at the vents. Every vessel that breathes during charging, heating or nitrogen purging carries solvent vapour out. Wit

s: Material and Energy Balance for Batch Plants
x: Starting with numbers before agreeing the boundary. Balancing total mass and never balancing the components. Forgetting gases given off by the reaction. Treating a 5 % gap as “normal losses” year after year. Estimating steam from the latent heat alone, without the losses and sensible heat.

s: Choosing materials of construction: SS304 and SS316L, duplex, Hastelloy, titanium, glass-lined steel, PTFE and FRP, corrosion types, PREN and gaskets.
x: Materials of Construction Plant Engineering · Materials · October 2026 “Use SS316, it’s stainless.” Many corrosion failures start with that sentence. Stainless steel resists a lot, but chlorides, hot caustic and reducing acids can destroy it quickly, while cheap carbon steel happily holds strong sulphuric acid. This article explains how the common plant materials behave, the forms of corrosion that catch people out, and how to choose. In this article The common materials Basics Forms of corrosion Basics Choosing by service Working level Gaskets, seals and linings Working level Checking and monitoring Going deeper Questions people ask The common materials Basics Carbon steel: cheap and strong. Fine for neutral solvents, steam, strong sulphuric acid at ambient, caustic at moderate temperature. Rusts in water and dilute acids. SS304 / SS316L: chromium forms a thin passive oxide film that pr

Carbon steel: cheap and strong. Fine for neutral solvents, steam, strong sulphuric acid at ambient, caustic at moderate temperature. Rusts in water and dilute acids. SS304 / SS316L: chromium forms a thin passive oxide film that protects the steel. Molybdenum in 316 improves resistance to chlorides. “L” means low carbon, which avoids corrosion at welds. Duplex stainless (2205): stronger and much more resistant to chloride stress-corrosion cracking than 316L. Nickel alloys (Hastelloy C-276, C-22): resist chlorides, many reducing acids and mixed acid streams. Expensive, used where stainless fails. Titanium: excellent in chlorides, wet chlorine a

General corrosion: even thinning, predictable from corrosion rate tables and coupons. See the corrosion coupon calculator . Pitting: local holes where the passive film breaks down, typically caused by chlorides. Can perforate a vessel while the rest looks perfect. The pitting resistance equivalent number, PREN = %Cr + 3.3 × %Mo + 16 × %N, ranks alloys: about 24 for 316L, 35 for duplex 2205, over 40 for super-duplex and Hastelloy. Stress-corrosion cracking (SCC): cracks from the combination of tensile stress and a specific environment, such as chlorides with 304/316 above about 50–60 °C, or hot caustic with carbon steel. Sudden and dangerous.

Try it: pick a service and see how the common materials generally behave. This is a first guide only; concentration, temperature and impurities change the answer. Selection should follow the worst condition the equipment will see, not the normal one: the cleaning cycle, the start-up with concentrated acid, the hot spot near the steam inlet, the chloride left from a previous product. In a multi-purpose plant, list every chemical the equipment may meet, including cleaning agents, and check them all. The materials compatibility tool helps with that list.

t: Gaskets, seals and linings Working level
x: A vessel in Hastelloy with the wrong gasket still leaks. Elastomers are usually the weakest link: EPDM: good for water, steam, dilute acids and alkali; swells in hydrocarbons and oils. Viton (FKM): good for hydrocarbons and many acids; poor in ketones, esters and amines. FFKM (perfluoroelastomer): resists almost everything; expensive. PTFE gaskets resist chemicals but creep under load; use filled or expanded PTFE and the right bolt torque.

Corrosion coupons in critical services, removed and weighed on a schedule. Ultrasonic thickness surveys on vessels and piping, compared with the minimum thickness from design. Material certificates and positive material identification (PMI) for alloy parts, so a carbon steel fitting doesn't end up in a Hastelloy line. Review materials through MOC whenever a new chemical or cleaning agent is introduced. On the plant Keep the failed part. A pitted gasket face, a cracked weld or a thinned elbow tells a corrosion specialist almost exactly what happened. Thrown into the scrap bin, it tells nobody anything.

Assuming stainless steel resists chlorides. Choosing material for the process but not for cleaning chemicals. Glass-lined vessels exposed to hot caustic. Elastomers chosen without checking every solvent. No PMI on alloy spares.

s: Permit to work and isolation basics: permit types, the isolation hierarchy, lockout-tagout, verification, gas testing, handover and Piper Alpha lessons.
x: Permit to Work and Isolation Process Safety · Safe Work · October 2026 Most serious accidents during maintenance happen at the boundary between operations and maintenance: a line opened that was still connected to pressure, a pump started that someone was working on, a permit that didn’t survive a shift change. A permit to work is the system that manages that boundary. This article explains how it works, and how to isolate equipment properly. In this article What a permit to work is for Basics Types of permit Basics The isolation hierarchy Working level Lockout, tagout and verification Working level Handover: the Piper Alpha lesson Going deeper Questions people ask What a permit to work is for Basics A permit to work is a written agreement between the person in control of the plant and the person doing the work. It records what will be done, where, what hazards exist, how the equipment h

t: What a permit to work is for Basics
x: A permit to work is a written agreement between the person in control of the plant and the person doing the work. It records what will be done, where, what hazards exist, how the equipment has been made safe, what precautions are needed, and who has checked each one. Its value is not the paper but the conversation and checks it forces: the plant is handed over in a defined state, and handed back only when the work is complete and the equipment ready.

Hot work: welding, grinding, cutting, anything that makes sparks or flames. Needs gas testing and fire watch. Cold work / line break: opening process lines and equipment. Confined space entry: vessels, tanks, pits. Needs isolation, ventilation, atmosphere testing for oxygen, flammables and toxics, a standby person and a rescue plan. Electrical work and work at height , often as certificates attached to a main permit. Where several jobs touch the same equipment, they must be cross-referenced so one permit isn't closed while another depends on the same isolation.

Valves leak and get opened by mistake. The more severe the hazard, the more secure the isolation must be: Single closed valve: only for low-hazard fluids and short, simple jobs. Double block: two closed valves in series. Double block and bleed: two closed valves with a vent or drain open between them, so any leak through the first valve goes to the bleed, not to the work. Positive isolation: a spade (blind) or spectacle blind inserted, or a spool removed and the open ends blanked. Toxic, flammable, high-pressure or hot fluids, and any confined space entry, generally need positive isolation. The isolation points must be marked on a P&ID copy a

t: Lockout, tagout and verification Working level
x: Every energy source that could hurt someone must be isolated and locked: electrical supply, pneumatic and hydraulic power, stored pressure, springs, gravity (raised parts), and process chemicals. Each person working puts their own lock on the isolation (a multi-lock hasp or lock box) and only they remove it. Then verify : try to start the motor locally; check the pressure gauge reads zero and open the bleed; test the atmosphere before entry. An isolation that hasn't been tested is an assumption.

t: Handover: the Piper Alpha lesson Going deeper
x: On 6 July 1988, on the Piper Alpha platform in the North Sea, a pressure safety valve had been removed from a condensate pump for maintenance and replaced with a blind flange that was not leak-tight. The permit for that work was not effectively communicated at the evening shift handover. When the other pump tripped, the night shift started the pump with the missing valve. Condensate leaked, ignited and exploded, and the fires that followed destroyed the platform. 167 men died. The inquiry found weaknesses in the permit to work system, especially in shift handover and in cross-referencing permits. The lesson for every plant: a permit is only a

Signing permits in the office without visiting the job. Treating a stop button or a closed valve as an isolation. Not verifying the isolation before starting work. Permits not discussed at shift handover. Closing a permit while another job depends on the same isolation.

s: PID control basics: P, I and D action, process gain, time constant and dead time, IMC tuning, cascade and split-range control and integral windup.
x: PID Control and Tuning Plant Engineering · Process Control · October 2026 A badly tuned temperature loop on a reactor shows up as a batch that swings 5 °C around its set point, a jacket valve that never stops moving, or a heat-up that overshoots into an exotherm. Most loops are tuned once at commissioning and never touched again. This article explains what a PID controller actually does and how to tune one sensibly. It repeats this many t

t: Feedback control in one paragraph Basics
x: A controller compares the measured value (the process variable, PV) with the set point (SP), and moves an output (usually a valve) to reduce the difference, the error. It repeats this many times a second. Everything else is about how much to move the valve for a given error, and how to avoid overreacting.

Output = Kc × [ e + (1/Ti) ∫ e dt + Td × de/dt ] Proportional (Kc): output proportional to the error now. More gain gives a faster response but, beyond a point, oscillation. Proportional action alone leaves a steady offset. Integral (Ti): keeps adding output while any error remains, so it removes the offset. A short integral time (strong integral action) causes overshoot and slow oscillation. Derivative (Td): reacts to how fast the error is changing, damping overshoot on slow processes. It amplifies noise, so it is often left at zero, except on slow temperature loops.

t: Know the process: gain, lag and dead time Working level
x: Most plant loops behave roughly like a first-order lag with dead time: Process gain K: how much the PV finally changes for a 1 % change in output. Time constant τ: how long it takes to get about 63 % of the way to its new value. Dead time θ: how long before anything happens at all. Thermowells, long pipes and jacket volumes add dead time. Dead time is what limits control. The bigger θ is compared with τ, the gentler the tuning must be. Find these three numbers with a simple step test: put the controller in manual, change the output by 5–10 %, and record the PV.

t: Tuning: a simple, safe method Working level
x: The IMC (internal model control) rules give robust PI settings from the step test, with one choice: the desired closed-loop speed λ. Choosing λ equal to the dead time is a reasonable start; a larger λ is gentler. Kc = τ / [K × (λ + θ)] Ti = τ For a process with K = 1, τ = 10 min and θ = 2 min, with λ = 2 min: Kc = 2.5 and Ti = 10 min. Compare that with a loop left at Kc = 1 and Ti = 5 min: slower to start, but overshooting because the integral is too strong. Try it: change gain, integral and derivative and watch the response to a set point step. Push the gain up until it oscillates, then press “Use IMC tuning”.

t: Reactor temperature control in practice Going deeper
x: Cascade control: the batch temperature controller (master) sets the jacket temperature set point; the jacket temperature controller (slave) moves the valves. The fast slave loop corrects utility disturbances before they reach the batch. Tune the slave first. Split range: one output drives cooling for 0–50 % and heating for 50–100 %. Check the overlap so both valves aren't open together, and that there's no dead band where nothing happens. Integral windup: during a long heat-up, the error stays large and the integral term keeps growing; when the batch reaches set point, the stored integral causes a big overshoot. Use anti-windup in the DCS, or

Tuning a loop without knowing the process dead time. Too much integral action, causing slow oscillation. No anti-windup on batch heat-up. Tuning the master loop before the slave loop. Blaming tuning for a sticky valve.

The same pump that ran for three years without trouble suddenly eats a seal every month. Usually the pump hasn't changed; the way it is being run has. This article explains how a centrifugal pump wants to be operated, what each symptom tells you, and why mechanical seals really fail. t: Where a pump likes to run Basics
x: A centrifugal pump has a curve: the head it makes falls as the flow rises. Where that curve crosses the system curve is where it actually runs. Each pump also has a best efficiency point (BEP) , the flow at which the liquid enters and leaves the impeller smoothly. Near the BEP, forces on the shaft are balanced, vibration is low and the seal and bearings last. Far left of BEP (throttled hard, below about 60–70 %): liquid recirculates inside the impeller, the shaft deflects, the liquid heats up, vibration rises. At zero flow (dead-heading) the pump can boil its own contents. Far right of BEP (discharge wide open, above about 120 %): the pump ne

t: How a mechanical seal works Basics
x: Where the shaft passes through the casing, something has to stop the liquid escaping. Old pumps used packing (gland rope) that was designed to drip. Mechanical seals instead use two very flat rings, one rotating with the shaft and one stationary, pressed together by springs. Between them runs a liquid film about one micrometre thick. That film lubricates and cools the faces. With it, a seal lasts years; without it, the faces rub, overheat and crack, sometimes within a minute. Everything about seal reliability comes back to that film: keep it present, clean, cool and stable.

Try it: pick a symptom. The pump shows where to look, with the likely causes in order and the first check to make. Three measurements solve most pump problems: suction pressure , discharge pressure and motor current . With the head (discharge minus suction) and the current, you can place the pump on its curve and see whether it is running where you think it is. Fit pressure gauges on both sides of every important pump, not only on the discharge. t: Why seals really fail Going deeper
x: Seal manufacturers say that most failures are not the seal's fault, and in my experience they are right. Look at the failed parts before ordering a replacement: Heat-checked or cracked faces: dry running. The pump ran on an empty tank, against a closed suction valve, or with vapour at the faces. Fit a low-level or dry-run trip (power monitor) and fill and vent the pump before starting. Swollen, hard or cracked O-rings: wrong elastomer for the solvent. Viton swells in ketones such as acetone; EPDM swells in hydrocarbons; FFKM (perfluoroelastomer) resists almost everything but costs much more. Check compatibility for every solvent the pump sees

Size for the real duty , not the worst case times a safety factor. Use a VFD where flows vary, rather than throttling. Alignment after every maintenance job, ideally with a laser, and with pipework supported so it doesn't pull on the pump. x: Reactor Selection: Batch, Semi-batch, CSTR or Flow Process Design · Reaction Engineering · October 2026 Most API and fine chemical plants are built around batch reactors, and for good reasons. But the choice of reactor type changes conversion, selectivity, safety and cost, and sometimes a different type solves a problem that no amount of batch optimisation can. This article compares the four basic reactor types and when each one makes sense. In this article The four basic types Basics Residence time and conversion Working level Selectivity: where the reactor type really matters Working level Heat removal and safety Working level Choosing in practice Going deeper Questions people ask The four basic types Basics Batch: everything charged, reacted, discharged. Flexible, simple, the standard multi-purpose plant reactor. Semi-batch: one reactant dosed into the other. The workhorse for exother

s: Reactor Selection: Batch, Semi-batch, CSTR or Flow
x: Batch: everything charged, reacted, discharged. Flexible, simple, the standard multi-purpose plant reactor. Semi-batch: one reactant dosed into the other. The workhorse for exothermic reactions because dosing controls the heat. See semi-batch dosing . Continuous stirred tank (CSTR): feed in and product out continuously, well mixed, so the whole contents sit at the outlet composition. Plug flow (PFR): a tube where each slice of fluid travels through without mixing with the slices before and after. Every slice behaves like a small batch reactor. Modern flow chemistry reactors approach this. See flow chemistry .

t: Residence time and conversion Working level
s: Reactor Selection: Batch, Semi-batch, CSTR or Flow
x: For a simple first-order reaction with rate constant k and residence time τ, the product kτ (the Damköhler number) sets conversion: Batch or plug flow: X = 1 - e^-kτ One CSTR: X = kτ / (1 + kτ) To reach 90 % conversion, a batch or plug flow reactor needs kτ = 2.3; a single CSTR needs kτ = 9, almost four times the volume. The reason is that the CSTR runs entirely at the outlet concentration, where the reactant is depleted and the rate is slow. Two CSTRs in series need about 1.9 times the plug flow volume; more tanks in series approach plug flow. Try it: set the conversion you need and compare the residence time each reactor type requires. The

t: Selectivity: where the reactor type really matters Working level
s: Reactor Selection: Batch, Semi-batch, CSTR or Flow
x: Conversion only costs volume. Selectivity costs yield and purity, and the reactor type affects it strongly: Consecutive reactions (A → desired B → unwanted C): plug flow or batch, stopped at the right time, gives the most B. A CSTR keeps B in the reactor with fresh conversion going on, so more C forms. Parallel reactions where the side reaction has a higher order in a reagent: keep that reagent dilute. Semi-batch dosing or a CSTR does this naturally. Fast reactions limited by mixing: local excess at the feed point gives impurities. Small, well-mixed flow reactors or good feed-point design help.

t: Heat removal and safety Working level
s: Reactor Selection: Batch, Semi-batch, CSTR or Flow
x: A large batch reactor has little cooling area per litre and holds the whole inventory of reactive material. A CSTR at steady state holds mostly converted material, so the energy available for a runaway is smaller. A flow reactor has a tiny volume and enormous area per volume, so it can run reactions that would be unsafe or impossible in batch: very fast, very exothermic, or with unstable intermediates that are made and consumed within seconds. The trade-off is complexity: continuous plants need steady feeds, accurate pumps, good analytics and a plan for start-up, shut-down and blockages.

x: Relief Valve Sizing Basics Process Design · Pressure Protection · October 2026 A relief valve sits on top of a vessel for years doing nothing, and then has a few seconds to do its one job. Whether it succeeds depends on decisions made long before: which scenario it was sized for, whether the pipe to it is too long, whether someone fitted a valve underneath it. This article explains how relief sizing works, from the basic idea to an API 520 calculation, and where the common traps are. Every vessel has a pressure it was designed for. Control systems, alarms and trips keep it well below that pressure most of the time. But all of them can fail: a control valve sticks open, cooling water stops, a fire starts under the vessel. The relief device is the last line of protection: a purely mechanical device that opens when the pressure reaches its set point and lets enough fluid out to stop the pressure rising further. “Enough” is the important word. A relief valve that opens but is too small simply slows the pressure rise, and the vessel still fails. Sizing is about matching the valve's capacity to the worst credible flow it must p

t: Set pressure, overpressure and MAWP Basics
x: MAWP (maximum allowable working pressure) is the highest pressure the vessel is certified for at its design temperature. It is on the nameplate. Set pressure is where the valve starts to open, normally at or below the MAWP. Overpressure is how far above MAWP the pressure may rise while the valve is discharging at full capacity: 10 % for a single valve on a process upset, 16 % with several valves, and 21 % for an external fire (ASME Section VIII and API 520/521). Relieving pressure = set pressure + overpressure. Sizing uses this pressure. Operating pressure should sit at least 10 % below set pressure, or the valve will simmer and leak.

t: Finding the governing scenario Working level
x: API 521 lists the causes of overpressure to consider. For a typical batch reactor in a pharma plant, the list usually narrows to: External fire around the vessel. Blocked outlet on a vent or condenser line while nitrogen or steam keeps flowing in. Control valve failure on the nitrogen supply, steam to the jacket, or a pump discharging into the vessel. Loss of cooling during reflux or reaction. Runaway reaction or decomposition. Tube rupture in a heat exchanger with a high-pressure side. Each credible scenario gives a relieving load. The largest one, the governing scenario , sets the size. Write all of them down with the reasoning: a future re

t: The fire case, worked through Working level
x: In a fire, the liquid inside boils and the vapour must escape. API 521 gives the heat absorbed by a vessel with adequate drainage and firefighting: Q = 43,200 × F × Awetted^0.82 (W) Awetted: wetted area in m², counted up to 7.6 m above grade. F: environment factor, 1.0 for a bare vessel, lower with approved insulation. Without adequate drainage, the constant is 70,900. Take a 6 m³ reactor holding toluene with a wetted area of about 12 m², set at 3 barg: Q = 43,200 × 12^0.82 ≈ 43,200 × 7.67 ≈ 331 kW. Relieving pressure = 3 × 1.21 + 1.01 ≈ 4.64 bar abs. Toluene boils at about 175 °C at this pressure, where its latent heat is about 310 kJ/kg. Re

Kd = 0.975 for a preliminary valve size; Kb = 1 for conventional valves with low back pressure; Kc = 0.9 with a rupture disc upstream, otherwise 1. For toluene, k ≈ 1.09 gives C ≈ 0.0247. t: Rupture discs and runaway reactions Going deeper
x: A rupture disc is a thin membrane that bursts at a set pressure. It opens fully in milliseconds, has no moving parts and is tight against leaks and corrosive vapours. But once burst, it stays open until replaced. Discs are used alone on reactors where a fast, large opening matters, and upstream of a relief valve to protect it from corrosion (with a pressure gauge between them to detect a leaking disc). A runaway reaction is a different problem from fire. As temperature climbs, the batch foams and swells, so the relief discharges a two-phase mixture of liquid and vapour. Two-phase flow needs a much larger area than vapour alone, often several

t: Installation: where good sizing goes wrong Going deeper
x: Inlet pressure loss above 3 % of set pressure makes the valve open and close rapidly (chatter), which can destroy it. Keep inlet lines short and at least the valve's inlet size. Back pressure from a long discharge line or a shared header reduces capacity. Above about 10 % of set pressure, use a balanced-bellows valve and the Kb correction. No isolation valve under a relief device unless it is locked or car-sealed open under a written procedure. A safe discharge: to a scrubber, flare, catch tank or a safe high point, never into a work area or back into a building. Testing: bench-test valves at the interval the inspection plan sets, and record

x: For HCl: NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H2O, so each kg of HCl uses 40/36.5 ≈ 1.1 kg of NaOH. A 2,000 kg charge of 10 % NaOH holds 200 kg of NaOH. x: A scrubber that handles the average flow can fail at the peak: the first minutes of a thionyl chloride distillation, a quench, or a relief event. Gas that bypasses the liquid goes straight to the stack.

x: Semi-Batch Reactions: Dosing Time, Accumulation and MTSR Scale-up · Reaction Safety · October 2026 “Dose the reagent over 4 hours.” Every batch card for an exothermic reaction has a line like this, and on a busy night someone always asks why it can't be 2 hours. The honest answer is not “because the SOP says so”. It is about how much unreacted reagent is sitting in the reactor at any moment, and what that reagent would do if the cooling failed. This article builds that answer from the ground up. In this article Why we dose instead of mixing everything Basics Accumulation: the reagent waiting to react Basics From accumulation to MTSR Working level Can the plant cool it? Working level Why colder is not always safer Going deeper Protecting a dosing step Going deeper Questions people ask Why we dose instead of mixing everything Basics If two reactants that release a lot of heat are mixed all

t: Why we dose instead of mixing everything Basics
s: Semi-Batch Reactions: Dosing Time, Accumulation and MTSR
x: If two reactants that release a lot of heat are mixed all at once (a batch reaction), the whole heat of reaction is available from the first minute. If cooling fails, there is nothing you can do: everything is already in the reactor. In a semi-batch reaction, one reactant is in the reactor and the other is dosed in slowly. Ideally each drop reacts almost as soon as it arrives, so the heat comes out at the rate you dose. That gives you a control handle: if the temperature rises or cooling fails, stop dosing, and the heat release stops too. At least, that is the idea. Whether it is true depends on accumulation.

t: Accumulation: the reagent waiting to react Basics
s: Semi-Batch Reactions: Dosing Time, Accumulation and MTSR
x: Reagent doesn't react instantly. At any moment during dosing, some of what has been added has reacted and some hasn't. The unreacted part is the accumulation . If the reaction is fast compared with the dosing, accumulation stays low and stopping the feed really does stop the heat. If the reaction is slow, reagent piles up, and stopping the feed doesn't help much: the reagent already in the reactor keeps reacting. Think of filling a bucket with a hole in it. The tap is the dosing rate; the hole is the reaction. The water level in the bucket is the accumulation. Open the tap faster, or make the hole smaller (a colder, slower reaction), and the

t: From accumulation to MTSR Working level

x: The worst case is a total cooling failure at the moment accumulation is highest. x: Solvent Selection and Solvent Swaps Scale-up · Solvents · October 2026 Many API processes use three or four solvents across a sequence of steps, and every change from one to the next costs time, energy and solvent. The swap is often the longest step in the batch and the one that most often leaves too much of the old solvent behind. This article covers how to choose solvents in the first place and how to swap them efficiently. The chemist picks a solvent for the chemistry: solubility, reactivity, selectivity. At scale, more questions matter: Safety: flash point, static (conductivity), peroxide formation (THF, ethers), toxicity, thermal stability with reagents (DMF and DMSO with strong bases and hydrides). Work-up: water miscibility, density difference from water, emulsion tendency. Recovery: boiling point, azeotropes with water and other solvents, ease of drying. t: Residual solvents and ICH classes Basics
x: ICH Q3C groups solvents by toxicity: Class 1 (avoid: benzene, carbon tetrachloride), Class 2 (limit, with a permitted concentration for each: toluene 890 ppm, methanol 3,000 ppm, DCM 600 ppm, acetonitrile 410 ppm), and Class 3 (low toxicity, generally up to 5,000 ppm: ethanol, acetone, ethyl acetate, IPA). The class of the last solvents used before isolation matters most, because they are the hardest to remove completely.

t: Two ways to swap Working level
x: To change from a low-boiling solvent (say THF) to a higher-boiling one (say toluene): Put-and-take: distil down to the minimum volume, add the new solvent back to the working volume, distil down again, repeat. Simple to run, with several “chases”. Concentrate, then constant volume: distil down to the minimum volume, then keep distilling while feeding new solvent at the same rate as distillate leaves, holding the volume constant. Finally top up to the working volume. Both work because the old solvent is more volatile: the vapour is richer in it than the liquid. With a relative volatility of 3.5, distilling down to half volume and swapping at t

t: Azeotropes and other traps Working level
x: Azeotropes: methanol and toluene, ethanol and toluene, IPA and water all form azeotropes. A swap that crosses one can't reach low residuals by simple distillation; the residual levels off. Check azeotrope data before designing a swap, and sometimes swap through a third solvent. Product stability: concentrating to a low volume at high temperature can degrade the product or crystallise it on the wall. Use vacuum to keep the temperature down. See vacuum systems . Water: water from a work-up often has to come out with the old solvent; toluene's heterogeneous azeotrope with water helps here (azeotropic drying with a Dean-Stark separator). Swapping

t: Doing it in the plant Going deeper
x: Define the end point by analysis (GC of the pot), not by the number of chases. Know the true minimum stirrable volume of the reactor, with the agitator covered and the temperature probe immersed. Watch the top temperature: as the old solvent runs out, it rises toward the new solvent's boiling point at that pressure. Collect the distillate separately for recovery; mixed distillate of two solvents is harder to recover than either alone. See distillation basics . On the plant If the residual old solvent stalls at the same value after each chase, suspect an azeotrope or a dead volume (a condenser leg, a dip pipe, a sample line) that keeps feeding

Fixing the number of chases instead of testing the residual. Ignoring an azeotrope between the two solvents. Not knowing the true minimum stirrable volume. Overheating the product during concentration. Mixing the distillates of different solvents.

s: How static builds up in plants: spark energy ½CV² vs MIE, low-conductivity solvents, bonding and earthing, filling and inerting, with the Barton case.
x: Static Electricity and Solvent Fires Process Safety · Ignition Sources · October 2026 Most solvent fires in pharma and fine chemical plants are not caused by a welding torch or a faulty motor. They start with a spark nobody saw: from a drum on a plastic pallet, an operator's body, or a plastic bag of powder tipped into a reactor. This article explains, from the beginning, how static charge builds up, why a spark too small to feel can ignite a solvent, and which simple controls stop it. In this article What static charge is Basics How charge builds up Basics How much energy is in a spark Working level Solvents that hold their charge Working level The controls that work Working level Powder into a solvent reactor Going deeper When earthing was not enough: Barton Solvents Going deeper Questions people ask What static charge is Basics Every material contains equal amounts of positive and neg

Every material contains equal amounts of positive and negative charge, so normally it is neutral. When two different materials touch, a few electrons cross from one to the other. Pull them apart and those electrons don't all go back: one side is left slightly positive, the other slightly negative. That separated charge is static electricity. It happens whenever things rub or separate: a solvent flowing along a pipe wall, powder sliding out of a bag, a person walking across the floor, a belt running over a pulley, nitrogen blowing through a hose. The more contact and the faster the separation, the more charge. A fine filter is one of the stron

Charge being generated is not, by itself, dangerous. It becomes dangerous only if it cannot escape. Think of a bucket under a running tap with a hole in the bottom. The tap is charge generation; the hole is the path to earth. If the hole is big (earthed metal, a conductive liquid), the level never rises. If the hole is tiny (a plastic container, an unbonded drum, toluene), the level rises until it overflows. In electrical terms, the voltage rises until the air breaks down, roughly 3 kV per millimetre, and the stored charge jumps as a spark. We can rarely stop generation in a process plant. The job is to make sure the leak is always bigger tha

t: How much energy is in a spark Working level
x: A charged object behaves like a capacitor. The energy it can release in one spark is: E = ½ C V² C capacitance in farads (a person about 100–300 pF, a 200 L drum about 100–200 pF, a road tanker about 1,000 pF), V voltage in volts. A person in ordinary shoes on a dry floor easily reaches 10 kV. With 200 pF that is ½ × 200×10^-12 × 10,000² = 0.01 J, or 10 mJ. You start to feel a spark at about 1 mJ. Now compare that with the minimum ignition energy (MIE) , the smallest spark that ignites the most easily ignited mixture of the vapour in air: Solvent MIE (mJ) Flash point Holds charge? Methanol 0.14 11 °C No, conductive Toluene 0.24 4 °C Yes, low

x: A liquid's electrical conductivity decides how fast charge drains from it. The standard IEC TS 60079-32-1 groups liquids into three classes: Low conductivity, below 50 pS/m: toluene, xylene, hexane, heptane, many hydrocarbons. Charge can stay in the liquid for tens of seconds, even inside an earthed metal tank. Medium, 50 to 10,000 pS/m: some esters and ethers. High, above 10,000 pS/m: alcohols, ketones, water. Charge drains in microseconds, but only if the container is earthed. In a plastic can, even methanol charges up. The time charge stays in a liquid is its relaxation time, τ = εε0/κ (permittivity divided by conductivity). For toluene it

t: The controls that work Working level
x: 1. Bond and earth every conductor Clamp drums, IBCs and tankers before the lid or valve opens, and remove the clamp last. Bond across anything that breaks the metal path: PTFE-gasketed flanges, glass sections, flexible hoses. Test it: a metal-to-metal bond below 10 Ω shows it is real, and below 1 MΩ to earth is enough to drain static. Earth monitoring clamps with a green light, interlocked to the transfer pump, remove the guesswork. Paint, rust and dirt under a clamp can break the path. 2. Fill slowly and from the bottom Splash filling from a top nozzle breaks the liquid into droplets and mist, which generates charge and fills the vapour spac

t: Powder into a solvent reactor Going deeper
x: Tipping powder from a plastic bag through an open manhole into a reactor that already contains solvent is the most common cause of flash fires in API and intermediate plants. Everything lines up at once: a flammable vapour at the manhole, air coming in, powder and bag both charging as the powder slides out, and an operator standing in the vapour. The discharge from a plastic bag or liner is a brush discharge , up to about 4 mJ. That is too weak to ignite most dusts but easily enough for solvent vapour. A non-antistatic FIBC or a plastic-lined chute can give a propagating brush discharge of 1,000 mJ or more, which ignites almost anything. Char

t: When earthing was not enough: Barton Solvents Going deeper
x: On 17 July 2007, a 15,000-gallon tank exploded at the Barton Solvents distribution facility in Valley Center, Kansas, while a tanker unloaded VM&P naphtha, a low-conductivity solvent. The tank was thrown into the air, fire spread through the tank farm and about 6,000 residents were evacuated. The US Chemical Safety Board found four conditions lined up: the naphtha was nonconductive and held its charge; stop–start filling introduced air and turbulence, adding charge; the tank headspace was flammable and not inerted; a loose linkage on the level float, an isolated conductor inside the tank, likely sparked. The bonding and grounding of the trans

“I didn't feel a spark, so there wasn't one.” Assuming a conductive solvent is safe in a plastic container or an unbonded drum. Assuming nitrogen protection without ever measuring the oxygen. Plastic buckets, funnels and scoops kept “just for small additions”. Thinking static is a winter problem: humidity helps surfaces, but does nothing for charge inside a flowing liquid.

s: How much heat steam gives in a jacket, why low-pressure steam heats better, steam consumption, and how to size a reactor condenser and vent condenser.
x: Steam Energy and Condenser Selection Plant Engineering · Heat Transfer · October 2026 Two questions come up in almost every new batch process: how much steam will this heating step need, and is the reactor condenser big enough for the distillation? Both come down to the same physics: latent heat, given up by steam when it condenses in the jacket, and taken up again by the solvent vapour that has to condense in the condenser. This article goes through both, with the numbers engineers actually use. In this article What steam gives you Basics Which steam pressure to use Basics Steam consumption for a duty Working level Selecting a reactor condenser Working level Vacuum, vent condensers and non-condensables Going deeper Questions people ask What steam gives you Basics The enthalpy of saturated steam has two parts. Sensible heat (hf) is what it took to heat the water to boiling. Latent heat (

The enthalpy of saturated steam has two parts. Sensible heat (hf) is what it took to heat the water to boiling. Latent heat (hfg) is what it took to boil it. In a jacket or coil, steam condenses and gives up its latent heat; the condensate leaves through the trap still carrying its sensible heat. So the useful heat per kg in ordinary heating is the latent heat, about 2,100 kJ/kg at typical process pressures. Try it: raise the steam pressure. The total enthalpy hardly changes, but more of it is sensible heat that leaves with the condensate, and the latent heat per kg falls.

t: Which steam pressure to use Basics
x: Higher pressure gives a higher temperature, so a bigger temperature difference and faster heating. But it gives less latent heat per kg, and the hot condensate carries more energy away (recoverable only as flash steam). The rule: use the lowest steam pressure that gives the temperature difference you need . Many plants distribute at 8–10 barg to keep pipe sizes small and reduce to 2–4 barg at the users. Remember the product's wall temperature limit and the glass-lined vessel's thermal shock limits when choosing.

t: Steam consumption for a duty Working level
x: Steam (kg/h) = Q (kW) × 3,600 / hfg (kJ/kg) × (1 + losses) 100 kW of heating at 3 barg (hfg ≈ 2,133 kJ/kg) needs about 169 kg/h of steam, plus 10–15 % for losses from the vessel and lines. To distil 1,850 kg of toluene, about 666 MJ of latent heat, needs roughly 360 kg of steam with losses. See material and energy balance and the steam and boiler calculators . Wet steam (with water droplets), a failed trap that waterlogs the jacket, or air in the steam all reduce the heat delivered. If a jacket heats slowly, check the trap and the condensate drain before blaming the steam pressure.

t: Selecting a reactor condenser Working level
x: The condenser must remove the latent heat of all the vapour the reactor boils off, at the highest rate the steam can produce it: Duty = vapour rate × [λ + cp (Tcondensing - Tcondensate)] Area = Duty / (U × LMTD) Start from the reboil rate : the jacket heat input at full steam sets the maximum vapour rate. A condenser sized for the “normal” rate will be overloaded the first time someone opens the steam valve fully. Use the latent heat of the solvent at the condensing temperature: methanol (about 1,100 kJ/kg) needs three times the condenser of toluene (about 363 kJ/kg) for the same mass. Check the approach to the cooling water outlet: with 32/3

t: Vacuum, vent condensers and non-condensables Going deeper
x: Under vacuum, the condensing temperature drops with the boiling point, the LMTD to cooling water shrinks and the area needed rises fast. Nitrogen bleed and air leaks add non-condensable gas that collects in the condenser and blankets the tubes, cutting U sharply. Keep a vent condenser on chilled water or brine after the main condenser to catch what the main one misses and to cut solvent loss to the vacuum pump. See vacuum systems . On the plant If the distillation rate stalls while the jacket still has steam, feel the condenser vapour outlet and check the vent. A hot outlet means the condenser is overloaded or blanketed with nitrogen, and the

Counting the total enthalpy of steam instead of the latent heat. Heating with high-pressure steam when low pressure would do. Sizing the condenser for the normal rather than the maximum boil-up. Ignoring non-condensables in vacuum condensers. No vent condenser on low-boiling solvents.

x: Steam System Efficiency: Calculations for the Plant Utilities · Steam & Boiler · Updated October 2026 Steam is the biggest fuel bill in most chemical and pharma plants, and most of the losses are invisible: a trap blowing into the condensate line, a flash vent at the feed tank, condensate going to drain because the return pump tripped months ago. This article walks through the numbers you need to put a rupee value on each of them, starting from what a tonne of steam actually costs. t: How a steam system works Basics
s: Steam System Efficiency: Calculations for the Plant
x: A steam system is a loop. The boiler burns fuel to turn water into steam. Steam travels through the mains to wherever heat is needed: reactor jackets, coils, heat exchangers, dryers. There it condenses back into water and gives up its latent heat , which is most of the energy it carries. The condensed water, called condensate, drains through a steam trap , a small automatic valve that lets water out but holds steam in, and in a good system flows back to the boiler feed tank to be used again. Every loss in that loop has to be paid for with more fuel at the boiler: steam escaping through a leak or a failed trap, heat lost through bare pipes, ho

s: Steam System Efficiency: Calculations for the Plant
x: Every loss calculation needs this one number. The fuel part of it comes from an energy balance on the boiler: Heat per kg of steam = hg (at boiler pressure) - hfw (feed water) Fuel per tonne of steam = 1,000 × (hg - hfw) / (η × GCV × 4.1868) Fuel cost per tonne of steam = Fuel per tonne × fuel price hg comes from steam tables (about 2,780 kJ/kg at 10 barg), hfw ≈ 4.186 × feed water temperature, η is the boiler efficiency and GCV the fuel's gross calorific value in kcal/kg. Worked example 10 barg steam, feed water 80 °C: 2,780 - 335 = 2,445 kJ/kg Coal at 4,000 kcal/kg, 75 % efficient: fuel = 1,000 × 2,445 / (0.75 × 4,000 × 4.1868) ≈ 195 kg per

t: Where the fuel goes Working level
s: Steam System Efficiency: Calculations for the Plant
x: A coal or biomass boiler at 75 % efficiency loses a quarter of the fuel's heat before the steam leaves the boiler house. The usual split: Dry flue gas: the biggest loss. It rises with stack temperature and with excess air. Check O₂ in the flue gas: about 3–4 % on oil and gas, 6–8 % on solid fuel. Moisture: water in the fuel and water formed from hydrogen leave as vapour up the stack. Wet husk or wet coal costs real money. Unburnt carbon in ash: shows up as black ash. Grate speed, air distribution and fuel sizing matter. Radiation and convection: small at full load, larger at low load. Blowdown: hot boiler water drained to control TDS.

s: Steam System Efficiency: Calculations for the Plant
x: Dissolved solids in the feed water stay behind when water boils, so the boiler water gets more concentrated until some of it is drained off. The blowdown needed to hold a TDS limit is: Blowdown (% of steam) = TDSfeed / (TDSboiler, max - TDSfeed) × 100 With 150 ppm feed water and a 3,000 ppm limit, blowdown is about 5.3 % of the steam. For a 5 t/h boiler at 10 barg that is about 263 kg/h of water at 184 °C, carrying (781 - 335) kJ/kg more heat than the feed water, about 33 kW or roughly 0.7 % of the fuel. Better feed water (more condensate return, a softener or RO) reduces it at the source; automatic TDS control and a flash vessel with a heat

t: Steam traps and leaks Working level
s: Steam System Efficiency: Calculations for the Plant
x: A trap that fails open passes live steam into the condensate line. Napier's formula gives an upper estimate of the steam through an orifice: Steam (kg/h) ≈ 0.412 × d² (mm²) × P (bar abs) Worked example: a trap survey A survey of 200 traps on 7 barg steam finds 15 % (30 traps) blowing through. Taking an equivalent 2 mm hole for each: Per trap: 0.412 × 4 × 8.0 ≈ 13 kg/h 30 traps: ≈ 400 kg/h, about 3,200 tonnes a year over 8,000 hours At ₹2,500 per tonne: up to ₹80 lakh a year The real figure is usually lower, because a failed trap rarely blows the full seat area all the time. Even half of it pays for a trap survey and spares many times over. Te

s: Steam System Efficiency: Calculations for the Plant
x: Condensate leaving a trap at 8 barg is at about 175 °C. In a return line at 0.5 barg water can only exist up to about 111 °C, so the extra heat boils part of it: Flash fraction = (hf,high - hf,low) / hfg,low = (743 - 467) / 2,226 ≈ 12 % That flash steam is ordinary low-pressure steam. If a flash vessel sends it to a low-pressure user such as a tank heater, an air heater or a deaerator, it replaces live steam. If not, it plumes from the feed tank vent, which also means the feed tank cannot be held at a high temperature.

s: Steam System Efficiency: Calculations for the Plant
x: Returned condensate is hot, already treated water. Each kilogram returned saves: the fuel to heat make-up water from ambient to the condensate temperature: m × 4.186 × (Tc - Tmakeup); the treated water itself, and its softener or RO cost; chemicals and blowdown, because condensate has almost no dissolved solids. Returning 3 t/h of condensate at 90 °C instead of 30 °C make-up recovers about 209 kW, roughly 60 kg/h of coal in a 75 % efficient boiler, plus 72 m³ a day of treated water. A rule of thumb worth remembering: every 6 °C rise in feed water temperature saves about 1 % of boiler fuel. Condensate from process heat exchangers can pick up p

s: Steam System Efficiency: Calculations for the Plant
x: Calculate the cost of steam per tonne and agree it with finance. Measure boiler efficiency monthly (direct method) and trend the evaporation ratio. Check flue gas O₂ and stack temperature every shift. Survey every steam trap at least once a year; keep a trap register. Walk the steam mains for leaks, missing insulation and wet lagging. Measure condensate return as a percentage of steam generated; most plants can reach 60–80 %. Look for vents with a steam plume: feed tank, condensate receivers, flash vessels. Set blowdown from boiler water TDS, not from habit.

x: Solvent Storage Tanks: Breathing Losses and Vents Process Design · Storage · October 2026 A solvent tank farm loses solvent every day without a single leak. Each time a tanker fills a tank, the gas pushed out of the vent carries vapour with it; each sunny afternoon, the tank warms and breathes out a little more. The amounts look small per event and add up to tonnes a year. This article explains where the losses come from and the equipment that controls them and keeps the tank safe. In this article Why tanks lose solvent Basics Estimating filling losses Working level Conservation vents and arresters Working level Nitrogen blanketing Working level Reducing losses Going deeper Questions people ask Why tanks lose solvent Basics The space above the liquid in a solvent tank is saturated with vapour. Whenever gas leaves the tank, vapour leaves with it: Filling (working) losses: each m³ of liqui

s: Solvent Storage Tanks: Breathing Losses and Vents
x: The space above the liquid in a solvent tank is saturated with vapour. Whenever gas leaves the tank, vapour leaves with it: Filling (working) losses: each m³ of liquid pumped in pushes out about one m³ of saturated headspace gas. Breathing losses: daytime heating expands the headspace and raises the vapour pressure; the tank breathes out. At night it cools and breathes in air, which then saturates again. The amount depends almost entirely on the solvent's vapour pressure at the tank temperature. Acetone, MDC and methanol lose far more than toluene or xylene.

s: Solvent Storage Tanks: Breathing Losses and Vents
x: Solvent in vented gas (kg/m³) = Pvap × M / (R × T) Pvap in Pa from the Antoine equation, M in kg/mol, R = 8.314 J/mol·K, T in K. Toluene at 30 °C has a vapour pressure of about 4.9 kPa, so each m³ of vented gas carries 4,890 × 0.092 / (8.314 × 303) ≈ 0.18 kg. Filling 100 m³ a month loses about 214 kg of toluene a year from filling alone. The same tank of acetone loses several times more. Try it: change the solvent, tank temperature and monthly throughput, and compare venting to air with a vent condenser and vapour balancing. For full estimates including breathing losses, use the US EPA AP-42 Chapter 7 methods, which account for tank colour, d

t: Conservation vents and arresters Working level
s: Solvent Storage Tanks: Breathing Losses and Vents
x: A pressure-vacuum conservation vent (breather valve) stays closed over a small pressure range, for example opening at +20 mbar and -5 mbar. Small daily temperature changes are absorbed without venting, which cuts breathing losses. It also protects the tank: storage tanks are very weak, often designed for only tens of millibars, and a blocked vent can collapse a tank under vacuum when it is pumped out or cooled by rain. On flammable solvent tanks, a flame arrester or an end-of-line deflagration arrester stops an external flame entering the tank through the vent. Arresters block with polymer, dust or ice, so they need inspection. A separate eme

s: Solvent Storage Tanks: Breathing Losses and Vents
x: A blanketing regulator admits nitrogen whenever tank pressure falls (during emptying or cooling) and the conservation vent releases gas when it rises. This keeps air out, so the headspace stays below the LOC and cannot burn, and keeps moisture out of hygroscopic solvents. See inerting and LOC . Blanketing does not reduce filling losses: the gas pushed out is now nitrogen saturated with vapour instead of air saturated with vapour. Set the blanketing pressure below the vent's opening pressure, with enough margin that nitrogen isn't vented continuously.

s: Solvent Storage Tanks: Breathing Losses and Vents
x: Vapour balancing: connect the tank vent back to the road tanker during unloading, so the displaced vapour goes into the tanker instead of the air. It is the cheapest large reduction. Vent condenser: cool the vented gas with chilled water or brine to condense most of the solvent. At 5 °C, toluene's vapour pressure falls to about 1.2 kPa, removing roughly three-quarters of the loss. Insulation and white paint reduce the daily temperature swing and breathing loss. x: Assuming nitrogen blanketing reduces filling losses. Blanketing pressure set above the conservation vent setting. Uninspected flame arresters blocked with polymer or ice. No vacuum protection, risking tank collapse when emptied. Unloading tankers without vapour balancing.

x: Vacuum Systems in Batch Plants Plant Engineering · Vacuum · October 2026 “Vacuum is not coming.” Every plant engineer gets this call, usually during a distillation that is already behind schedule. The answer is almost always one of four things: the pump, a leak, the condenser, or something boiling that shouldn't be. This article explains how a vacuum system works from the basics, how to calculate what it should achieve, and how to find out why it doesn't. In this article What vacuum really is Basics The pumps you'll meet Basics Pump-down time Working level Air leaks and the rate-of-rise test Working level The condenser decides the solvent loss Going deeper When vacuum won't come: a checklist Going deeper Questions people ask What vacuum really is Basics Vacuum is just a pressure below atmospheric. Always talk in absolute pressure (mbar abs or torr), not “mm vacuum” or “-0.95 kg/cm²”. The

Vacuum is just a pressure below atmospheric. Always talk in absolute pressure (mbar abs or torr), not “mm vacuum” or “-0.95 kg/cm²”. The same gauge reading means a different absolute pressure on a rainy day and at a different site altitude, and only absolute pressure tells you the boiling point. In process plants we mostly work in rough vacuum : from atmospheric (1,013 mbar) down to about 1 mbar. That covers solvent distillation (usually 50–200 mbar), drying (5–50 mbar) and deodorising or high-vacuum stripping (1–5 mbar). Why bother? Lower pressure lowers the boiling point. x: Three electrical terms come up again and again in a plant review, so it helps to be clear about them. kW (real power) is the power that does useful work: turning a pump, heating a batch. It includes current that flows back and forth to magnetise motors and transformers without doing any work. Power factor (PF) is kW ÷ kVA. x: Work-up and Phase Separation at Scale Scale-up · Work-up · October 2026 In the lab, you shake the separating funnel, wait a minute and run off the lower layer. In the plant, the same work-up can take hours to settle, leave a cloudy rag layer at the interface, and lose product down the drain with the aqueous layer. This article explains why, and how to make a work-up that separates cleanly at scale. s: Work-up and Phase Separation at Scale
x: Water and an immiscible solvent such as toluene, ethyl acetate or MDC form two phases because they don't dissolve in each other (much). Mixing breaks one phase into droplets dispersed in the other. When mixing stops, droplets fall or rise according to density, meet, merge (coalesce) and form a continuous layer. Separation needs both steps: settling to bring droplets together, and coalescence to merge them.

t: Settling: the Stokes law picture Basics
s: Work-up and Phase Separation at Scale
x: v = g × d² × Δρ / (18 μ) v settling velocity, d droplet diameter, Δρ density difference between phases, μ viscosity of the continuous phase. Droplet size counts most, because it is squared. With a toluene-water density difference of about 130 kg/m³ and a water-like viscosity: 100 µm droplets settle at about 0.7 mm/s: 2–3 minutes across a 10 cm separating funnel, but about 35 minutes across a 1.5 m plant reactor. 30 µm droplets take about 26 minutes in the funnel and over 6 hours in the plant. That is the scale-up problem: settling distance grows 15-fold, and plant agitators often make smaller droplets than a hand-shaken funnel. Try it: change

t: Emulsions and rag layers Working level
s: Work-up and Phase Separation at Scale
x: An emulsion forms when droplets are stabilised against coalescing. A rag layer is a band of emulsion, often with fine solids, that sits at the interface and won't resolve. Common causes: Fine solids (catalyst fines, inorganic salts, polymeric by-products) collecting at the interface. Surface-active species: amphiphilic intermediates, soaps formed at high pH, residual surfactant. Small density difference: MDC with heavy brine, or solvents close to water's density. Over-mixing: high-speed agitation before settling makes very fine droplets. A pH near the pKa of the product, where it partitions into both phases.

s: Work-up and Phase Separation at Scale
x: Add salt (brine): increases the density difference and reduces the solubility of organics in water. Change pH away from the problem range, or adjust temperature (viscosity falls and solubilities change). Filter the mixture through a filter aid to remove interface solids, often the real cause. Add more solvent or a different co-solvent to change density and viscosity. Wait, gently: slow agitation helps droplets meet; no agitation at all can leave them suspended. Test these in the lab on a plant sample before the campaign, and write the chosen remedy into the batch record.

t: Running separations in the plant Going deeper
s: Work-up and Phase Separation at Scale
x: Mix enough, not more: extraction needs contact, but not violent mixing. Lower the agitator speed for extractions, and reduce it further before stopping. Specify settling time from plant experience, not from the lab funnel. See the interface: a sight glass on the bottom outlet line, conductivity probes (water conducts, most solvents don't) or a capacitance probe. Run the lower layer slowly as the interface approaches. Decide where the rag goes: keep it with the product layer, send it to a separate drum, or recycle it to the next batch. x: Copying the lab settling time into the plant batch record. Mixing extractions at full agitator speed. Ignoring interface solids as the cause of a rag layer. Draining the lower layer fast as the interface approaches. Not checking the aqueous layer for product loss.

The CH syllabus has ten sections. For 2027 IIT Madras has revised the syllabus; the main addition is fundamentals of AI and machine learning (linear regression and PCA) under Engineering Mathematics. Read the official CH syllabus for the full topic list. Section and formula sheet Typical marks Our questions Engineering Mathematics 13 (fixed) 14 Practise Process Calculations 5–8 7 Practise Thermodynamics 6–9 9 Practise Fluid Mechanics and Mechanical Operations 9–12 11 Practise Heat Transfer 7–10 9 Practise Mass Transfer 9–12 10 Practise Chemical Reaction Engineering 9–12 10 Practise Instrumentation and Process Control 7–9 9 Practise Plant Desi

Give about two hours a day to the subject of the week and 30 minutes to General Aptitude. End each week with that section in practice mode and the matching questions from the last five official papers. Week Subject Focus 1–2 Engineering Mathematics Linear algebra, calculus, ODEs, probability, numerical methods, and the new AI/ML basics. 3 Process Calculations Balances with recycle, bypass and purge; combustion; phase rule. 4–5 Thermodynamics Laws, property relations, fugacity and activity, VLE, reaction equilibrium. 6–7 Fluid Mechanics and Mechanical Operations Pipe flow, pumps, meters, settling, fluidisation, filtration, size reduction. 8–9

Do the NATs and MSQs you can solve first. They carry no negative marks, so a careful attempt never costs you. Guess MCQs only when you can rule out two options. With four options and a 1/3 penalty, a blind guess has an expected value of zero. Practise on the virtual calculator. It is slower than a handheld one; our mock test has a similar on-screen calculator. Read the rounding instruction in every NAT. Keep full precision until the last step. Bank General Aptitude. Fifteen marks for an hour of practice a week is the best return in the paper.

x: GATE CH mock test A full-length mock in the real pattern: 65 questions, 100 marks, 3 hours, with the on-screen calculator and negative marking. Each attempt draws a new set from our question bank. Overview Formula sheets Practice questions Mock test How this mock test works The mock follows the GATE Chemical Engineering (CH) pattern: 65 questions for 100 marks in 3 hours. The first 10 questions are General Aptitude (5 one-mark and 5 two-mark, 15 marks). The other 55 are Chemical Engineering, worth 85 marks, of which 13 marks come from Engineering Mathematics. One-mark questions come before two-mark questions in each part, as in the real paper. Question types and marking MCQ: one correct option out of four. A wrong answer costs 1/3 of the question's marks. MSQ: one or more options are correct. You must pick all the correct ones and nothing else. No negative marking and no partial credit.
