t: Choose the word closest in meaning to ubiquitous .
x: Q1. MCQ · 1 mark Choose the word closest in meaning to ubiquitous . rare found everywhere very old easily broken Show answer and solution Answer: (B) found everywhere Ubiquitous means present everywhere.

t: Neither the operators nor the shift supervisor ____ aware of the change in the batch sheet.
x: Q2. MCQ · 1 mark Neither the operators nor the shift supervisor ____ aware of the change in the batch sheet. were was are have been Show answer and solution Answer: (B) was With neither … nor , the verb agrees with the nearer subject, the shift supervisor (singular): was .
Q3. MCQ · 1 mark Find the next number: 3, 8, 15, 24, 35, ? 46 47 48 49 Show answer and solution Answer: (C) 48 The terms are n² - 1 for n = 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. The next is 7² - 1 = 48 .

t: Pipe A fills a tank in 6 hours and pipe B fills it in 9 hours. With both pipes open, how many hours does it take to fill the empty tank? (round to 2 decimals)
x: Q4. NAT · 1 mark Pipe A fills a tank in 6 hours and pipe B fills it in 9 hours. With both pipes open, how many hours does it take to fill the empty tank? (round to 2 decimals) Show answer and solution Answer: 3.6 (accepted range 3.58 to 3.62) Combined rate = 1/6 + 1/9 = 5/18 tank per hour, so time = 18/5 = 3.60 h .

t: Which word does not belong with the others?
x: Q5. MCQ · 1 mark Which word does not belong with the others? Litre Gallon Kilogram Barrel Show answer and solution Answer: (C) Kilogram Litre, gallon and barrel measure volume; kilogram measures mass.

t: P is taller than Q. R is shorter than Q. S is taller than P. Who is the shortest?
x: Q6. MCQ · 1 mark P is taller than Q. R is shorter than Q. S is taller than P. Who is the shortest? P Q R S Show answer and solution Answer: (C) R Order from tallest: S > P > Q > R. R is the shortest.

t: The price of a solvent rises by 20% and then falls by 20%. What is the net percentage change in price? (enter a negative number for a fall)
x: Q7. NAT · 2 marks The price of a solvent rises by 20% and then falls by 20%. What is the net percentage change in price? (enter a negative number for a fall) Show answer and solution Answer: -4 (accepted range -4.01 to -3.99) 1.20 × 0.80 = 0.96, so the price falls by 4% : answer -4.

t: Eight identical reactors produce 1200 t of product in 30 days. How many days do ten such reactors take to produce 1800 t at the same rate per reactor?
x: Q8. MCQ · 2 marks Eight identical reactors produce 1200 t of product in 30 days. How many days do ten such reactors take to produce 1800 t at the same rate per reactor? 30 36 40 45 Show answer and solution Answer: (B) 36 Rate = 1200 / (8 × 30) = 5 t per reactor-day. Days = 1800 / (10 × 5) = 36 .

t: Statements: All pumps are machines. Some machines are noisy. Which conclusion(s) follow?
x: Q9. MSQ · 2 marks Statements: All pumps are machines. Some machines are noisy. Which conclusion(s) follow? Some pumps are noisy. All pumps are machines. Some machines are pumps. No pump is noisy. Show answer and solution Answer: (B) All pumps are machines., (C) Some machines are pumps. All pumps are machines, so some machines are pumps (B, C follow). Nothing links pumps to the noisy machines, so A and D do not follow.

t: Two fair dice are thrown. What is the probability that the sum is 8? (round to 3 decimals)
x: Q10. NAT · 2 marks Two fair dice are thrown. What is the probability that the sum is 8? (round to 3 decimals) Show answer and solution Answer: 0.138889 (accepted range 0.137 to 0.14) Sums of 8: (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2), i.e. 5 of 36 outcomes. P = 5/36 = 0.139 .

t: What is the angle between the hour and minute hands of a clock at 3:40?
x: Q11. MCQ · 2 marks What is the angle between the hour and minute hands of a clock at 3:40? 120° 125° 130° 140° Show answer and solution Answer: (C) 130° Angle = |30H - 5.5M| = |90 - 220| = 130° .

t: A plant cut its steam use per tonne of product by 15% while its output rose by 10%. Total steam use has:
x: Q12. MCQ · 2 marks A plant cut its steam use per tonne of product by 15% while its output rose by 10%. Total steam use has: fallen by 6.5% fallen by 5% fallen by 15% risen by 6.5% Show answer and solution Answer: (A) fallen by 6.5% New total = 0.85 × 1.10 = 0.935 of the old, so it fell by 6.5% .

t: The eigenvalues of the matrix [[2, 1], [1, 2]] are:
x: Q1. MCQ · 1 mark The eigenvalues of the matrix [[2, 1], [1, 2]] are: 0 and 4 1 and 3 2 and 2 -1 and 3 Show answer and solution Answer: (B) 1 and 3 det(A - λI) = (2 - λ)² - 1 = 0, so λ = 1 and 3 .

t: Find the determinant of the matrix [[1, 2, 0], [0, 3, 1], [2, 0, 1]].
x: Q2. NAT · 1 mark Find the determinant of the matrix [[1, 2, 0], [0, 3, 1], [2, 0, 1]]. Show answer and solution Answer: 7 (accepted range 6.99 to 7.01) Expanding along row 1: 1(3·1 - 1·0) - 2(0·1 - 1·2) + 0 = 3 + 4 = 7 .

t: The value of limx→0 sin(3x)/x is:
x: Q3. MCQ · 1 mark The value of limx→0 sin(3x)/x is: 0 1 3 1/3 Show answer and solution Answer: (C) 3 sin(3x)/x = 3 · sin(3x)/(3x) → 3 .

t: The Laplace transform of e^-2t is:
x: Q4. MCQ · 1 mark The Laplace transform of e^-2t is: 1/(s + 2) 1/(s - 2) 2/s s/(s + 2) Show answer and solution Answer: (A) 1/(s + 2) L{e^at} = 1/(s - a); with a = -2 this is 1/(s + 2) .
Q5. NAT · 1 mark Evaluate ∫0^2 (3x² + 1) dx. Show answer and solution Answer: 10 (accepted range 9.99 to 10.01) [x³ + x] from 0 to 2 = 8 + 2 = 10 .

t: Breakdowns of a pump follow a Poisson distribution with a mean of 2 per month. The probability of no breakdown in a month is closest to:
x: Q6. MCQ · 1 mark Breakdowns of a pump follow a Poisson distribution with a mean of 2 per month. The probability of no breakdown in a month is closest to: 0.135 0.270 0.368 0.050 Show answer and solution Answer: (A) 0.135 P(0) = e^-λ = e^-2 = 0.135 .

t: In principal component analysis (PCA), the first principal component is the direction along which the data has the:
x: Q7. MCQ · 1 mark In principal component analysis (PCA), the first principal component is the direction along which the data has the: minimum variance maximum variance largest mean smallest correlation Show answer and solution Answer: (B) maximum variance PC1 is the eigenvector of the covariance matrix with the largest eigenvalue: the direction of maximum variance .

t: A straight line y = a + bx is fitted to data by ordinary least squares, with an intercept. Which statement(s) are true?
x: Q8. MSQ · 1 mark A straight line y = a + bx is fitted to data by ordinary least squares, with an intercept. Which statement(s) are true? The residuals sum to zero. The line passes through (x̄, ȳ). b = cov(x, y) / var(x). R² on the fitted data can be negative. Show answer and solution Answer: (A) The residuals sum to zero., (B) The line passes through (x̄, ȳ)., (C) b = cov(x, y) / var(x). With an intercept, the residuals sum to zero and the line passes through (x̄, ȳ); the slope is cov(x, y)/var(x). On the fitted data, R² lies between 0 and 1, so D is false.

t: Solve dy/dx = -2y with y(0) = 5. Find y(1). (round to 3 decimals)
x: Q9. NAT · 2 marks Solve dy/dx = -2y with y(0) = 5. Find y(1). (round to 3 decimals) Show answer and solution Answer: 0.676676 (accepted range 0.672 to 0.682) y = 5e^-2x, so y(1) = 5e^-2 = 0.677 .

t: Newton–Raphson is used to solve x² - 2 = 0, starting at x0 = 1. Find x2, the value after two iterations. (round to 4 decimals)
x: Q10. NAT · 2 marks Newton–Raphson is used to solve x² - 2 = 0, starting at x0 = 1. Find x2, the value after two iterations. (round to 4 decimals) Show answer and solution Answer: 1.41667 (accepted range 1.4165 to 1.4168) x1 = 1 - (1 - 2)/2 = 1.5; x2 = 1.5 - (2.25 - 2)/3 = 1.4167 .

t: Estimate ∫0^1 e^x dx by the trapezoidal rule with two equal intervals. (round to 3 decimals)
x: Q11. NAT · 2 marks Estimate ∫0^1 e^x dx by the trapezoidal rule with two equal intervals. (round to 3 decimals) Show answer and solution Answer: 1.75393 (accepted range 1.75 to 1.758) h = 0.5: (h/2)[f(0) + 2f(0.5) + f(1)] = 0.25(1 + 3.2974 + 2.7183) = 1.754 (exact 1.718).

t: The purity of a product is normally distributed with mean 50 and standard deviation 5 (arbitrary units). The probability that a sample exceeds 60 is closest to:
x: Q12. MCQ · 2 marks The purity of a product is normally distributed with mean 50 and standard deviation 5 (arbitrary units). The probability that a sample exceeds 60 is closest to: 0.159 0.050 0.023 0.001 Show answer and solution Answer: (C) 0.023 z = (60 - 50)/5 = 2; P(Z > 2) ≈ 0.023 .

t: For f(x, y, z) = x²y + yz, find the magnitude of ∇f at the point (1, 2, 3).
x: Q13. NAT · 2 marks For f(x, y, z) = x²y + yz, find the magnitude of ∇f at the point (1, 2, 3). Show answer and solution Answer: 6 (accepted range 5.99 to 6.01) ∇f = (2xy, x² + z, y) = (4, 4, 2); |∇f| = √(16 + 16 + 4) = 6 .

t: The general solution of y″ + 4y = 0 is:
x: Q14. MCQ · 2 marks The general solution of y″ + 4y = 0 is: Ae^2x + Be^-2x A cos 2x + B sin 2x (A + Bx)e^2x A cos 4x + B sin 4x Show answer and solution Answer: (B) A cos 2x + B sin 2x m² + 4 = 0 gives m = ±2i, so y = A cos 2x + B sin 2x .

t: The number of degrees of freedom (Gibbs phase rule) for pure water at its triple point is:
x: Q1. MCQ · 1 mark The number of degrees of freedom (Gibbs phase rule) for pure water at its triple point is: 0 1 2 3 Show answer and solution Answer: (A) 0 F = C - P + 2 = 1 - 3 + 2 = 0 .

t: 100 kg/h of a 20 wt% NaCl solution is concentrated to 50 wt% NaCl in an evaporator. How much water is evaporated, in kg/h?
x: Q2. NAT · 1 mark 100 kg/h of a 20 wt% NaCl solution is concentrated to 50 wt% NaCl in an evaporator. How much water is evaporated, in kg/h? Show answer and solution Answer: 60 (accepted range 59.9 to 60.1) Salt = 20 kg/h; product = 20/0.5 = 40 kg/h; water evaporated = 100 - 40 = 60 kg/h .

t: Methane is burned completely with 20% excess air (air: 21 mol% O2, 79 mol% N2). What is the mol% CO2 in the flue gas on a dry basis? (round to 1 decimal)
x: Q3. NAT · 2 marks Methane is burned completely with 20% excess air (air: 21 mol% O2, 79 mol% N2). What is the mol% CO2 in the flue gas on a dry basis? (round to 1 decimal) Show answer and solution Answer: 9.58904 (accepted range 9.5 to 9.7) Per mol CH4: O2 fed = 2 × 1.2 = 2.4; N2 = 2.4 × 79/21 = 9.029. Dry flue gas: CO2 1, O2 0.4, N2 9.029 → total 10.429. CO2 = 9.6 mol% .

t: Fresh feed of 100 mol/h of A goes to a reactor with 25% single-pass conversion. A separator after the reactor recycles all unreacted A, so the overall conversio
x: Q4. NAT · 2 marks Fresh feed of 100 mol/h of A goes to a reactor with 25% single-pass conversion. A separator after the reactor recycles all unreacted A, so the overall conversion is 100%. What is the recycle flow of A, in mol/h? Show answer and solution Answer: 300 (accepted range 299 to 301) Reactor feed F: 0.25F = 100, so F = 400 mol/h. Recycle = 400 - 100 = 300 mol/h .

t: A fresh feed of 100 mol/h contains 1 mol% inert. The inert leaves only in a purge taken from the recycle, and the recycle may hold at most 5 mol% inert. What is
x: Q5. NAT · 2 marks A fresh feed of 100 mol/h contains 1 mol% inert. The inert leaves only in a purge taken from the recycle, and the recycle may hold at most 5 mol% inert. What is the minimum purge flow, in mol/h? Show answer and solution Answer: 20 (accepted range 19.9 to 20.1) Inert balance: 100 × 0.01 = P × 0.05, so P = 20 mol/h .

t: In a material balance, a tie component is a material that:
x: Q6. MCQ · 1 mark In a material balance, a tie component is a material that: reacts completely is present only in the product passes from one stream to another unchanged is added as a catalyst Show answer and solution Answer: (C) passes from one stream to another unchanged A tie component passes from one stream to another without change in amount, so it links the two streams in the balance.

t: How much heat, in MJ, is needed to heat 500 kg of water from 25 °C to 85 °C? Take cp = 4.18 kJ/kg·K.
x: Q7. NAT · 1 mark How much heat, in MJ, is needed to heat 500 kg of water from 25 °C to 85 °C? Take cp = 4.18 kJ/kg·K. Show answer and solution Answer: 125.4 (accepted range 125 to 125.8) Q = m cp ΔT = 500 × 4.18 × 60 = 125,400 kJ = 125.4 MJ .

t: For a reversible isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, the change in internal energy is:
x: Q1. MCQ · 1 mark For a reversible isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, the change in internal energy is: positive negative zero equal to the work done Show answer and solution Answer: (C) zero U of an ideal gas depends only on T, so ΔU = 0 ; the work done equals the heat absorbed.

t: The fugacity of a pure ideal gas is equal to its:
x: Q2. MCQ · 1 mark The fugacity of a pure ideal gas is equal to its: volume pressure chemical potential activity coefficient Show answer and solution Answer: (B) pressure For an ideal gas the fugacity coefficient is 1, so f = P .

t: Which of these are state functions?
x: Q3. MSQ · 1 mark Which of these are state functions? Enthalpy Entropy Work Gibbs energy Show answer and solution Answer: (A) Enthalpy, (B) Entropy, (D) Gibbs energy Enthalpy, entropy and Gibbs energy are state functions; work depends on the path.

t: A Carnot engine works between 500 K and 300 K and takes in 1000 kJ of heat. How much work, in kJ, does it produce?
x: Q4. NAT · 2 marks A Carnot engine works between 500 K and 300 K and takes in 1000 kJ of heat. How much work, in kJ, does it produce? Show answer and solution Answer: 400 (accepted range 399.5 to 400.5) η = 1 - TC/TH = 1 - 300/500 = 0.4; W = 0.4 × 1000 = 400 kJ .

t: A benzene–toluene liquid with xbenzene = 0.4 is at its bubble point. The vapour pressures are 100 kPa (benzene) and 40 kPa (toluene). Assuming Raoult's law, fin
x: Q5. NAT · 2 marks A benzene–toluene liquid with xbenzene = 0.4 is at its bubble point. The vapour pressures are 100 kPa (benzene) and 40 kPa (toluene). Assuming Raoult's law, find ybenzene in the first vapour. (round to 3 decimals) Show answer and solution Answer: 0.625 (accepted range 0.62 to 0.63) P = 0.4 × 100 + 0.6 × 40 = 64 kPa; y = 0.4 × 100 / 64 = 0.625 .

t: Find the entropy change, in J/K, when 2 mol of an ideal gas (Cp = 29.1 J/mol·K) is heated at constant pressure from 300 K to 600 K. (round to 1 decimal)
x: Q6. NAT · 2 marks Find the entropy change, in J/K, when 2 mol of an ideal gas (Cp = 29.1 J/mol·K) is heated at constant pressure from 300 K to 600 K. (round to 1 decimal) Show answer and solution Answer: 40.3412 (accepted range 40.1 to 40.6) ΔS = n Cp ln(T2/T1) = 2 × 29.1 × ln 2 = 40.3 J/K .

Q7. MCQ · 1 mark The Gibbs–Duhem equation relates: the partial molar properties of the components of a mixture heat and work in a cycle pressure and temperature along a phase boundary the rate constant and temperature Show answer and solution Answer: (A) the partial molar properties of the components of a mixture At constant T and P, Σ xi dM̄i = 0: it links the partial molar properties of the components in a mixture .

t: For a reaction at 500 K, ΔG° = -10 kJ/mol. Find the equilibrium constant K. Take R = 8.314 J/mol·K. (round to 2 decimals)
x: Q8. NAT · 2 marks For a reaction at 500 K, ΔG° = -10 kJ/mol. Find the equilibrium constant K. Take R = 8.314 J/mol·K. (round to 2 decimals) Show answer and solution Answer: 11.0849 (accepted range 10.95 to 11.2) K = exp(-ΔG°/RT) = exp(10000 / (8.314 × 500)) = exp(2.4056) = 11.08 .

t: A binary liquid follows the one-parameter Margules model, ln γ1 = A x2², with A = 1.0. Find γ1 at x1 = 0.3. (round to 3 decimals)
x: Q9. NAT · 2 marks A binary liquid follows the one-parameter Margules model, ln γ1 = A x2², with A = 1.0. Find γ1 at x1 = 0.3. (round to 3 decimals) Show answer and solution Answer: 1.63232 (accepted range 1.625 to 1.64) x2 = 0.7; ln γ1 = 0.49; γ1 = e^0.49 = 1.632 .

t: For laminar flow in a circular pipe, the Fanning friction factor is:
x: Q1. MCQ · 1 mark For laminar flow in a circular pipe, the Fanning friction factor is: 64/Re 16/Re 0.079 Re^-0.25 8/Re Show answer and solution Answer: (B) 16/Re fFanning = 16/Re (the Darcy factor is 64/Re).

t: In fully developed laminar flow in a pipe, the maximum velocity is how many times the average velocity?
x: Q2. MCQ · 1 mark In fully developed laminar flow in a pipe, the maximum velocity is how many times the average velocity? 1.0 1.22 2.0 0.82 Show answer and solution Answer: (C) 2.0 The profile is parabolic: vmax = 2 vavg.

t: Water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, μ = 0.001 Pa·s) flows at an average velocity of 0.02 m/s through a 50 mm ID pipe. Find the pressure drop over 10 m, in Pa. (round to 2 de
x: Q3. NAT · 2 marks Water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, μ = 0.001 Pa·s) flows at an average velocity of 0.02 m/s through a 50 mm ID pipe. Find the pressure drop over 10 m, in Pa. (round to 2 decimals) Show answer and solution Answer: 2.56 (accepted range 2.54 to 2.58) Re = 1000 × 0.02 × 0.05 / 0.001 = 1000, so the flow is laminar. Hagen–Poiseuille: ΔP = 32 μ L v / D² = 32 × 0.001 × 10 × 0.02 / 0.0025 = 2.56 Pa .

t: Water drains from a large open tank through a small hole 5 m below the free surface. Neglecting losses, find the jet velocity in m/s. (g = 9.81 m/s², round to 2
x: Q4. NAT · 2 marks Water drains from a large open tank through a small hole 5 m below the free surface. Neglecting losses, find the jet velocity in m/s. (g = 9.81 m/s², round to 2 decimals) Show answer and solution Answer: 9.90454 (accepted range 9.85 to 9.95) Torricelli: v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 9.81 × 5) = 9.90 m/s .

Q5. MCQ · 1 mark A Bingham plastic fluid: needs a yield stress before it flows has viscosity that falls with time has viscosity that rises with shear rate behaves as a Newtonian fluid at all stresses Show answer and solution Answer: (A) needs a yield stress before it flows A Bingham plastic does not flow until the shear stress exceeds a yield stress ; above it, stress rises linearly with shear rate.

t: A pump delivers 36 m³/h of water against a total head of 30 m with an overall efficiency of 60%. Find the power input in kW. (g = 9.81 m/s², round to 2 decimals
x: Q6. NAT · 2 marks A pump delivers 36 m³/h of water against a total head of 30 m with an overall efficiency of 60%. Find the power input in kW. (g = 9.81 m/s², round to 2 decimals) Show answer and solution Answer: 4.905 (accepted range 4.85 to 4.95) Q = 0.01 m³/s. P = ρ g Q H / η = 1000 × 9.81 × 0.01 × 30 / 0.6 = 4905 W = 4.91 kW .

t: In the Stokes' law regime, the terminal settling velocity of a sphere is proportional to:
x: Q7. MCQ · 1 mark In the Stokes' law regime, the terminal settling velocity of a sphere is proportional to: d d² d^0.5 1/d Show answer and solution Answer: (B) d² vt = g d² (ρp - ρ) / 18μ, so vt ∝ d² .

t: Find the terminal settling velocity, in mm/s, of a 50 µm sand particle (ρp = 2650 kg/m³) in water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, μ = 0.001 Pa·s), assuming Stokes' law. (round
x: Q8. NAT · 2 marks Find the terminal settling velocity, in mm/s, of a 50 µm sand particle (ρp = 2650 kg/m³) in water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, μ = 0.001 Pa·s), assuming Stokes' law. (round to 2 decimals) Show answer and solution Answer: 2.24812 (accepted range 2.2 to 2.3) vt = 9.81 × (50 × 10^-6)² × 1650 / (18 × 0.001) = 2.25e-03 m/s = 2.25 mm/s . Check: Re ≈ 0.11, so Stokes applies.

x: Q9. NAT · 2 marks A bed of particles (ρp = 2500 kg/m³) is fluidised by air (ρ = 1.2 kg/m³). At minimum fluidisation the bed is 1.0 m deep with a voidage of 0.45. Find the pressure drop across the bed, in kPa. (g = 9.81 m/s², round to 1 decimal) Show answer and solution Answer: 13.4823 (accepted range 13.4 to 13.6) ΔP = (1 - ε)(ρp - ρ) g L = 0.55 × 2498.8 × 9.81 × 1.0 = 13.5 kPa : the weight of the bed per unit area.

t: Which law of size reduction states that the energy needed is proportional to the new surface area created?
x: Q10. MCQ · 1 mark Which law of size reduction states that the energy needed is proportional to the new surface area created? Rittinger's law Kick's law Bond's law Stokes' law Show answer and solution Answer: (A) Rittinger's law Rittinger's law : E = KR(1/D2 - 1/D1).

t: In constant-pressure cake filtration, a plot of t/V against V (t = time, V = filtrate volume) is a straight line. Its slope is proportional to:
x: Q11. MCQ · 2 marks In constant-pressure cake filtration, a plot of t/V against V (t = time, V = filtrate volume) is a straight line. Its slope is proportional to: the filter medium resistance only the filtrate density the specific cake resistance the square of the filter area Show answer and solution Answer: (C) the specific cake resistance t/V = (μ α c / 2A²ΔP) V + μ Rm/(AΔP). The slope contains the specific cake resistance α ; the intercept gives the medium resistance.

t: The conduction resistance of a plane wall of thickness L, conductivity k and area A is:
x: Q1. MCQ · 1 mark The conduction resistance of a plane wall of thickness L, conductivity k and area A is: L/(kA) kA/L k/(LA) 1/(hA) Show answer and solution Answer: (A) L/(kA) R = L/(kA) .

t: A furnace wall has 0.2 m of brick (k = 0.7 W/m·K) and 0.05 m of insulation (k = 0.05 W/m·K). The inner face is at 600 °C and the outer face at 50 °C. Find the h
x: Q2. NAT · 2 marks A furnace wall has 0.2 m of brick (k = 0.7 W/m·K) and 0.05 m of insulation (k = 0.05 W/m·K). The inner face is at 600 °C and the outer face at 50 °C. Find the heat loss in W/m². (round to the nearest whole number) Show answer and solution Answer: 427.778 (accepted range 425 to 431) q = ΔT / ΣR = 550 / (0.2/0.7 + 0.05/0.05) = 550 / 1.2857 = 428 W/m² .

t: In a counter-current exchanger the hot fluid cools from 150 °C to 90 °C and the cold fluid heats from 30 °C to 70 °C. Find the LMTD in °C. (round to 1 decimal)
x: Q3. NAT · 2 marks In a counter-current exchanger the hot fluid cools from 150 °C to 90 °C and the cold fluid heats from 30 °C to 70 °C. Find the LMTD in °C. (round to 1 decimal) Show answer and solution Answer: 69.5212 (accepted range 69.3 to 69.7) ΔT1 = 150 - 70 = 80, ΔT2 = 90 - 30 = 60; LMTD = 20 / ln(80/60) = 69.5 °C .

t: The Nusselt number represents the ratio of:
x: Q4. MCQ · 1 mark The Nusselt number represents the ratio of: momentum to thermal diffusivity convective to conductive heat transfer buoyancy to viscous forces inertial to viscous forces Show answer and solution Answer: (B) convective to conductive heat transfer Nu = hL/k: convective to conductive heat transfer across the fluid layer.

t: Water is heated in turbulent flow in a tube with Re = 10,000 and Pr = 5. Using the Dittus–Boelter equation, find the Nusselt number. (round to the nearest whole
x: Q5. NAT · 2 marks Water is heated in turbulent flow in a tube with Re = 10,000 and Pr = 5. Using the Dittus–Boelter equation, find the Nusselt number. (round to the nearest whole number) Show answer and solution Answer: 69.393 (accepted range 68.5 to 70.5) Nu = 0.023 Re^0.8 Pr^0.4 (heating) = 0.023 × 1584.9 × 1.904 = 69 .

t: The total emissive power of a black body is proportional to its absolute temperature raised to the power:
x: Q6. MCQ · 1 mark The total emissive power of a black body is proportional to its absolute temperature raised to the power: 1 2 3 4 Show answer and solution Answer: (D) 4 Stefan–Boltzmann: E = σT^4.

t: A small pipe is insulated with a material of k = 0.08 W/m·K; the outside coefficient is h = 8 W/m²·K. Find the critical radius of insulation, in mm.
x: Q7. NAT · 2 marks A small pipe is insulated with a material of k = 0.08 W/m·K; the outside coefficient is h = 8 W/m²·K. Find the critical radius of insulation, in mm. Show answer and solution Answer: 10 (accepted range 9.95 to 10.05) rc = k/h = 0.08/8 = 0.01 m = 10 mm . Below this radius, adding insulation increases the heat loss.

t: A single-effect evaporator receives feed at its boiling point and evaporates 1000 kg/h of water (latent heat 2257 kJ/kg). The heating steam gives up 2200 kJ/kg.
x: Q8. NAT · 2 marks A single-effect evaporator receives feed at its boiling point and evaporates 1000 kg/h of water (latent heat 2257 kJ/kg). The heating steam gives up 2200 kJ/kg. Neglecting losses, find the steam economy (kg evaporated per kg steam). (round to 3 decimals) Show answer and solution Answer: 0.974745 (accepted range 0.97 to 0.98) Steam = 1000 × 2257 / 2200 = 1025.9 kg/h; economy = 1000 / 1025.9 = 0.975 .

t: Which of these increase the overall heat transfer coefficient of an exchanger?
x: Q9. MSQ · 1 mark Which of these increase the overall heat transfer coefficient of an exchanger? Raising the fluid velocity Fouling on the tubes A thinner wall of higher conductivity Dropwise instead of filmwise condensation Show answer and solution Answer: (A) Raising the fluid velocity, (C) A thinner wall of higher conductivity, (D) Dropwise instead of filmwise condensation Higher velocity raises film coefficients, a thin high-k wall lowers wall resistance, and dropwise condensation gives a much higher coefficient than filmwise. Fouling adds resistance.

t: Fick's first law states that the molar diffusion flux is proportional to the:
x: Q1. MCQ · 1 mark Fick's first law states that the molar diffusion flux is proportional to the: concentration square of concentration concentration gradient temperature gradient Show answer and solution Answer: (C) concentration gradient J = -DAB dCA/dz: proportional to the concentration gradient .

t: According to Higbie's penetration theory, the mass transfer coefficient varies with diffusivity as:
x: Q2. MCQ · 1 mark According to Higbie's penetration theory, the mass transfer coefficient varies with diffusivity as: D D^0.5 D^2/3 D^0 Show answer and solution Answer: (B) D^0.5 kL = 2√(D/πt): k ∝ D^0.5 (film theory gives D^1).

t: A binary mixture with constant relative volatility α = 2.5 is fed as saturated liquid with xF = 0.5. The distillate is xD = 0.95. Find the minimum reflux ratio.
x: Q3. NAT · 2 marks A binary mixture with constant relative volatility α = 2.5 is fed as saturated liquid with xF = 0.5. The distillate is xD = 0.95. Find the minimum reflux ratio. (round to 2 decimals) Show answer and solution Answer: 1.1 (accepted range 1.08 to 1.12) For a saturated-liquid feed the pinch is at x = 0.5: y* = 2.5 × 0.5 / (1 + 1.5 × 0.5) = 0.7143. Rmin = (xD - y*)/(y* - x*) = 0.2357 / 0.2143 = 1.10 .

t: Using the Fenske equation, find the minimum number of theoretical stages (including the reboiler) to separate a binary with α = 2.5 into xD = 0.95 and xB = 0.05
x: Q4. NAT · 2 marks Using the Fenske equation, find the minimum number of theoretical stages (including the reboiler) to separate a binary with α = 2.5 into xD = 0.95 and xB = 0.05. (round to 2 decimals) Show answer and solution Answer: 6.42687 (accepted range 6.4 to 6.46) Nmin = ln[(0.95/0.05)(0.95/0.05)] / ln 2.5 = ln 361 / 0.9163 = 6.43 .

t: In gas absorption with an equilibrium line y = mx, the absorption factor is:
x: Q5. MCQ · 1 mark In gas absorption with an equilibrium line y = mx, the absorption factor is: L/(mG) mG/L G/(mL) mL/G Show answer and solution Answer: (A) L/(mG) A = L/(mG) ; A > 1 makes complete absorption possible with enough stages.

t: A dilute solute is absorbed in a packed column into pure solvent with a very large absorption factor (equilibrium back-pressure negligible). For 98% removal wit
x: Q6. NAT · 2 marks A dilute solute is absorbed in a packed column into pure solvent with a very large absorption factor (equilibrium back-pressure negligible). For 98% removal with HOG = 0.5 m, find the packed height in m. (round to 2 decimals) Show answer and solution Answer: 1.95601 (accepted range 1.94 to 1.97) With y* ≈ 0, NOG = ln(y1/y2) = ln(1/0.02) = 3.912. Z = HOG NOG = 1.96 m .

t: During the constant-rate period of drying, the drying rate is controlled by:
x: Q7. MCQ · 1 mark During the constant-rate period of drying, the drying rate is controlled by: diffusion of moisture inside the solid external heat and mass transfer at the surface the bound moisture content the equilibrium moisture content Show answer and solution Answer: (B) external heat and mass transfer at the surface The surface is covered with free water, so the rate is set by external heat and mass transfer to and from the surface, as for a free water surface.

t: Air at 101.325 kPa is saturated with water vapour at 25 °C, where the vapour pressure of water is 3.17 kPa. Find the absolute humidity in kg water per kg dry ai
x: Q8. NAT · 2 marks Air at 101.325 kPa is saturated with water vapour at 25 °C, where the vapour pressure of water is 3.17 kPa. Find the absolute humidity in kg water per kg dry air. (round to 4 decimals) Show answer and solution Answer: 0.020088 (accepted range 0.0199 to 0.0203) H = 0.622 pw/(P - pw) = 0.622 × 3.17 / 98.155 = 0.0201 kg/kg .

t: In a single equilibrium extraction stage, the distribution coefficient (solute-free mass ratio basis) is K = 4, and the solvent-to-feed ratio (solute-free basis
x: Q9. NAT · 2 marks In a single equilibrium extraction stage, the distribution coefficient (solute-free mass ratio basis) is K = 4, and the solvent-to-feed ratio (solute-free basis) is 0.5. Find the percentage of solute extracted. (round to 1 decimal) Show answer and solution Answer: 66.6667 (accepted range 66.4 to 66.9) Extraction factor E = K S/F = 2; fraction extracted = E/(1 + E) = 2/3 = 66.7% .

t: For distillation of a binary mixture, which statement(s) are true?

A higher α needs fewer stages. α > 1 means the heavy key is more volatile. Show answer and solution Answer: (A) α = 1 means distillation cannot separate the mixture., (B) α can change with temperature., (C) A higher α needs fewer stages. α = 1 means vapour and liquid have the same composition, so distillation cannot separate them; α can change with temperature; a higher α needs fewer stages. t: The units of the rate constant of a second-order reaction (rate in mol/L·s) are:
x: Q1. MCQ · 1 mark The units of the rate constant of a second-order reaction (rate in mol/L·s) are: s^-1 L/(mol·s) mol/(L·s) L²/(mol²·s) Show answer and solution Answer: (B) L/(mol·s) k = r/C² → (mol/L·s)/(mol/L)² = L/(mol·s) .

t: A first-order reaction with k = 0.1 min^-1 runs in a batch reactor. How long, in minutes, for 90% conversion? (round to 2 decimals)
x: Q2. NAT · 2 marks A first-order reaction with k = 0.1 min^-1 runs in a batch reactor. How long, in minutes, for 90% conversion? (round to 2 decimals) Show answer and solution Answer: 23.0259 (accepted range 22.9 to 23.1) t = ln(1/(1 - X))/k = ln 10 / 0.1 = 23.03 min .

t: A liquid-phase first-order reaction (k = 0.5 min^-1) is run to 80% conversion. Find the ratio of the CSTR volume to the PFR volume needed for the same feed rate
x: Q3. NAT · 2 marks A liquid-phase first-order reaction (k = 0.5 min^-1) is run to 80% conversion. Find the ratio of the CSTR volume to the PFR volume needed for the same feed rate. (round to 2 decimals) Show answer and solution Answer: 2.48534 (accepted range 2.47 to 2.5) CSTR: τ = X/(k(1 - X)) = 0.8/0.1 = 8.00 min. PFR: τ = -ln(1 - X)/k = 3.219 min. Ratio = 2.49 .

t: A reaction rate doubles when the temperature rises from 300 K to 310 K. Find the activation energy in kJ/mol. (R = 8.314 J/mol·K, round to 1 decimal)
x: Q4. NAT · 2 marks A reaction rate doubles when the temperature rises from 300 K to 310 K. Find the activation energy in kJ/mol. (R = 8.314 J/mol·K, round to 1 decimal) Show answer and solution Answer: 53.5943 (accepted range 53.2 to 54) ln 2 = (E/R)(1/300 - 1/310), so E = 8.314 × 0.6931 / 1.0753 × 10^-4 = 53.6 kJ/mol .

t: The exit age distribution E(t) of an ideal CSTR with mean residence time τ is:
x: Q5. MCQ · 1 mark The exit age distribution E(t) of an ideal CSTR with mean residence time τ is: δ(t - τ) 1/τ for t ≤ τ (1/τ) e^-t/τ t/τ² e^-t/τ Show answer and solution Answer: (C) (1/τ) e^-t/τ For a perfectly mixed vessel, E(t) = (1/τ) e^-t/τ .

t: An enzyme follows Michaelis–Menten kinetics with Vmax = 10 µmol/min and Km = 2 mM. Find the rate, in µmol/min, at a substrate concentration of 2 mM.
x: Q6. NAT · 1 mark An enzyme follows Michaelis–Menten kinetics with Vmax = 10 µmol/min and Km = 2 mM. Find the rate, in µmol/min, at a substrate concentration of 2 mM. Show answer and solution Answer: 5 (accepted range 4.99 to 5.01) r = VmaxS/(Km + S) = 10 × 2/(2 + 2) = 5 µmol/min : at S = Km, the rate is half of Vmax.

t: For a first-order reaction in a porous catalyst slab, when the Thiele modulus φ is large the effectiveness factor approaches:
x: Q7. MCQ · 1 mark For a first-order reaction in a porous catalyst slab, when the Thiele modulus φ is large the effectiveness factor approaches: 1 1/φ φ 0 exactly Show answer and solution Answer: (B) 1/φ η = tanh(φ)/φ → 1/φ for large φ: strong pore-diffusion resistance.

t: A first-order reaction (k = 0.2 min^-1) runs in two equal CSTRs in series with a total mean residence time of 10 min. Find the overall conversion. (round to 2 d
x: Q8. NAT · 2 marks A first-order reaction (k = 0.2 min^-1) runs in two equal CSTRs in series with a total mean residence time of 10 min. Find the overall conversion. (round to 2 decimals) Show answer and solution Answer: 0.75 (accepted range 0.745 to 0.755) Each tank: τ = 5 min, kτ = 1. X = 1 - 1/(1 + kτ)² = 1 - 1/4 = 0.75 .

t: Parallel reactions: A → R (desired, rate ∝ CA²) and A → S (rate ∝ CA). Which choice favours R?
x: Q9. MCQ · 2 marks Parallel reactions: A → R (desired, rate ∝ CA²) and A → S (rate ∝ CA). Which choice favours R? A plug flow or batch reactor, without dilution A single large CSTR Diluting the feed with inert Recycling product to the reactor inlet Show answer and solution Answer: (A) A plug flow or batch reactor, without dilution The desired reaction has the higher order, so keep CA high : use a PFR or batch reactor, avoid dilution and back-mixing.

t: Which of these raise the equilibrium conversion of a reversible exothermic reaction?
x: Q10. MSQ · 1 mark Which of these raise the equilibrium conversion of a reversible exothermic reaction? Lowering the temperature Adding a catalyst Removing a product as it forms Raising the temperature Show answer and solution Answer: (A) Lowering the temperature, (C) Removing a product as it forms Lower temperature shifts equilibrium towards products for an exothermic reaction, and removing product shifts it forward. A catalyst only changes the rate, not the equilibrium.

t: After a step change, a first-order system reaches what fraction of its final change in one time constant?
x: Q1. MCQ · 1 mark After a step change, a first-order system reaches what fraction of its final change in one time constant? 36.8% 50% 63.2% 86.5% Show answer and solution Answer: (C) 63.2% 1 - e^-1 = 63.2% .

t: A process has G(s) = 2/(5s + 1). The input steps by 3 units at t = 0. Find the output change at t = 5 s. (round to 2 decimals)
x: Q2. NAT · 2 marks A process has G(s) = 2/(5s + 1). The input steps by 3 units at t = 0. Find the output change at t = 5 s. (round to 2 decimals) Show answer and solution Answer: 3.79272 (accepted range 3.78 to 3.81) y(t) = K M (1 - e^-t/τ) = 2 × 3 × (1 - e^-1) = 3.79 .

t: A proportional-only controller on a self-regulating process, after a step change in set point, gives:
x: Q3. MCQ · 1 mark A proportional-only controller on a self-regulating process, after a step change in set point, gives: no offset a steady-state offset an unstable response always an inverse response Show answer and solution Answer: (B) a steady-state offset P-only control leaves a steady-state offset ; integral action removes it.

t: A second-order underdamped system has damping ratio ζ = 0.5. Find the overshoot (as a fraction) for a step input. (round to 3 decimals)
x: Q4. NAT · 2 marks A second-order underdamped system has damping ratio ζ = 0.5. Find the overshoot (as a fraction) for a step input. (round to 3 decimals) Show answer and solution Answer: 0.163034 (accepted range 0.16 to 0.166) OS = exp(-πζ/√(1 - ζ²)) = exp(-1.814) = 0.163 .

t: A loop has ultimate gain Ku = 4 and ultimate period Pu = 10 min. Using Ziegler–Nichols settings for a PI controller, find the controller gain Kc. (round to 2 de
x: Q5. NAT · 2 marks A loop has ultimate gain Ku = 4 and ultimate period Pu = 10 min. Using Ziegler–Nichols settings for a PI controller, find the controller gain Kc. (round to 2 decimals) Show answer and solution Answer: 1.8 (accepted range 1.79 to 1.81) Z-N PI: Kc = 0.45 Ku = 1.80 , τI = Pu/1.2 = 8.33 min.

t: An air-to-open control valve, on loss of instrument air, will:
x: Q6. MCQ · 1 mark An air-to-open control valve, on loss of instrument air, will: fail open fail closed stay in its last position open to 50% Show answer and solution Answer: (B) fail closed Air opens it, so with no air the spring closes it: fail closed.

t: The closed-loop characteristic equation is s³ + 2s² + 3s + K = 0. The system is stable for:
x: Q7. MCQ · 2 marks The closed-loop characteristic equation is s³ + 2s² + 3s + K = 0. The system is stable for: K > 0 0 0 K > 6 Show answer and solution Answer: (C) 0 Routh array: rows (1, 3), (2, K), ((6 - K)/2, 0), (K). Stability needs 6 - K > 0 and K > 0: 0 .

t: In cascade control, the inner (secondary) loop should be:
x: Q8. MCQ · 1 mark In cascade control, the inner (secondary) loop should be: faster than the outer loop slower than the outer loop tuned with integral action only open loop Show answer and solution Answer: (A) faster than the outer loop The secondary loop must be faster than the primary so it can correct disturbances before they reach the primary variable.

t: In ISA 5.1 P&ID symbols, an instrument bubble (circle) with a single solid horizontal line through it means the instrument is:
x: Q9. MCQ · 1 mark In ISA 5.1 P&ID symbols, an instrument bubble (circle) with a single solid horizontal line through it means the instrument is: field mounted in the main control room, accessible to the operator behind the panel, not accessible a software function only Show answer and solution Answer: (B) in the main control room, accessible to the operator A plain circle is field-mounted; a solid line means it is in the main control room or panel, accessible to the operator .

t: Equipment costing ₹10 lakh has a salvage value of ₹1 lakh after a 9-year life. Using straight-line depreciation, find its book value in ₹ lakh after 4 years.
x: Q1. NAT · 2 marks Equipment costing ₹10 lakh has a salvage value of ₹1 lakh after a 9-year life. Using straight-line depreciation, find its book value in ₹ lakh after 4 years. Show answer and solution Answer: 6 (accepted range 5.99 to 6.01) Annual depreciation = (10 - 1)/9 = 1 lakh. Book value after 4 years = 10 - 4 = ₹6 lakh .

t: A 2000 L reactor costs ₹5 lakh. Using the six-tenths rule, estimate the cost of an 8000 L reactor of the same type, in ₹ lakh. (round to 2 decimals)
x: Q2. NAT · 2 marks A 2000 L reactor costs ₹5 lakh. Using the six-tenths rule, estimate the cost of an 8000 L reactor of the same type, in ₹ lakh. (round to 2 decimals) Show answer and solution Answer: 11.487 (accepted range 11.4 to 11.6) C2 = C1(V2/V1)^0.6 = 5 × 4^0.6 = ₹11.49 lakh .

t: Equipment cost ₹20 lakh when the cost index was 500. The index is now 650. Estimate its present cost in ₹ lakh.
x: Q3. NAT · 1 mark Equipment cost ₹20 lakh when the cost index was 500. The index is now 650. Estimate its present cost in ₹ lakh. Show answer and solution Answer: 26 (accepted range 25.9 to 26.1) Present cost = 20 × 650/500 = ₹26 lakh .

t: The payback period is the time needed for:
x: Q4. MCQ · 1 mark The payback period is the time needed for: the plant to reach design capacity the loan interest to be paid the cash flow to recover the fixed capital investment equipment to be fully depreciated Show answer and solution Answer: (C) the cash flow to recover the fixed capital investment Payback = fixed capital investment / annual cash flow (profit after tax + depreciation): the time to recover the fixed capital from cash flow.

t: Find the present worth, in ₹ lakh, of ₹1 lakh to be received 5 years from now at 10% interest compounded annually. (round to 3 decimals)
x: Q5. NAT · 2 marks Find the present worth, in ₹ lakh, of ₹1 lakh to be received 5 years from now at 10% interest compounded annually. (round to 3 decimals) Show answer and solution Answer: 0.620921 (accepted range 0.619 to 0.622) PW = 1 / 1.1^5 = ₹0.621 lakh .

t: The optimum economic pipe diameter balances:
x: Q6. MCQ · 1 mark The optimum economic pipe diameter balances: pumping cost against the fixed cost of the pipe velocity against density insulation against heat loss only corrosion against erosion Show answer and solution Answer: (A) pumping cost against the fixed cost of the pipe A larger pipe costs more to buy and install but less to pump through: the optimum minimises the sum of pumping and fixed pipe costs .

t: Three batches are made in one reactor (4 h per batch) followed by one filter (3 h per batch). A batch can be filtered while the next one reacts. What is the min
x: Q7. MCQ · 2 marks Three batches are made in one reactor (4 h per batch) followed by one filter (3 h per batch). A batch can be filtered while the next one reacts. What is the minimum time to finish all three batches? 12 h 15 h 18 h 21 h Show answer and solution Answer: (B) 15 h The reactor is the bottleneck: it finishes batch 3 at 12 h, and filtering that batch ends at 15 h .

t: In the contact process for sulfuric acid, SO2 is oxidised to SO3 over:
x: Q1. MCQ · 1 mark In the contact process for sulfuric acid, SO2 is oxidised to SO3 over: nickel platinum gauze only vanadium pentoxide iron oxide Show answer and solution Answer: (C) vanadium pentoxide Promoted vanadium pentoxide (V2O5) .

t: The catalyst used in Haber–Bosch ammonia synthesis is:
x: Q2. MCQ · 1 mark The catalyst used in Haber–Bosch ammonia synthesis is: promoted iron silver copper–zinc oxide zeolite Show answer and solution Answer: (A) promoted iron Promoted iron (with K2O and Al2O3).

t: Urea is made from ammonia and carbon dioxide through the intermediate:
x: Q3. MCQ · 1 mark Urea is made from ammonia and carbon dioxide through the intermediate: ammonium nitrate ammonium carbamate cyanamide ammonium sulfate Show answer and solution Answer: (B) ammonium carbamate 2NH3 + CO2 → ammonium carbamate → urea + H2O.

t: In a membrane-cell chlor-alkali plant, the products at the cathode are:

t: The cooking liquor (white liquor) in kraft pulping is mainly:
x: Q5. MCQ · 1 mark The cooking liquor (white liquor) in kraft pulping is mainly: Na2SO3 + SO2 NaOH + Na2S H2SO4 Ca(HSO3)2 Show answer and solution Answer: (B) NaOH + Na2S Kraft white liquor is NaOH + Na2S .

t: Ethylene oxide is made commercially by direct oxidation of ethylene over a catalyst of:
x: Q6. MCQ · 1 mark Ethylene oxide is made commercially by direct oxidation of ethylene over a catalyst of: silver vanadium nickel platinum Show answer and solution Answer: (A) silver Silver on alumina.

x: Process modelling for scale-up Simple models answer most lab-to-plant questions before the first plant batch: how long the heat-up takes, whether the dosing is safe, how fast the reaction runs at plant temperature, what agitator speed suspends the solids, and how much solvent a swap needs. These five tools run in your browser, free, with your own data, and every result downloads to Excel. 🌡️ Heating and Cooling Time Simulator How long a jacketed batch takes to heat or cool, with the temperature curve, jacket duty and steam or TR. Fit the kinetics from two or three lab runs at different temperatures. Simulate the dosing at plant scale with the fitted k and Ea, the heat of reaction from RC1 and the plant jacket. Check accumulation, MTSR and the cooling margin. Check the heat-up and cool-down steps so the batch record times are realistic. Check the mixing : solids suspension for slurries, kLa for gas reactions, and the process-side heat transfer coefficient for the jacket. s: Free batch heating and cooling time simulator for jacketed reactors: temperature curve, jacket duty, steam use and TR, for steam, brine or glass-lined vessels.
x: Batch heating and cooling time simulator How long will the batch take to reach temperature? Enter the batch, the jacket and the utility, and the simulator steps through time to give the temperature curve, the jacket duty and the steam or refrigeration needed. It handles a steam jacket, brine or water with limited flow, and glass-lined vessels where the jacket must stay within a set ΔT of the batch. How it works m cp dT/dt = Qjacket + Pagitator - UAloss (T - Tamb) Fixed utility temperature (condensing steam, high-flow brine): Q = UA (Tu - T). The time has a closed form, t = (m cp/UA) ln[(Tu - T0)/(Tu - Ttarget)], which the tool shows as a check. Limited utility flow : the utility warms or cools as it passes through the jacket, so Q = ṁcp,u (Tu - T)(1 - e^-UA/ṁcp,u). Low flow can be the real bottleneck, not the area. t: Why plant batches heat and cool slower than the lab
s: Batch heating and cooling time simulator
x: The time scales with m cp/UA. Volume grows with the cube of the vessel size but jacket area only with the square, so a 10 KL reactor has roughly one tenth of the area per kg of a 10 L lab reactor. A step that heats in 20 minutes in the lab can take hours in the plant. Use this tool before tech transfer to set realistic heat-up and cool-down times in the batch record.

x: Mixing and mass transfer scale-up Enter the lab vessel and the plant vessel side by side. The toolbox compares power per volume, blend time, the speed needed to suspend solids (Njs), the gas-liquid mass transfer coefficient (kLa) and the process-side heat transfer coefficient, then gives the plant speed you need to keep each one the same. The retreat-curve value is an estimate. Blend ti

Correlations are only as good as their constants. Two simple lab observations make the plant prediction far more reliable: the speed at which no solid rests on the base for more than 1 to 2 seconds (enter it as the lab Njs and the tool back-calculates S), and if gas matters, a measured kLa. Keep the plant geometry similar (same D/T, impeller type and clearance) for the scaling to hold.

No single speed keeps everything the same on scale-up. Keep N/Njs for slurries and crystallisation, P/V for blending and gas dispersion, tip speed for shear-sensitive crystals, and look at blend time when fast competing reactions are involved. For more on the rules, read mixing scale-up from lab to plant .

s: Free reaction kinetics fitting tool: paste conversion vs time at several temperatures, fit rate constant and activation energy, and predict plant batch time.
x: Reaction kinetics fitting Paste HPLC or GC conversion results from lab runs at two or more temperatures. The tool fits the rate constant at each temperature, draws the Arrhenius plot to get the activation energy, and predicts the time to your target conversion at the plant temperature. It is the first step of any process model. How it works First order : X = 1 - e^-kt. Second order, A + B , with M = [B]0/[A]0: ln[(M - X)/(M(1 - X))] = [A]0(M - 1) k t (and X = k[A]0t/(1 + k[A]0t) when M = 1). nth order : (1 - X)^1-n = 1 + (n - 1) k [A]0^n-1 t, with n fitted across all temperatures. For each temperature, k is found by least squares on conversion. With two or more temperatures, a straight line through ln k against 1/T gives the activation energy: ln k = ln A - Ea/(RT) . Getting good data Run at least three temperatures, 10 to 15 °C apart, around the planned plant temperature. Take 6 to 10 s

For each temperature, k is found by least squares on conversion. With two or more temperatures, a straight line through ln k against 1/T gives the activation energy: ln k = ln A - Ea/(RT) .

Run at least three temperatures, 10 to 15 °C apart, around the planned plant temperature. Take 6 to 10 samples per run, more at the start when conversion changes fastest, and quench each sample immediately. Keep the temperature steady. Add the reagent quickly (or all at once) so the start time is clear. Use the same stoichiometry and concentration as the plant process. The sample data loaded in the tool is made up for illustration. Replace it with your own.

Try each rate law and keep the one with the highest R² at every temperature and no pattern in the misfit. A rate that changes about 2× per 10 °C is typical (Ea around 50 to 70 kJ/mol). Use the fitted k and Ea in the semi-batch dosing simulator to check heat release and accumulation at plant scale.

s: Free semi-batch dosing simulator: heat release, accumulation and MTSR during dosing from your kinetics, cooling capacity check and shortest safe dosing time.
x: Semi-batch dosing simulator Dose reagent B into substrate A and watch what happens through the dose: how much heat the reaction gives, whether the jacket can remove it, how much unreacted reagent builds up, and how hot the batch would get if cooling failed at any moment (the MTSR). One click finds the shortest dosing time that keeps the MTSR below your limits. How it works The tool integrates the mole balances for A and B with the dosing profile and the rate law (second order, rate = k[A][B], or first order in B), with k following Arrhenius. The reactor is assumed to stay at the set temperature. MTSR(t) = Tr + nunreacted(t) × (-ΔHr) / (m(t) cp) Accumulation is the reagent that has been dosed but has not reacted yet, as a percentage of the limiting reagent. It is the fuel for a runaway if cooling fails. Cooling needed = heat of reaction + heat to bring the feed to the reaction temperature

Fit k and Ea from lab samples with the kinetics fitting tool , or from RC1 heat flow. ΔHr comes from RC1, and TD24 from DSC or ARC data. If you only have RC1 accumulation at one dosing time, use the addition time calculator .

Lower the reaction temperature in the tool and watch the accumulation rise. A slower reaction lets dosed reagent pile up, so a cooling failure late in the dose can release more heat than at a higher temperature. The right temperature keeps the reaction fast enough to consume the reagent as it is added, while the MTSR stays below the limits.

s: Free solvent swap simulator: compare put-and-take and constant-volume distillation for 86 solvents, with solvent used, distillate, time and residual solvent.
x: Solvent swap simulator Changing from one solvent to another in the reactor is one of the longest steps in many API processes. Choose the two solvents, the pressure and the volumes, and the simulator works out how much new solvent and distillation time each method needs to bring the old solvent below your limit. How it works The batch is treated as a single-stage still (no column). At each step the bubble point is found from Raoult’s law with Antoine vapour pressures, the vapour composition is yA = xA PA^sat/P, and a small amount of vapour is removed. Put-and-take : distil down to the minimum stirrable volume, refill with the new solvent to the maximum volume, repeat until the residual target is met. Constant volume : distil down to a set level, then feed the new solvent at the same rate as the distillate so the level stays constant. Constant volume almost always needs less new solvent be

The batch is treated as a single-stage still (no column). At each step the bubble point is found from Raoult’s law with Antoine vapour pressures, the vapour composition is yA = xA PA^sat/P, and a small amount of vapour is removed. Put-and-take : distil down to the minimum stirrable volume, refill with the new solvent to the maximum volume, repeat until the residual target is met. Constant volume : distil down to a set level, then feed the new solvent at the same rate as the distillate so the level stays constant. Constant volume almost always needs less new solvent because every litre of distillate removes old solvent at its highest concentra

It assumes an ideal mixture. Alcohols or water with hydrocarbons, esters, ketones, ethers or chlorinated solvents often form azeotropes, which make the swap harder than shown. The tool warns you about likely pairs. The dissolved product is ignored. It raises the boiling point a little and may crystallise as the solvent changes, so check solubility at each stage. A real reactor gives some reflux on the walls and vapour line, so the separation is slightly better than a single stage. Confirm the end point by GC. Vapour pressure data is from our solvent data pages . For the background, read solvent selection and solvent swaps .

x: Chiller & VAM Calculations Find the real tonnage and kW/TR of a chiller from field readings, work out the steam or hot water a vapour absorption machine (VAM) needs, and compare what an electric chiller and a VAM cost to run. Full article Chiller TR & kW/TR VAM steam Chiller vs VAM cost How it works Two ways to make chilled water An electric (vapour compression) chiller uses a compressor to push refrigerant from the evaporator, where it boils and takes heat from the chilled water, to the condenser, where it gives that heat to the cooling water. It runs on electricity. A vapour absorption machine (VAM) uses water as the refrigerant and lithium bromide solution to absorb it. Instead of a compressor, heat drives the water back out of the solution: steam, hot water, exhaust gas or a burner. It uses very little electricity, so it makes sense where heat is cheap or free. t: Two ways to make chilled water
x: An electric (vapour compression) chiller uses a compressor to push refrigerant from the evaporator, where it boils and takes heat from the chilled water, to the condenser, where it gives that heat to the cooling water. It runs on electricity. A vapour absorption machine (VAM) uses water as the refrigerant and lithium bromide solution to absorb it. Instead of a compressor, heat drives the water back out of the solution: steam, hot water, exhaust gas or a burner. It uses very little electricity, so it makes sense where heat is cheap or free.

Cooling (kW) = flow (m³/h) × ρ / 3,600 × cp × ΔT TR = Cooling (kW) / 3.517 (for water: TR ≈ m³/h × ΔT / 3.024) kW/TR = power input (kW) / TR COP = cooling (kW) / power input (kW) One ton of refrigeration (TR) is 3.517 kW, the heat to melt one short ton of ice in a day. Use a calibrated flow meter or a clamp-on ultrasonic meter and accurate temperature sensors: at a 5 °C difference, a 0.25 °C sensor error is a 5 % error in TR. Worked example 120 m³/h of water, 12 °C → 7 °C: cooling = 120 × 1,000 / 3,600 × 4.186 × 5 ≈ 698 kW ≈ 198 TR Measured power 140 kW → 140 / 198 ≈ 0.71 kW/TR, COP ≈ 5.0 For glycol or brine, choose the fluid in the calculato

Heat input (kW) = TR × 3.517 / COP Steam (kg/h) = Heat input × 3,600 / hfg at the steam pressure Heat to cooling tower = cooling + heat input = TR × (1 + 1/COP) A 200 TR double-effect machine with COP 1.3 on 8 barg steam needs about 541 kW of heat, or about 960 kg/h of steam (4.8 kg/h per TR). Its cooling tower must reject about 1.77 times the cooling load, against about 1.2–1.25 times for an electric chiller, so a VAM needs a bigger tower, more condenser water and a bigger condenser water pump.

Compare the yearly power cost of the chiller (TR × kW/TR × hours × ₹/kWh) with the VAM's steam cost plus its pump and fan power. The break-even steam cost tells you how cheap steam must be before the VAM wins. With 0.85 kW/TR including the chiller's share of pumps and fans, power at ₹8/kWh and a VAM using 4.6 kg/h per TR, the break-even is about ₹1,200 per tonne of steam. Steam from a coal or biomass boiler can come close to this; waste heat or back-pressure steam from a turbine easily beats it.

Machine Typical efficiency Notes Water-cooled centrifugal 0.55–0.65 kW/TR Large loads, chilled water 6–7 °C Water-cooled screw 0.65–0.8 kW/TR Common in process plants Air-cooled screw or scroll 1.0–1.3 kW/TR No cooling tower, worse in hot weather Brine chiller, -10 to -20 °C Much higher per TR Compare only with machines at the same temperature VAM single-effect COP 0.65–0.75 Low-pressure steam or 85–95 °C hot water, ≈ 8 kg/h steam per TR VAM double-effect COP 1.2–1.4 8–9 barg steam, ≈ 4.5–5 kg/h steam per TR A VAM makes chilled water down to about 5–7 °C; it cannot make sub-zero brine. For brine duties use a vapour compression chiller.

t: Simple ways to save chiller energy
x: Raise the chilled water supply temperature as far as the process allows: each 1 °C saves roughly 2–3 % of compressor power. Keep the condenser water cold and the tubes clean: each 1 °C lower condenser water also saves about 2–3 %. Run one chiller well loaded rather than two at half load. Fix a low chilled water ΔT: it usually means too much flow or bypassing through three-way valves. Insulate chilled water and brine lines; check for condensation and wet insulation.

s: Free compressed air and nitrogen calculators: leak flow and cost, receiver size, compressor specific power, N2 for pressure, vacuum and sweep purging.
x: Compressed Air & Nitrogen Calculations Compressed air is one of the most expensive utilities per unit of useful energy, and nitrogen is a safety utility. Work out what leaks cost, size a receiver, estimate compressor power and plan nitrogen for purging and blanketing. Full article Air leak cost Receiver size Compressor power N₂ purging N₂ blanketing How it works Why compressed air is expensive Only about 10–15 % of the electricity a compressor draws comes out as useful work at the tool; the rest becomes heat in the compressor. A compressor making 10 m³/min at 7 barg draws about 60–65 kW. Leaks, pressure set higher than needed and air used for cleaning or cooling waste a large share of it. Only about 10–15 % of the electricity a compressor draws comes out as useful work at the tool; the rest becomes heat in the compressor. A compressor making 10 m³/min at 7 barg draws about 60–65 kW. Leaks, pressure set higher than needed and air used for cleaning or cooling waste a large share of it.

Air through a hole (choked flow): m = Cd × A × P0 × √[k / (R T) × (2/(k+1))^(k+1)/(k-1)] Power wasted (kW) = leak (m³/min free air) × specific power (kW per m³/min) Above about 0.9 barg the flow through a hole is choked, so it rises in step with the absolute pressure. With a discharge coefficient of 0.65, a 3 mm hole at 7 barg leaks about 0.43 m³/min. Ten such leaks waste about 4.3 m³/min, roughly 28 kW, or about ₹18 lakh a year at ₹8/kWh. A simple check: with all users stopped, time how fast the receiver pressure falls, or how long the compressor stays loaded.

V (m³) = Q (m³/min free air) × t (min) × 1.013 / (P1 - P2) To cover a 10 m³/min demand for 1 minute while the pressure falls from 7.5 to 6.5 barg needs about 10 m³ of storage. A receiver near a large intermittent user, such as a filter press, centrifuge or bag filter pulse cleaning, smooths peaks and stops a second compressor starting for a few seconds of demand.

Adiabatic power = n × k/(k-1) × P1 × Q × [(P2/P1)^(k-1)/(n k) - 1] Shaft power = adiabatic power / overall efficiency n is the number of stages and k = 1.4 for air. For 10 m³/min to 7 barg in one stage, the adiabatic power is about 48 kW and the shaft power about 64 kW at 75 % efficiency, about 6.4 kW per m³/min. Every extra 1 bar of discharge pressure costs roughly 6–8 % more power, so set the compressor to the lowest pressure the users need.

Pressure or vacuum purge: O₂ after n cycles = O₂start × (Plow / Phigh)^n (absolute pressures) N₂ per cycle (Nm³) = V × (Phigh - Plow) / 1.013 Sweep purge (well mixed): N₂ (Nm³) = V × ln(O₂start / O₂target) For a 6 m³ reactor headspace purged to 2 barg and vented to atmosphere, each cycle cuts oxygen to about a third: 7.1 % after one cycle and 2.3 % after two. Most solvent vapours cannot burn below about 10 % oxygen (the limiting oxygen concentration), and plants commonly aim for 8 % or less, so one cycle leaves almost no margin. Two cycles use about 24 Nm³. Always confirm with an oxygen analyser; a sweep purge with poor mixing can leave pocke

s: Free cooling tower calculators: range, approach, heat rejected in kW and TR, evaporation loss, make-up and blowdown from cycles of concentration.
x: Cooling Tower Calculations Check how well a cooling tower is working, how much water it consumes and what higher cycles of concentration would save, and size the cooling water for a condenser or cooler. Full article Range & approach Make-up & blowdown Water for a heat load How it works How a cooling tower works Hot return water is sprayed over the fill while fans draw air through it. A small part of the water evaporates, and its latent heat cools the rest. That is why a cooling tower can cool water below the dry-bulb air temperature but never below the wet bulb temperature: the wet bulb is the limit set by how much more moisture the air can take. Range, approach and effectiveness Range = Thot in - Tcold out Approach = Tcold out - Twet bulb Effectiveness = Range / (Range + Approach) Heat rejected (kW) = flow (kg/s) × 4.186 × Range Range is set by the plant's heat load and the water flow.

Hot return water is sprayed over the fill while fans draw air through it. A small part of the water evaporates, and its latent heat cools the rest. That is why a cooling tower can cool water below the dry-bulb air temperature but never below the wet bulb temperature: the wet bulb is the limit set by how much more moisture the air can take.

Range = Thot in - Tcold out Approach = Tcold out - Twet bulb Effectiveness = Range / (Range + Approach) Heat rejected (kW) = flow (kg/s) × 4.186 × Range Range is set by the plant's heat load and the water flow. Approach shows the tower's condition: a tower that held 4 °C approach when new and now gives 7 °C at the same wet bulb has fouled fill, blocked nozzles or weak fans.

Evaporation E (m³/h) = 0.00085 × 1.8 × Circulation (m³/h) × Range (°C) Cycles of concentration COC = TDS (or conductivity) of circulating water / that of make-up Blowdown B = E / (COC - 1) - Drift Make-up M = E + B + Drift = E × COC / (COC - 1) Evaporation removes pure water and leaves the dissolved salts behind, so the circulating water gets more concentrated. Blowdown bleeds off some of it to keep the salts below the scaling limit. More cycles means less blowdown and less make-up, but only as far as the water chemistry and treatment programme allow. Worked example 500 m³/h circulation, hot water 37 °C, cold water 32 °C, wet bulb 28 °C, COC

Item Typical Notes Approach 3–5 °C Under 2.5 °C is expensive to build; over 6 °C points to a problem Range 4–8 °C Set by the heat load and water flow Evaporation ≈ 0.15 % of flow per °C of range About 1 % of flow for a 6–7 °C range Drift loss 0.005–0.02 % (modern eliminators) 0.1–0.2 % on old towers without eliminators Cycles of concentration 3–6 Limited by hardness, silica and chloride in the make-up The heat rejected is shown in kW and in refrigeration tons (1 TR = 3.517 kW). Some cooling tower makers rate towers in “cooling tower tons” of 15,000 BTU/h, which already includes the chiller's compressor heat, so check which ton a datasheet use

t: Simple checks that save energy and water
x: Log hot, cold and wet bulb temperatures every shift and trend the approach. Clean the hot water basin nozzles and replace broken fill and drift eliminators. Control blowdown on conductivity, not on a fixed valve opening. Use fan VFDs or switch fans by cold water temperature in winter. Check the cooling water pump is not throttled against a half-closed valve.

s: Free steam and boiler calculators: fuel consumption, evaporation ratio, boiler efficiency (direct method), flash steam, condensate savings and leak loss.
x: Steam & Boiler Calculations Work out what your steam costs and where it goes: fuel for a steam load, boiler efficiency from a test, flash steam, the value of returned condensate, and what a leaking trap throws away. Results update as you type. Full article Boiler fuel Boiler efficiency Flash steam Condensate recovery Steam leak loss How it works How a steam system works The boiler burns fuel to turn feed water into steam. Steam travels through the mains to jackets, coils and heat exchangers, where it condenses and gives up its latent heat. The condensate drains through steam traps and, in a good system, returns hot to the boiler feed tank. Every kilogram of steam that leaks, every trap that blows through and every litre of condensate sent to drain has to be made again from cold water with more fuel. Boiler fuel consumption Fuel (kg/h) = S × (hg - hfw) / (η × GCV × 4.1868) Evaporation rat

The boiler burns fuel to turn feed water into steam. Steam travels through the mains to jackets, coils and heat exchangers, where it condenses and gives up its latent heat. The condensate drains through steam traps and, in a good system, returns hot to the boiler feed tank. Every kilogram of steam that leaks, every trap that blows through and every litre of condensate sent to drain has to be made again from cold water with more fuel.

Fuel (kg/h) = S × (hg - hfw) / (η × GCV × 4.1868) Evaporation ratio = S / Fuel S is steam flow (kg/h), hg the enthalpy of saturated steam at the boiler pressure (kJ/kg, from steam tables), hfw ≈ 4.186 × feed water temperature (kJ/kg), η the boiler efficiency as a fraction and GCV the fuel's gross calorific value in kcal/kg. The 4.1868 converts kcal to kJ. Worked example 5,000 kg/h of steam at 10 barg, feed water at 80 °C, Indian coal at 4,000 kcal/kg, boiler efficiency 75 %: hg at 10 barg (11 bar abs) ≈ 2,780 kJ/kg; hfw = 4.186 × 80 ≈ 335 kJ/kg Heat per kg = 2,780 - 335 = 2,445 kJ/kg Fuel = 5,000 × 2,445 / (0.75 × 4,000 × 4.1868) ≈ 973 kg/h →

Measure steam (from a flow meter or feed water meter) and fuel (weighed or metered) over the same few hours at steady load, then turn the fuel formula around: η = S × (hg - hfw) / (Fuel × GCV × 4.1868). It is quick, but a 5 % error in the steam meter is a 5 % error in efficiency. The indirect (heat loss) method, which adds up flue gas, moisture, unburnt and radiation losses, tells you why efficiency is low.

Flash fraction = (hf,1 - hf,2) / hfg,2 Condensate leaving a trap is at the saturation temperature of the higher pressure. When it drops to the return line pressure it carries more heat than water can hold there, so part of it boils. From 8 barg to 0.5 barg about 12 % flashes: 2,000 kg/h of condensate gives roughly 250 kg/h of low-pressure steam. Collect it in a flash vessel and use it for a low-pressure heater, or it simply vents from the feed tank.

Returned condensate saves treated water, chemicals and the fuel to heat cold make-up water. A rule of thumb: every 6 °C rise in feed water temperature saves about 1 % of boiler fuel. Returning 3,000 kg/h at 90 °C instead of 30 °C make-up recovers about 209 kW, worth roughly 60 kg/h of coal.

Napier's formula gives the steam through a sharp hole: m (kg/h) ≈ 0.412 × d² (mm²) × P (bar abs). A 3 mm hole at 7 barg passes about 30 kg/h, around 240 tonnes a year. Treat it as an upper estimate for a trap blowing through; a proper trap survey with ultrasound or temperature tells you which ones.

Fuel GCV (typical) Boiler efficiency Evaporation ratio Indian coal 3,500–4,500 kcal/kg 70–80 % 4–5.5 Biomass briquette 3,500–4,000 kcal/kg 68–75 % 4–5 Rice husk 3,000–3,400 kcal/kg 65–72 % 3.5–4.5 Furnace oil ≈ 10,200 kcal/kg 82–88 % 13–15 Natural gas / PNG ≈ 9,500 kcal/Sm³ 85–90 % ≈ 14 kg/Sm³ Ranges depend on the fuel lot, boiler type and load. Use your own fuel analysis and test data when you have them.

t: Where steam money is usually lost
x: Failed-open steam traps: a survey often finds 10–20 % failed in systems without a programme. Condensate sent to drain instead of back to the feed tank. Flash steam venting from the feed tank or condensate receivers. Bare or wet insulation on mains, valves and flanges. Too much excess air: aim for about 3–4 % O₂ in flue gas on oil or gas, 6–8 % on solid fuel. Continuous blowdown set by habit instead of by the boiler water TDS.

Recovery (%) = permeate / feed × 100 Salt rejection (%) = (1 - permeate TDS / feed TDS) × 100 Reject TDS = (feed × feed TDS - permeate × permeate TDS) / reject flow A 20 m³/h feed at 900 ppm giving 15 m³/h of 25 ppm permeate runs at 75 % recovery and 97.2 % rejection; the 5 m³/h reject carries about 3,500 ppm. Pushing recovery higher concentrates the reject further and raises the scaling risk, which is why antiscalant dosing and the reject LSI (Langelier saturation index) set the limit. Falling rejection points to membrane damage, leaking O-rings or scaling; rising feed pressure at the same flow points to fouling.

t: DG set: what a unit of DG power costs
x: Cost per kWh = diesel price (₹/litre) / specific energy (kWh per litre) Loading (%) = kW / (kVA rating × 0.8) × 100 Read the specific energy from the DG log: kWh from the energy meter divided by litres from the day tank. A healthy diesel set gives about 3.2–3.8 kWh per litre at 60–80 % load, so at ₹90 per litre DG power costs ₹24–28 per kWh, three times grid power. Below about 40 % load the engine wastes fuel and wet-stacks, so run fewer DG sets at higher load.

kVAR = kW × (tan φ1 - tan φ2), where φ = cos^-1(PF) Raising 800 kW from 0.82 to 0.98 power factor needs about 396 kVAR and cuts the kVA from 976 to 816 and the current by about 16 %. That lowers the kVA demand charge, cable and transformer losses, and frees transformer capacity. Where there are many VFDs, use detuned (reactor-protected) capacitors or an active filter, because harmonics can overload plain capacitors.

Input power (kW) = √3 × V × I × PF / 1,000 Loading (%) = input × efficiency / rated kW A 37 kW motor drawing 52 A at 415 V and 0.85 PF takes about 31.8 kW and is about 80 % loaded. Motors below about 50 % load lose efficiency and power factor; a smaller motor or a VFD may pay.

t: VFD savings on pumps and fans
x: Flow ∝ speed Head ∝ speed² Power ∝ speed³ (no static head) A pump throttled to 70 % flow with a valve still draws most of its full power. Slowing it to 70 % speed with a VFD needs only about 34 % of the power, plus 2–3 % VFD losses. For a 45 kW pump that is about 16 kW instead of about 40 kW. Where most of the head is static (lifting to an overhead tank), the cube law overstates the saving, because the pump still has to lift the water at low speed; enter the static head share in the calculator.
